bills.headline: Gives Chickamauga seniors 70 and older a $50,000 city property tax homestead exemption.
bills.recap: This law gives Chickamauga homeowners who are 70 or older, and who have lived in the city at least five years, a $50,000 exemption on the assessed value of their home for city property taxes. It covers up to five acres, renews each year once approved, and continues for a surviving spouse who is 67 or older, has not remarried, and stays in the home. It does not reduce state, county, or school taxes, and it replaces any other city homestead exemption rather than adding to it. It needed voter approval in November 2025 and, if approved, starts with the 2026 tax year, so Realtors working with older buyers and sellers in Chickamauga should note the lower city tax bills.

bills.headline: Creates a Brunswick city tax homestead exemption that grows with years of ownership.
bills.recap: This law creates a new homestead exemption from City of Brunswick property taxes, based on how long the owner has owned the home. The discount on assessed value is 5% for five years or less, 10% for six to ten years, 20% for 11 to 20 years, 30% for 21 to 29 years, and 50% for 30 years or more. It applies only to city taxes, not county, state, school, or city bond debt taxes, and it stacks on top of other city exemptions. Brunswick voters had to approve it in November 2025, and if approved it starts January 1, 2026, so Realtors should note that buyers start at the lowest tier while long-time owners gain the most.

The exemption is $7,000 of assessed value for ages 62-64, $14,000 for ages 65-72, $21,000 for ages 73-79, and the full assessed value for ages 80 and up. It covers up to five acres, requires a one-time application, replaces other school homestead exemptions rather than adding to them, and applies only to tax years 2026 through 2030 if local voters approve it in November 2025. Realtors may find it useful when talking with older buyers and sellers in Dublin about carrying costs and whether to stay or move.

bills.recap: This bill gives homeowners in the City of Dublin school district a homestead exemption from school property taxes for tax years 2026 through 2030. The taxable value of a homestead can rise by no more than 20 percent per year over its base value, plus the value of any major improvements. Taxes to pay off school bonds are not covered. The exemption does not transfer to a new buyer, though a surviving spouse who stays in the home keeps it. Voters had to approve it in a November 2025 election. Realtors should note that buyers will start fresh at current assessed values, so the seller's tax bill may not match what a buyer will pay.

bills.title: Buildings and housing; revise process by which a local governing body may propose amendments to state minimum standard codes
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Part 2 of Article 1 of Chapter 2 of Title 8 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to state building, plumbing, and electrical codes, so as to revise the process by which a local governing body may propose amendments to state minimum standard codes; to require the approval of the Department of Community Affairs for amendments to such codes; to amend Chapter 7 of Title 12 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to control of soil erosion and sedimentation, so as to revise provisions regarding denial or nonacceptance of permits; to require local issuing authorities to provide rejected permit applicants with a written list of reasons for denial within specified time frames; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: H: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The committee version drops the original plan to make local code amendments need state approval; instead, the state must post all local code amendments and its decisions on its website in real time. Starting January 1, 2027, cities and counties that issued more than 250 building permits the prior year must run a free public website showing live status for each permit application, including any missed deadlines and the legal basis for any denial. The bill also widens the use of private engineers, architects, and inspectors for plan reviews and inspections, including erosion control work, and cuts local permit fees by 50 percent when an applicant uses one. A private provider's approved inspection report is accepted unless the local government flags problems within five business days. For land-disturbance permits, localities must post a list of required application materials and decide within five days whether an application is complete, or it is treated as complete. They also face set deadlines to act on resubmitted applications.

bills.headline: Speeds up building and land-disturbance permits and expands use of private plan reviewers and inspectors.
bills.recap: Starting January 1, 2027, cities and counties that issued more than 250 building permits the year before must run a free public website showing real-time permit status, including missed deadlines and reasons for denials. Builders can hire licensed private engineers, architects, or qualified inspectors to do plan reviews and inspections, including erosion control. When they do, local permit fees are cut in half, and approved private inspection reports are accepted automatically unless the local government flags problems within five business days. Local governments must also publish a list of what a complete application needs, give written reasons with code citations for any denial, and meet tighter review deadlines. For Realtors, this could mean faster, more predictable new construction and renovation timelines, though only local governments can still issue certificates of occupancy.

bills.title: Georgia Taxpayer Privacy Protection Act; enact
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Article 1 of Chapter 5 of Title 48 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to general provisions relative to ad valorem taxation of property, so as to prohibit the disclosure of taxpayer telephone numbers in property tax records sold, transferred, or shared with third parties; to provide for penalties for violations; to provide for complaints; to provide for policies and procedures; to provide for a short title; to provide for legislative findings and purposes; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: H: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The committee version keeps the core rule: taxpayer phone numbers may not appear in tax rolls, assessment records, or other public property tax records, including data sales and open records requests. It also keeps the civil penalty of up to $5,000. The main change is about complaints. The original let affected taxpayers file a complaint with the Attorney General's office. The new version drops that and instead treats a violation as an unfair or deceptive practice under Georgia's Fair Business Practices Act.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: This new version comes from the House Rules Committee instead of the Ways and Means Committee. The one real change is the penalty standard: a person can now be fined up to $5,000 only for disclosing a taxpayer's phone number in a public tax record recklessly or knowingly, not just negligently. That raises the bar for penalties, so a simple careless mistake would no longer be enough. The other edits are formatting and document labels.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: Nothing of substance changed in this version. The only edits are formatting: the header now lists the sponsors (Representatives Huddleston, Chastain, Fleming, Jones, and McCollum) and labels it a Rules Committee substitute, and page footers were added. The rules on keeping taxpayer phone numbers out of public tax record sales, and the penalties, stay the same.

bills.headline: Bans taxpayer phone numbers from public property tax records and data sales.
bills.recap: This bill bars anyone from including property owners' phone numbers in tax rolls, assessment records, or other public property tax documents, including bulk data sales and open records requests. Exceptions apply for internal government tax use, court orders, and uses the owner agrees to in writing. Reckless or knowing disclosure can bring a civil penalty of up to $5,000, and violations count as unfair business practices under state law. Realtors and lead-generation services that pull owner phone numbers from tax data would lose that source, while homeowners get more privacy from unwanted calls.

bills.title: Property; tenant seeking to limit public access to records of the court relating to dispossessory actions to be sealed under certain circumstances; provide
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Article 3 of Chapter 7 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to dispossessory proceedings, so as to provide for a tenant seeking to limit public access to records of the court relating to dispossessory actions to be sealed under certain circumstances; to provide for exemptions; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Lets tenants ask courts to seal eviction case records in certain situations.
bills.recap: This bill lets tenants ask a court to seal eviction (dispossessory) records so the public cannot see them. A tenant who wins the case can ask right away, and a tenant who settles can ask once they meet the deal's terms or the landlord gets paid by a government or nonprofit program. A tenant who lost can ask three years later if the case happened during a public health emergency, came from hardships beyond their control, or no other eviction cases are pending against them. Landlords, tenants, and their lawyers can still see sealed records, which could make it harder for landlords and property managers to screen applicants for past evictions.

bills.title: Property; provide residential tenants with the right to complete repairs required by landlord and offset rental installments by the reasonable cost of such repairs under certain circumstances
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 7 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to landlord and tenant, so as to provide residential tenants with the right to complete repairs required by the landlord and offset rental installments by the reasonable cost of such repairs under certain circumstances; to provide residential tenants with the right to terminate a rental agreement under certain circumstances; to prohibit the landlord from taking adverse action against residential tenants under certain circumstances; to provide for a civil right of action and remedies; to provide a definition; to provide for applicability; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Lets Georgia renters make repairs and deduct the cost from rent if landlords don't act.
bills.recap: If a landlord fails to fix a serious defect, such as broken plumbing, HVAC, electrical, appliances, or code violations, within 14 days of written notice, the tenant can hire a licensed professional to fix it. The tenant can then deduct the reasonable repair cost from rent, up to 50% of each rent payment, until the cost is recovered. If the problem isn't fixed within 60 days, the tenant may end the lease with 30 days' written notice, as long as they haven't started the repair themselves. Landlords cannot evict, refuse to renew, or retaliate against tenants for using these rights, and the bill applies to leases signed or renewed on or after July 1, 2025.

bills.title: Property; transfer-on-death deeds; modify certain provisions
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 17 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to transfer-on-death deeds, so as to modify certain provisions regarding transfer-on-death deeds; to provide for a definition; to provide for the acceptance of a real estate transfer; to provide for revocation; to provide for limitations; to provide for curing defects; to amend Chapter 3 of Title 53 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to year's support, so as to provide for precedence of transfer-on-death deeds; to provide for related matters; to provide for an effective date; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.lastAction: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute

timeline.text: H: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The House Judiciary Committee rewrote HB 899. Agents acting under a power of attorney can no longer sign transfer-on-death deeds at all, and the death certificate access rule for beneficiaries moves into the vital records law. Title still passes only after a beneficiary signs and records the acceptance affidavit within nine months, and that affidavit must now list the deed book and page. A beneficiary who dies after the owner but before accepting loses their share, which is split among the living beneficiaries. The deed now wins over the estate's unsecured debts rather than a year's support petition, and the one-person-accepts-for-all grace period moves to July 1, 2026. The estate must give beneficiaries notice of the deed. A solvent estate can pay the mortgage, taxes and urgent repairs and then claim a special lien. That lien ranks below tax liens and earlier security deeds, and it must be filed, mailed and foreclosed like a mechanic's lien. An insolvent estate facing foreclosure can record a notice and sell the home if no beneficiary has accepted.

bills.headline: Updates Georgia's transfer-on-death deed rules for accepting, revoking, and protecting inherited property.
bills.recap: This bill changes how transfer-on-death deeds work in Georgia. Ownership passes only after a named beneficiary signs an affidavit and records it, with the death certificate, within nine months of the owner's death. A power of attorney can't create these deeds, and a revocation now needs only one witness plus an officer. Selling the property or the death of the only beneficiary automatically cancels the deed. Beneficiaries can get death certificates, and these deeds take priority over the estate's unsecured debts and year's support claims. The estate's personal representative may pay the mortgage, taxes, and urgent repairs and later claim a lien for those costs. Realtors listing or selling inherited homes should watch these steps, since they affect when title is clear and who can sign.

bills.recap: This bill says all property held by the Lake Lanier Islands Development Authority is public property used for public purposes and is exempt from property taxes. It also says leases or other property interests the authority grants to private people or businesses count as public property and are exempt from property taxes. This would mainly affect businesses and others who lease land from the authority at Lake Lanier Islands, along with local governments that might otherwise tax those leaseholds. Realtors working near Lake Lanier may want to note how this could affect leasehold values and local tax revenue.

bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 14 of Title 44 and Chapter 4 of Title 48 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to mortgages, conveyances to secure debt, and liens and tax sales, respectively, so as to provide for debtors in foreclosures to receive certain information and forms in a notice of foreclosure; to provide for tax sale notices to comply with foreclosure notice requirements; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: H: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The House Judiciary Committee version drops the tax sale part of the bill, so tax sale notices no longer must follow the foreclosure notice rules. Foreclosure notices must still tell borrowers they can claim surplus funds after the sale. Instead of listing deadlines and claim forms, the notice must give instructions on how to make a first claim. It must also include a bold warning that unclaimed surplus funds may go to the State after the legal time limit, currently five years. The new version also requires tracking on the mailed notice, and it updates the surplus funds law to say the surplus is paid to the borrower or their agent after the mortgage and other liens with priority, including statutory liens, are paid.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed in this version. Only the header was updated, swapping the committee substitute line for a title listing the bill's sponsors: Representatives Camp, Crowe, Mathiak, Powell, and Leverett. The bill's rules on what foreclosure notices must tell debtors are the same.

bills.headline: Foreclosure notices must tell homeowners how to claim leftover sale money.
bills.recap: This bill requires lenders' 30-day foreclosure notices to tell homeowners they can claim any surplus money left after a foreclosure sale, with instructions on how to start a claim. The notice must also warn in bold that unclaimed surplus funds may go to the state after the legal deadline, currently five years. It clarifies that surplus is paid to the former owner only after the mortgage and other priority liens, including statutory liens, are paid. Realtors working with distressed sellers may find this helps clients recover equity they might otherwise lose.

bills.title: Essential Services for Renters Act; enact
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 7 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to landlord and tenant, so as to provide residential tenants with the right to complete repairs required by the landlord and offset rental installments by the reasonable cost of such repairs under certain circumstances; to provide residential tenants with the right to terminate a rental agreement under certain circumstances; to provide for definitions; to provide a short title; to provide for applicability; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Lets renters fix ignored repairs and deduct costs, or end leases after delays.
bills.recap: If a landlord does not fix a needed repair within 14 days of written notice, the tenant could hire a licensed professional and take the reasonable cost out of rent, with receipts. Repairs covered include problems inside the unit that the lease requires the landlord to fix, plus essential services like plumbing, electric, gas, HVAC, and running water. If the repair is still not done after 60 days, a tenant who has not started the repair could end the lease with 30 days' written notice. The rules do not apply to damage the tenant caused and would cover leases signed or renewed on or after July 1, 2026, so agents who manage rentals should review repair procedures and consider naming preapproved repair professionals in leases.

bills.title: Magistrate courts; expand existing remedies regarding unauthorized possession of real property
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Article 1 of Chapter 10 of Title 15, Article 2 of Chapter 7 of Title 16, and Article 2 of Chapter 11 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to general provisions relative to magistrate courts, criminal trespass and damage to property, and proceedings against intruders, respectively, so as to expand existing remedies regarding the unauthorized possession of real property; to require that any person subject to removal or arrest for the unauthorized possession of real property be given 30 calendar days to present a counteraffidavit prior to any such removal or arrest; to provide for legislative findings and intent; to provide for definitions; to make conforming changes; to provide for an effective date and applicability; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.lastAction: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute

timeline.text: H: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The House Judiciary Committee version drops the plan to give accused squatters 30 calendar days to show proof they can be there. It keeps the current three-day window in both the general intruder removal process and the criminal squatting law, which is no longer changed by the bill. The new process that lets other condo or HOA owners seek removal of a squatter in their community now uses three-day timelines instead of 30. That covers both the advance written notice to the unit's owner and the wait before officers remove the occupant. Overall, removals would move much faster than under the original bill.

bills.headline: Lets condo and HOA neighbors start squatter removal and adds a three-day waiting period.
bills.recap: This bill changes Georgia's process for removing people who occupy property without a right to be there. It requires officers to show the owner's affidavit to the occupant and wait at least three days before removal, giving the occupant time to file a counteraffidavit claiming a legal right to stay. It also lets other owners in the same condo or HOA community start the removal process, but only after sending the property owner three days' written notice by certified mail or overnight delivery. The process stops if the owner says no, and the association must help with the notice. Realtors with listings, vacant homes, or clients in condo and HOA communities should know these new squatter rules, which take effect July 1, 2026.

bills.title: Property; prohibit certain business enterprises from purchasing or acquiring an interest in a single-family residential property
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 3 of Title 44 and Chapter 5 of Title 48 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to regulation of specialized land transactions and ad valorem taxation of property, respectively, so as to prohibit certain business enterprises from purchasing or acquiring an interest in a single-family residential property; to provide for construction; to provide for the assessment of real property purchased or acquired by certain business enterprises at 100 percent of its fair market value; to provide for penalties; to provide for certification of ownership; to provide for forms and applications; to provide for definitions; to provide for effective dates and automatic repeal; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Bans large rental-home investors from buying Georgia single-family homes and raises their property taxes.
bills.recap: Starting January 1, 2027, companies that own 100 or more single-family rental homes in Georgia, along with their affiliates, could not buy any more single-family homes, townhouses, condos, or manufactured homes. Lenders can still hold mortgages and take homes through foreclosure, but must sell those homes within three years. If voters approve a constitutional amendment in November 2026, these investors' property would also be taxed at 100 percent of fair market value instead of the usual 40 percent. Owners would have to certify ownership with county tax assessors and face double-tax penalties if they don't. Realtors should note that this could cut investor competition for buyers but shrink the pool of cash buyers for sellers.

bills.title: Senior Stabilization Act; enact
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 7 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to landlord and tenant, so as to provide for rent increase limits for certain senior citizens; to provide for a short title; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Caps rent increases at 10 percent for certain seniors on Social Security through 2028.
bills.recap: From July 1, 2026, through December 31, 2028, landlords could not raise rent by more than 10 percent for existing tenants who are 62 or older and rely mainly on Social Security income. The cap applies when renewing a lease or signing a new lease with the same tenant, and it is measured against the rent in effect on June 30, 2026. It covers only tenants with a rental agreement in place on that date. Realtors who manage rentals or advise investors should note this would limit rent growth on units with qualifying senior tenants.

bills.title: Property; debtor's aggregate interest in real property or personal property used as a residence; revise exemption
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Code Section 44-13-100 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to exemptions for purposes of bankruptcy and intestate insolvent estates, so as to revise the exemption for a debtor's aggregate interest in real property or personal property that the debtor or a dependent of the debtor uses as a residence, in a cooperative that owns property that the debtor or a dependent of the debtor uses as a residence, or in a burial plot; to provide for such exemption for the primary residence of spouses; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: H: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute
H: House Date Signed by Governor

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The House Judiciary Committee's substitute keeps the higher homestead exemption in bankruptcy: up to $50,000 for one debtor, and $100,000 when the home is titled in one spouse and is both spouses' primary residence. The new version adds yearly inflation adjustments to both amounts starting July 1, 2031. The state revenue commissioner would set the inflation rate, possibly using the federal Consumer Price Index. For homeowners in financial trouble, this means the protected home equity would keep pace with the cost of living over time.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed in this version. The only edit is to the header: the line saying the House Judiciary Committee offered the substitute was replaced with the bill title and the sponsors' names (Representatives Hong, Reeves, and Leverett). The rules on the homestead exemption for a debtor's residence are the same as before.

versions.name: Enrolled
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed between the committee version and the final enrolled version. The only edits are labels showing the bill passed both the House and Senate. The rules on the debtor's home exemption, including yearly inflation updates starting July 1, 2031, are the same.

bills.headline: Raises Georgia's homestead bankruptcy exemption from $21,500 to $50,000, with future inflation increases.
bills.recap: This law raises how much home equity a person can protect from creditors in bankruptcy, from $21,500 to $50,000. If the home is titled in one spouse's name and is the primary residence of both spouses, the protected amount rises from $43,000 to $100,000. Starting July 1, 2031, these amounts will be adjusted each year for inflation, using a method set by the state revenue commissioner. Realtors may care because homeowners facing financial trouble can keep more of their equity, which can affect distressed sales and how much equity sellers walk away with.

bills.title: Landlord and tenant; limitations on increasing rent on residential properties; provide
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Article 1 of Chapter 7 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to landlord and tenant in general, so as to provide for limitations on increasing rent on residential properties; to provide for an effective date and applicability; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Caps rent increases at 5 percent when landlords renew residential leases.
bills.recap: This bill would bar residential property owners from raising rent more than 5 percent when renewing a tenant's lease. Landlords could set any rent for a new tenancy once no tenant from the prior lease remains in the home. It would take effect July 1, 2026, and apply to leases signed or renewed on or after that date. Realtors who manage rentals or advise investors should note how this could affect rental income and property values.

bills.title: Georgia Homeownership Protection Act of 2026; enact
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Titles 36, 44, 46, and 48 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to local government, property, public utilities and public transportation, and revenue and taxation, respectively, so as to prohibit local governments from adding unpaid service charges to the ad valorem tax roll for purposes of tax execution or tax sale of an owner occupied dwelling; to provide for civil remedies and penalties; to make conforming changes; to provide for a short title; to provide for an effective date and applicability; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Bars HOAs, condo associations, utilities, and local governments from foreclosing on owner-occupied homes over unpaid fees.
bills.recap: This bill stops HOAs and condo associations from foreclosing on owner-occupied homes for unpaid assessments or fines. Those debts could only be collected through a lawsuit for a money judgment, though associations could still suspend amenity use, charge reasonable late fees, and record a notice of delinquency. It also bars local governments and utilities from adding unpaid water, sewer, trash, or other service charges to the tax roll or forcing a tax sale of an owner-occupied home. Homeowners could sue for damages of up to $5,000 per violation, the Attorney General could seek penalties of up to $10,000, and sales made in violation would be void, which matters for title and closings starting July 1, 2026.

bills.title: Property Rights Through the Ballot Act; enact
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 3 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to regulation of specialized land transactions, so as to establish a binding referendum process allowing homeowners residing in communities governed by property owners' or homeowners' associations to vote on the continuation or dissolution of such associations; to provide for definitions; to provide for the legal effects of dissolution; to require transparency, nonretaliation, and consumer protections; to provide for the transition of essential shared infrastructure; to provide for enforcement and remedies; to provide for a short title; to provide for related matters; to provide for severability; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Lets homeowners vote to dissolve their HOA and bans HOA foreclosures on owner-occupied homes.
bills.recap: This bill lets owner-occupants in HOA, condo, and similar communities petition for a binding vote on whether their association should keep existing. A vote is triggered when 20 percent of eligible owners sign, and a simple majority can dissolve the association. Dissolution voids its covenants and rules, turns its liens into unsecured debt, and sends shared roads and utilities to the local government or other arrangements. The bill also bars associations from foreclosing on owner-occupied homes over unpaid dues or fines and requires open meetings, record access, and annual audits. That could change how HOA communities are marketed, what buyers get in disclosures, and how sellers handle unpaid dues at closing.

bills.title: Real Estate Security and Title Act; enact
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Titles 9, 15, and 23 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to civil practice, courts, and equity, respectively, so as to provide for certain purchasers at judicial sales to submit a credit bid; to provide for the removal of the restriction on personally identifiable information after the death of a protected person; to provide penalties; to provide for the qualification of special masters in certain quiet title actions; to provide for definitions; to provide a short title; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.lastAction: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute

H: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The House Judiciary Committee's substitute changes the rules for paying at judicial sales. The original version would have required buyers to pay with a cashier's or certified check. The new version keeps cash as an option and also allows certified funds, including from institutions insured by the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund. The foreclosing lender can still submit a credit bid instead of paying, and the rest of the bill, including privacy protections for judges and their spouses and the special master rules for quiet title cases, is basically unchanged.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: This new version adds a carve-out to the privacy rules that hide personal information of protected people, such as judges, in public records. County clerks, tax offices and other government offices may still give unredacted copies of recorded property documents and property tax records to title insurers, title agents, their attorneys, and those attorneys' agents. To get these copies, the requester must state that they need the information to provide title insurance. This helps title searches and closings move forward even when a protected person's details are restricted. The rest of the bill, including the special master rules for quiet title cases, is unchanged.

bills.headline: Allows lender credit bids at judicial sales, shields judges' property records, and tightens quiet title rules.
bills.recap: This bill lets the lender foreclosing on a property make a credit bid at a judicial sale instead of paying cash or a certified check. It also expands privacy protections for current and former judges and their spouses, so government offices must hide their home addresses, parcel numbers, and phone numbers. Real property indexes must show when that information has been restricted, but title insurers, title agents, and their attorneys can still get full copies for title work. The bill also requires special masters in certain quiet title cases to be Georgia lawyers with at least five years of land title experience, which may affect title searches and closings involving protected owners.

bills.title: Student Housing Affordability Act; enact
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Part 3 of Article 7 of Chapter 3 of Title 20 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to the Georgia Student Finance Authority, so as to establish a financial aid program to provide grants to eligible students to assist with off-campus housing expenses; to provide definitions; to provide for a maximum award amount; to provide for applications; to provide for rules, regulations, and procedures; to provide for a short title; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Creates state grants to help college students pay off-campus housing costs.
bills.recap: This bill would set up a new grant program, run by the Georgia Student Finance Commission, to help college students who live off campus pay for housing. To qualify, students must attend an eligible school, live off campus, be eligible for a HOPE-type scholarship or grant, and fill out the FAFSA. The most a student could get is the gap between the school's listed on-campus and off-campus housing costs, and the program only runs if lawmakers fund it. Realtors and landlords in college towns may care because it could boost demand for off-campus rentals near campuses.

bills.title: Neighborhood Ownership, Transparency, and Accountability (NOTA) Act; enact
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 7 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to landlord and tenant, so as to prohibit certain entities from owning 25 or more single-family homes; to provide for the filing of certain information with the Secretary of State; to provide for inspections; to provide for civil actions by the Attorney General to enforce the provisions; to provide for private rights of action; to provide for damages and remedies; to provide for equitable and injunctive relief; to provide for joinder; to provide for joint and several liability; to provide for construction; to provide for definitions; to provide for a short title; to provide for legislative purpose; to provide for legislative findings; to provide for related matters; to provide for an effective date and applicability; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Bars business entities owning 25+ rental homes from buying more homes in large counties.
bills.recap: This bill stops companies and their affiliates that own 25 or more single-family rental homes from buying more single-family homes in Georgia counties with over 150,000 people, unless the home is for their own residence. Covered companies would have to file yearly reports with the Secretary of State listing their properties, rents, evictions, large financing sources, and management companies. They would also need inspections on each home and must publish results within 30 days of a request. The Attorney General, local governments, and private parties could sue, with penalties of up to $100 per day per home, damages, and punitive damages. Realtors working with institutional investors or sellers in metro markets could see fewer large-investor buyers.

bills.title: West Point, City of; ad valorem tax for municipal purposes; provide homestead exemption
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to provide a homestead exemption from City of West Point ad valorem taxes for municipal purposes in the amount of $100,000.00 of the assessed value of the homestead for residents of that city who are 65 years of age or older and whose income does not exceed $50,000.00; to provide for definitions; to specify the terms and conditions of the exemption and the procedures relating thereto; to provide for applicability; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Creates a $100,000 West Point city tax homestead exemption for lower-income seniors.
bills.recap: This bill gives West Point homeowners age 65 or older a $100,000 exemption off the assessed value of their home for city property taxes. It applies only if the owner's household income, including a spouse living there, is $50,000 or less for the prior year. It covers city taxes only, not county, school, or state taxes, and adds to any other exemptions. Voters in West Point must approve it in November 2026, and it would start January 1, 2027, which could lower costs for qualifying senior owners and may matter when they decide to stay or sell.

bills.title: West Point, City of; ad valorem tax for municipal purposes; provide homestead exemption
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to provide a homestead exemption from City of West Point ad valorem taxes for municipal purposes in the amount of $10,000.00 of the assessed value of the homestead for residents of that city; to provide for definitions; to specify the terms and conditions of the exemption and the procedures relating thereto; to provide for applicability; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: H: House Date Signed by Governor

versions.name: Enrolled
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed between the introduced and enrolled versions of this bill. The only edits are labels showing it passed the House and Senate. The West Point homestead exemption from city property taxes, starting with tax years on or after January 1, 2027, reads the same as when it was introduced.

bills.headline: Creates a $10,000 West Point city homestead exemption, pending a November 2026 local vote.
bills.recap: This law gives West Point homeowners a $10,000 exemption off the assessed value of their home for city property taxes. It covers up to five contiguous acres and does not reduce state, county, or school taxes. Owners must apply once with the city, and the exemption then renews each year while they live there. It only takes effect if West Point voters approve it in November 2026, starting with the 2027 tax year, and Realtors can mention it as a possible cost savings for buyers in West Point.

bills.title: Suwanee, City of; ad valorem taxes for municipal purposes; provide homestead exemption
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to provide a homestead exemption from City of Suwanee ad valorem taxes for municipal purposes for residents of that city; to provide for definitions; to specify the terms and conditions of the exemption and the procedures relating thereto; to provide for applicability; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: H: House Date Signed by Governor

versions.name: Enrolled
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed between the introduced and enrolled versions. The only edits are header labels showing the bill passed both the House and Senate. The Suwanee homestead exemption from city property taxes, starting with tax years on or after January 1, 2027, and the local election paid for by the city, read the same as first filed.

bills.headline: Creates a $15,000 Suwanee city homestead exemption if voters approve in November 2026.
bills.recap: This law gives Suwanee homeowners a $15,000 break on the assessed value of their home for city property taxes. It does not cut state, county, or school taxes, and it stacks on top of any other city homestead exemptions. Owners must apply once with the city, and the exemption then renews each year while they live in the home. It only takes effect if Suwanee voters approve it in November 2026, starting with the 2027 tax year, so agents may want to remind buyers in Suwanee to file for homestead exemptions after closing.

bills.title: Ad valorem tax; state-wide homestead tax exemption for a portion of the value of the homestead for certain senior residents; provide
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 5 of Title 48 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to ad valorem taxation of property, so as to provide for a state-wide homestead tax exemption from ad valorem taxes for a portion of the value of the homestead for certain senior residents; to specify the terms and conditions of the exemption and the procedures relating thereto; to provide for applicability; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, and automatic repeal; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Creates a $500,000 statewide homestead tax exemption for homeowners age 60 and older.
bills.recap: This bill would exempt $500,000 of a home's assessed value from state and local property taxes for Georgia residents age 60 or older, though taxes that pay off bonds would still apply. Seniors who already had a homestead exemption in 2025 and still qualify in 2026 would get it automatically, and a surviving spouse keeps it as long as they live in the home. The exemption does not transfer to a new buyer, and it cannot be combined with local exemptions that cap assessment increases, so the owner gets whichever is better. It needs a two-thirds vote in both chambers and statewide voter approval in November 2026, and would start January 1, 2027. Realtors may care because it could sharply cut taxes for older owners, which might make them less likely to sell, while buyers of those homes would not inherit the break.

bills.title: Ad valorem tax; education purposes of homesteads of qualified individuals who are 65 years of age or older; provide exemption
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Part 1 of Article 2 of Chapter 5 of Title 48 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to tax exemptions, so as to provide an exemption from ad valorem taxation for education purposes of homesteads of qualified individuals who are 65 years of age or older; to specify certain terms, conditions, and procedures relating thereto; to provide for applicability; to provide that falsifying information with regard to such exemption shall be unlawful; to provide for penalties; to provide for related matters; to provide for a referendum; to provide for effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Exempts homeowners 65 and older from all school property taxes on their homes.
bills.recap: This bill would fully exempt the homes of Georgia residents age 65 or older from school property taxes, including taxes that pay off school bonds. Owners file a one-time affidavit with the local tax office, and the exemption then renews each year unless the owner becomes ineligible. It also covers homes held by co-owners, a personal representative, or a trustee when a qualifying person lives there, and lying on the form counts as false swearing. Voters would decide in a November 2026 statewide referendum, and if approved it would take effect January 1, 2027, which could lower costs for older buyers and owners and affect decisions about selling or downsizing.

bills.title: Homeownership Opportunity and Market Equalization Act of 2026; enact
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapters 5 and 8 of Title 48 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to ad valorem taxation of property and sales and use taxes, respectively, so as to provide for the acceptance of tax digests in the event of a publication error made by a newspaper; to amend Part 4 of Article 6 of Chapter 2 of Title 20 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to financing under the "Quality Basic Education Act," so as to exclude amounts attributable to certain exemptions from ad valorem taxation from the equalized adjusted school property tax digest for the purpose of calculating the local five mill share and equalization grants; to amend Article 1 of Chapter 81 of Title 36 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to local government budgets and audits; to provide for a short title; to provide for an effective date and applicability; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
