timeline.text: H: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute
H: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute
S: Senate Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute
H: House Agreed Senate Amend or Sub As Amended

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The committee version greatly expands the bill: the statewide homestead exemption still rises in steps ($10,000 in 2027–28, $30,000 in 2029–30, $60,000 in 2031), but now fully exempts the home's value starting in 2032, with some local opt-out delays. Starting in 2032, new homestead owners would pay full property tax in their first year before the exemption begins, and major improvements would be fully taxed in the year they are first assessed. The new version adds a Local Homestead Option Sales Tax (LHOST) to pay for these exemptions, raises the overall local sales tax cap from 2% to 5% starting July 2027, allows SPLOST and LOST at rates below 1%, and creates non-property-based 'local finance assessments' that must be paid or the owner loses homestead exemptions. It also softens the failure-to-report penalty to a flat 50%, ties the voter-approval budget cap to the greater of 3% or inflation (with a local Act as another option), drops the earlier tax bill, notice, and newspaper-error changes, and makes major parts depend on voters passing a constitutional amendment.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The new version drops the plan to phase in a full statewide homestead exemption, the first-year tax on new owners after a sale, the local 'finance assessments,' and the voter approval rule for big school and local budget increases. Instead, homestead property would be assessed at a lower share of market value, falling 3 percent a year starting in 2027 until it reaches 10 percent of fair market value (down from today's 40 percent), if voters approve a constitutional amendment. LOST and HOST sales taxes would convert into a new local homestead sales tax (LHOST) on January 1, 2028. The bill also creates separate homestead sales taxes for schools (S-LHOST, up to 2 percent) and for cities (M-HOST, up to 1 percent), and adds a new excise tax on certain data centers to fund a Homeowner's Tax Relief Fund.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The House Rules Committee rewrote HB 1116 and dropped several big pieces from the Ways and Means version. Gone are the plan to cut the taxable value of homesteads from 40 percent to 10 percent of market value, the school and city homestead sales taxes (S-LHOST and M-HOST), the data center excise tax and its homeowner relief fund, the education funding study committee, the 50 percent penalty for not reporting loss of homestead eligibility, and the need for a constitutional amendment to take effect. What remains is a single county-level LHOST of 1 percent starting in 2028. Existing LOST, HOST, EHOST and RHOST taxes would convert into the LHOST, FLOST could convert if local voters approve, and the local sales tax cap would rise to 5 percent, with these deadlines moved from mid-2027 to the end of 2027. New items include voter approval for city, county and school budgets that raise property tax revenue by more than 3 percent or inflation, limits on the dates for those special elections, a ban on back-billing homeowners for homestead exemptions applied by mistake through no fault of their own, a nonbinding November 2026 statewide vote on fully exempting homesteads from property tax, and a statement that future sales tax on data center computer equipment should fund homestead tax relief.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed in this version. The only edits are to the document's formatting: a new header listing the bill's sponsors (Representatives Blackmon, Burns, Efstration, Hatchett, Cannon, and others), an updated document code, and "H. B. 1116 (SUB)" added to each page footer. The bill's actual content is the same, including the new LHOST sales tax, the property tax revenue limits, and the advisory referendum.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The Senate Finance version drops the House plan to raise the local sales tax cap to 5 percent and to automatically convert LOST, HOST, EHOST, and RHOST into the new LHOST in 2028. It also removes the statewide advisory vote on ending homestead property taxes, the data center sales tax intent language, and the homestead application deadline changes. Instead, a county could adopt a 1 percent LHOST only through a local Act approved by local voters, for up to 10 years. The proceeds would fund a yearly homestead exemption figured by the tax commissioner, and any existing FLOST would end when the LHOST starts. The 3 percent revenue-cap referendum rules for school boards and local governments now start January 1, 2027 instead of 2028, and revenue from economic growth no longer counts toward the cap. New items also require owners of income-producing property to give actual income and expense data when tax assessors ask, and change how certain local homestead exemptions count in school funding formulas.

bills.headline: Creates a local sales tax to cut homestead property taxes and caps local tax growth.
bills.recap: This bill lets counties ask voters to approve a new 1 percent local sales tax, starting in 2028, that is used only to lower property taxes on primary homes. It also requires voter approval when cities, counties, or school boards want property tax revenue to grow more than 3 percent or inflation, whichever is higher, not counting growth from new development. Homeowners can't be billed back taxes if a homestead exemption was applied by mistake through no fault of their own. Owners of commercial income property must give tax assessors income and expense data when asked, and that data stays confidential. Realtors may see lower and more predictable tax bills on primary homes, which can help with affordability talks with buyers and sellers.

bills.title: Sales and use tax; exempt materials used in construction, renovation, and rehabilitation of affordable housing by purely public charities
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Part 1 of Article 1 of Chapter 8 of Title 48 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to general provisions relative to state sales and use tax, so as to exempt from state and local sales and use taxation materials used in construction, renovation, and rehabilitation of affordable housing by purely public charities; to provide for requirements; to provide for related matters; to provide for an effective date; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: H: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The House Ways & Means Committee version drops the local sales tax break, so the exemption now covers only state sales tax on building materials bought by qualifying charities for affordable homes. It also changes the 30-year deed restriction: instead of barring any sale, the home can be resold, but only to a buyer earning 80% or less of the county median income. The exemption would now end on December 31, 2031, and the bill still takes effect January 1, 2027.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed in the bill's substance. The only edit is to the header: the line saying the House Ways & Means Committee offered the substitute was replaced with the bill number and a list of sponsors, starting with Representative Franklin of the 160th. The proposed sales tax break on building materials for affordable housing built or fixed up by purely public charities appears unchanged.

bills.headline: Exempts building materials for charity-built affordable starter homes from state sales tax.
bills.recap: This bill lets certain 501(c)(3) charities skip state sales tax on materials that stay permanently in affordable homes they build, renovate, or rehab. It applies only to single-family homes sold to first-time buyers with zero-interest loans from the charity, like a Habitat for Humanity-style model. Buyers must earn 80 percent or less of the county median income, live in the home, and accept a 30-year resale limit to other buyers at that income level. The break would start January 1, 2027, and would expire December 31, 2031, which could lower costs and expand starter-home supply in some markets.

bills.title: Ad valorem tax; state-wide homestead exemption for certain public service employees; provisions
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Part 1 of Article 2 of Chapter 5 of Title 48 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to tax exemptions, so as to provide for a state-wide homestead exemption for certain public service employees from ad valorem taxes in an amount equal to the amount by which the current year assessed value of a homestead exceeds the base year value of such homestead; to provide for definitions; to specify the terms and conditions of the exemption and the procedures relating thereto; to provide for applicability; to provide for related matters; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, and automatic repeal; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Freezes home assessed values for property taxes for qualifying teachers, first responders, and hospital workers.
bills.recap: This bill creates a statewide homestead exemption that freezes the taxable value of a home at its base year level for certain public service workers. It covers firefighters, paramedics, police officers, teachers and other school staff, and hospital employees who earn 150% or less of their area's median income. The freeze does not cover new improvements or added land, does not pass to a new owner, and replaces any other homestead exemption the owner has. It needs a two-thirds vote in both chambers and statewide voter approval in November 2026, and would start January 1, 2027. Realtors may see it as a draw for these workers to buy homes.

bills.title: Income tax; donation of real property for conservation purposes; revise tax credits
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Article 2 of Chapter 7 of Title 48 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to income tax imposition, rate, computation, exemptions, and credits, so as to revise tax credits for donation of real property for conservation purposes; to revise required filings; to repeal provisions regarding the State Properties Commission; to revise the aggregate amount of tax credits allowed; to extend the date for acceptance of new applications; to repeal penalty provisions; to repeal a definition; to provide for related matters; to provide for an effective date; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: H: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The committee version moves appraisal review for conservation land donations from the State Properties Commission to the Department of Natural Resources. The Department would now check each appraisal for a major overvaluation, meaning the claimed value is 150 percent or more of the correct value. If it finds one, it must report the appraiser to the Georgia Real Estate Commission for investigation and possible discipline. The rest of the bill is unchanged from the introduced version, including the higher credit limits ($1 million or 50 percent of value), the $30 million yearly program cap, and the extension of the program through 2031.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed in this version. The only edit is to the header, which now lists the bill's sponsors (Representatives Cannon, Dickey, Corbett, Rhodes, Meeks, and others) instead of the line saying the House Ways and Means Committee offered the substitute. The rules on tax credits for donating land for conservation are the same.

bills.headline: Expands Georgia's tax credit for donating land or conservation easements and extends it to 2031.
bills.recap: This bill raises the state income tax credit for donating land or conservation easements. The cap per donation goes from $500,000 or 25% of value to $1 million or 50% of value. The yearly cap per taxpayer doubles, and the statewide total rises from $4 million to $30 million a year through 2031. It also removes the State Properties Commission from appraisal review and repeals the special dollar penalty for appraisers who overvalue land, though overvalued appraisals still go to the Georgia Real Estate Commission for possible discipline. Realtors working with rural, farm, or timber landowners may see more interest in conservation donations, and those deals may involve appraisers licensed under the Real Estate Commission.

bills.title: Local government; authorize establishment of local homeowner's incentive adjustment grant programs
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Title 36 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to local government so as to authorize the establishment of local homeowner's incentive adjustment grant programs; to amend Article 7 of Chapter 5 of Title 48 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to miscellaneous local administrative provisions, so as to authorize the establishment of local homeowner's incentive adjustment grant funds; to provide for a contingent effective date and automatic repeal; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Lets counties and cities use surplus funds for homestead property tax credits after voter approval.
bills.recap: This bill lets a Georgia county or city create a local homeowner tax credit program, but only if local voters approve it in a referendum. When the local government has a budget surplus, it can put money into a special fund and use it to give a dollar-for-dollar credit on county or city property taxes for homes with a homestead exemption. The credit cannot exceed the tax owed, will be shown on the tax bill, and does not apply to school or bond taxes. The bill only takes effect on January 1, 2027, if voters ratify a state constitutional amendment removing the $18,000 assessed value cap. Realtors may care because it could lower yearly tax bills for homestead owners in places that adopt it.

bills.title: Health Care Homestead Protection Act; enact
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 13 of Title 51 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to recovery in medical malpractice actions, so as to provide for an exemption in medical malpractice actions for the primary residences of health care providers; to provide for exceptions; to provide for a short title; to provide for an effective date and applicability; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Shields doctors' and health providers' primary homes from medical malpractice judgment collections.
bills.recap: This bill protects the primary home of an individual health care provider from being seized or sold to pay a medical malpractice judgment, claim, or lien. The protection covers houses, other real property, and mobile homes used as a primary residence. It does not block tax liens, government debts, mortgages or other voluntary loans on the home, or criminal restitution orders. For Realtors, it means mortgage lenders keep their rights, and provider-owned homes would be less likely to face forced sales from malpractice judgments starting July 1, 2026.

bills.title: Georgia Urban Sustainable Gardens Act; enact
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 8 of Title 50 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to Department of Community Affairs, so as to require such department to compile a list of state owned real property that may be used for community gardens; to provide for the establishment and maintenance of community gardens in certain municipalities; to provide requirements for such community gardens; to provide for funding of such community gardens by the municipality; to authorize the lease or other availability of state owned real property for use as community gardens; to provide for construction; to require cooperation from state agencies; to provide for definitions; to provide for legislative findings; to provide for a short title; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Requires larger Georgia cities to create free community gardens, possibly on unused state land.
bills.recap: This bill has the Department of Community Affairs list unused state-owned land that could work as community gardens by the end of 2026. By the end of 2027, every city with 25,000 or more people must set up and run at least one community garden, if suitable state land is available. Cities may also use their own land, and garden plots must be free to residents. Realtors may care because the bill changes how some vacant public land is used, which could affect neighborhood appeal and local land use.

bills.title: Heard County; ad valorem tax for educational purposes; provide homestead exemption
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to provide a homestead exemption from Heard County school district ad valorem taxes for educational purposes in the amount of the total assessed value of the homestead for residents of that school district who are 70 years of age or older; to provide for definitions; to specify the terms and conditions of the exemption and the procedures relating thereto; to provide for applicability; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: H: House Date Signed by Governor

versions.name: Enrolled
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed between the introduced and enrolled versions. The only edits are header labels showing the bill passed the House and Senate. The Heard County school tax homestead exemption, its link to other exemptions, and the local vote with a January 1, 2027 start date all stay the same.

bills.headline: Heard County homeowners 70 and older would pay no school property taxes on their homes.
bills.recap: This bill gives Heard County homeowners age 70 or older a full exemption from school district property taxes on their primary home. Owners must apply once with the county tax commissioner, and the exemption then renews automatically each year while they live there. It does not cover state, county, or city taxes, and it only takes effect if local voters approve it in a November referendum, starting January 1, 2027. Realtors may find it useful when working with older buyers and sellers, since it can sharply lower yearly costs for seniors who stay in or move to Heard County.

bills.title: Landlord and tenant; establish minimum habitability standards consistent with recognized housing standards
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Article 1 of Chapter 7 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to general provisions regarding landlord and tenant, so as to establish minimum habitability standards consistent with recognized housing standards; to prohibit waivers of such standards; to provide for enforcement and clarification of existing landlord duties; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Sets minimum habitability standards for rentals and gives tenants new remedies for unfixed problems.
bills.recap: This bill says every Georgia residential lease includes a promise, which cannot be waived, that the home is fit to live in. Landlords would have to follow health and safety codes, keep common areas clean and safe, and keep plumbing, electrical, heating, AC, and appliances they supply working. They would also have to provide trash containers and pickup, running water, hot water, and reasonable heat. If a serious problem is not fixed within one week of notice, the tenant could end the lease, withhold rent, sue for damages, make repairs and deduct the cost from rent, or get substitute housing. Tenants must still keep the unit reasonably clean and avoid damage beyond normal wear and tear. Realtors who manage rentals or advise investors should note the added landlord duties and tenant remedies.

bills.title: Development authorities; certain affordable housing uses of property qualify as projects; provide
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 62 of Title 36 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to development authorities, so as to provide that certain affordable housing uses of property qualify as projects that may be undertaken by development authorities; to provide for legislative findings and declarations; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.lastAction: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute

timeline.text: H: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The House Governmental Affairs Committee changed who can qualify for affordable housing projects backed by development authorities. The original bill capped household income at 80 percent of the local median income. The new version caps it at 175 percent of the federal poverty level instead. It also adds a second test: the authority must find that a business has shown a reasonable need for workforce housing in the county or city that created the authority.

bills.headline: Lets local development authorities build, buy, lease, or finance affordable workforce housing.
bills.recap: This bill adds housing to the list of projects that Georgia's local development authorities can take on. Authorities could acquire, build, improve, lease, or finance single-family, two-family, or multifamily homes. There are two conditions: the homes must be mainly for households earning no more than 175 percent of the federal poverty level, and a business must show a reasonable need for workforce housing in that city or county. Realtors may see more new affordable housing projects and public financing tools in areas where employers need housing for workers.

bills.title: Georgia Housing and Finance Authority; eliminate outstanding bond limit
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 26 of Title 50 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to the Georgia Housing and Finance Authority, so as to eliminate the outstanding bond limit; to provide for a statement on bonds regarding the full faith and credit of the State; to provide for related matters; to provide for an effective date; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Removes the $6 billion cap on Georgia housing authority single-family bonds.
bills.recap: This bill removes the $6 billion limit on bonds the Georgia Housing and Finance Authority can have outstanding for its single-family home program. It also drops older caps on bonds for business and health care financing. Every bond must now state that it is not a debt of the State and is not backed by the State's full faith and credit. For Realtors, this could let the authority raise more money for home loan programs that help Georgia buyers, including first-time buyers.

bills.title: Commerce and trade; encourage transparency and fairness with respect to rent pricing for residential properties
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Part 2 of Article 15 of Chapter 1 of Title 10 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to the "Fair Business Practices Act of 1975," so as to encourage transparency and fairness with respect to rent pricing for residential properties; to prohibit landlords from failing to disclose the total rental price of any residential property and charging hidden fees for any residential property; to provide for definitions; to provide for statutory construction; to provide for related matters; to provide for an effective date and applicability; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Requires landlords to disclose total rent upfront and bans hidden rental fees.
bills.recap: This bill would make it an unfair business practice for a landlord to sign a lease or take payment before clearly showing the total rental price, including all mandatory and government fees. It also bans hidden fees, such as fees that exceed actual cost, fees for services not provided, fees for things the landlord must already provide, fees tied to required vendors, or fees not written in the lease. It covers homes, apartments, hotels, and short-term and vacation rentals, and applies to leases and renewals signed after it becomes law. Agents who handle leasing or property management would need to make sure listings and leases show the full price and only charge fees that are spelled out and reasonable.

bills.title: Chatham County; City of Savannah; school district ad valorem tax; homestead exemption; provisions
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend an Act providing for a base year assessed value homestead exemption from Chatham County and City of Savannah School District ad valorem taxes for educational purposes, approved April 12, 1999 (Ga. L. 1999, p. 4215), as amended, so as to prevent any increases in the adjusted base year assessed value of properties above the value set in tax year 2025; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: H: House Date Signed by Governor

versions.name: Enrolled
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed between the introduced and enrolled versions. The only edits are header labels showing the bill passed the House and Senate. The rules on the Chatham County school district homestead exemption in Savannah are the same as when the bill was introduced.

bills.headline: Freezes Savannah-Chatham school tax homestead value at 2025 level, pending voter approval.
bills.recap: This bill changes an existing homestead exemption for Chatham County and City of Savannah school taxes. Today, the taxable base value of a homestead can rise each year with inflation. Under this bill, that adjusted base value could not go above its tax year 2025 level after 2026, which in effect freezes school taxable values for homesteads. Voters in the school district must approve it at the 2026 general primary for it to take effect on July 1, 2026. Realtors should note that this could lower school tax bills for owner-occupants and may make homeownership in the area more appealing.

bills.title: Chatham County; school district ad valorem tax; homestead exemption; provisions
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend an Act providing a homestead exemption from Chatham County school district ad valorem taxes for educational purposes in an amount equal to the amount by which the current year assessed value of a homestead exceeds the base year assessed value of such homestead, approved May 9, 2025 (Ga. L. 2025, p. 3649), so as to provide that any homeowner receiving the homestead exemption provided for in Ga. L. 1999, p. 4215, as amended, shall automatically receive the exemption provided for in this Act; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: H: House Date Signed by Governor

versions.name: Enrolled
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed between the introduced and enrolled versions. The only edits are to the header labels, which now mark the bill as passed by the House and Senate. The homestead exemption rules for Chatham County school district property taxes read the same as when the bill was introduced.

bills.headline: Chatham County homeowners with existing school tax freeze automatically get newer homestead exemption.
bills.recap: This law changes a 2025 Chatham County school tax homestead exemption that limits school taxes to the home's base year value. Homeowners who, as of December 31, 2026, have applied for and qualify for the older 1999 base year school tax exemption will get the newer exemption automatically, with no new application needed. Everyone else must still apply with the Chatham County tax commissioner. Realtors can tell Chatham clients that existing exemption holders keep their savings without extra paperwork, while new buyers still need to file.

bills.title: Ad valorem tax; assessment of real property purchased or acquired by certain business enterprises at 100 percent of its fair market value; provide
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 5 of Title 48 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to ad valorem taxation of property, so as to provide for the assessment of real property purchased or acquired by certain business enterprises at 100 percent of its fair market value; to require that proceeds from taxation of such property be used to reduce the ad valorem tax bill on homesteads in the same tax jurisdiction as such property; to provide for penalties; to provide for certification of ownership; to provide for forms and applications; to provide for definitions; to provide for contingent effectiveness and automatic repeal; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Taxes big corporate single-family rental owners at full value to cut homestead tax bills.
bills.recap: This bill would tax property owned by companies holding 1,000 or more single-family rental homes in Georgia at 100 percent of fair market value, instead of the usual 40 percent. Those owners must certify their properties with the county tax assessors by January 1, 2027, or within 90 days of buying. If they don't, they face a penalty of twice the unpaid tax plus interest, and it becomes a lien on the property. The extra tax money must first go toward credits that lower tax bills on homesteads in the same area. It only takes effect if voters approve a constitutional amendment in November 2026. Realtors may care because it could cool large investor buying of starter homes and lower taxes for owner-occupants.

bills.title: Local government; waive development impact fees for certain projects related to development of affordable or workforce housing; authorize
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 71 of Title 36 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to development impact fees, so as to authorize local governments to waive development impact fees for certain projects related to the development of affordable or workforce housing without increasing other impact fees to offset such lost funds; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Lets local governments waive impact fees for owner-occupied workforce housing projects.
bills.recap: Under current law, a city or county can exempt affordable housing projects from development impact fees only if it covers that project's share of road, water, or other infrastructure costs from another funding source. This bill lets local governments skip that backfill rule for workforce housing made up of single-family homes meant mainly for owner occupancy, as long as the exemption is supported in the local comprehensive plan. If a city or county uses this waiver, it cannot raise impact fees on other projects just to make up the lost money. Realtors may care because lower impact fees could reduce building costs and help bring more entry-level homes for buyers to market.

bills.title: Right to Information for Homeowners Act; enact
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 3 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to regulation of specialized land transactions, so as to provide for community associations to disclose documents to unit owners upon request; to provide for community associations to maintain certain records; to provide for the creation of an online database; to provide for annual reports; to provide for a civil action; to provide for attorney's fees; to provide for penalties; to provide for definitions; to provide a short title; to provide for related matters; to provide for an effective date and applicability; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Requires HOAs and condo associations to share financial, insurance, and governing records with owners.
bills.recap: This bill would require homeowners', condo, and property owners' associations to give owners key records within 14 days of a request, keep a secure online database of those records, and send an annual report on insurance, reserves, and debts. Associations would need an independent audit at least every two years, must share unredacted bank statements on request, keep bank records for seven years, and tell owners about major insurance changes within seven days. Owners could sue for damages, including punitive damages, and associations could be fined up to $500 per violation. For Realtors, easier access to an association's finances, reserves, and insurance could help buyers and sellers spot problems before closing, though associations may face higher costs that could show up in dues.

bills.title: Sales and use tax; limit number of local sales and use taxes by authorizing counties; revise provisions
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 8 of Title 48 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to sales and use taxes, so as to revise provisions limiting the number of local sales and use taxes by authorizing counties to collect an enhanced homestead option sales tax as well as a local option sales tax; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Lets counties levy both a homestead sales tax and a local option sales tax.
bills.recap: This bill changes Georgia's cap on local sales taxes. It lets counties collect an enhanced homestead option sales tax along with a regular local option sales tax, by grouping these taxes under a separate 1 percent limit outside the general 2 percent cap. Homestead option sales taxes are generally used to lower property taxes on owner-occupied homes. Realtors may care because more counties could use sales tax money to ease homeowners' property tax bills, which can affect the cost of owning a home.

bills.title: Brookhaven, City of; increase existing homestead exemption for senior citizens and disabled persons to $200,000.00
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend an Act to incorporate the City of Brookhaven in DeKalb County, approved April 16, 2012 (Ga. L. 2012, p. 5527), as amended, so as to increase the existing homestead exemption for senior citizens and disabled persons to $200,000.00; to specify the terms and conditions of the exemption and the procedures relating thereto; to provide for applicability; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: H: House Date Signed by Governor

versions.name: Enrolled
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed between the introduced and enrolled versions. The only edits are header labels showing the bill passed the House and Senate. The bill still raises Brookhaven's city homestead exemption for senior citizens and disabled persons to $200,000 of assessed value, subject to a local vote.

bills.headline: Raises Brookhaven's senior and disabled homestead exemption from $160,000 to $200,000, pending voter approval.
bills.recap: This local bill raises the City of Brookhaven homestead exemption for eligible seniors and disabled residents from $160,000 to $200,000 of assessed value. It applies only to city property taxes, not county or school taxes. Brookhaven voters must approve it in the November 2026 election, and if they do, it takes effect January 1, 2027. Realtors working with older or disabled buyers and sellers in Brookhaven may want to note the possible lower city tax bills for those who qualify.

bills.title: Georgia Landowners Protection Act; enact
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 66 of Title 36 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to zoning procedures, so as to provide for the maximum period of time a local government may enforce certain moratoria; to prohibit reimposition of certain moratoria within a certain period of time; to waive sovereign immunity on claims related to damages arising from moratoria exceeding such limitations; to provide for recoverable damages and attorney's fees; to provide for legislative findings; to provide a short title; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Limits local zoning and permit moratoria to 180 days and lets owners sue.
bills.recap: This bill caps local zoning and building permit moratoria at 180 days. A city or county could not bring back the same type of zoning moratorium within 365 days after one ends, and must give 30 days' public notice before voting on a new one. Owners whose property loses value from a moratorium lasting over 180 days could sue in superior court for lost development value, carrying costs like interest, higher property taxes, and possibly attorney's fees. Emergencies, natural disasters, and imminent health or safety threats are exempt. Realtors may care because shorter delays could help builders, land sellers, and housing supply.

bills.title: Walker County; school district ad valorem tax; remove five year residency requirement for homestead exemption
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend an Act to provide a homestead exemption from Walker County school district ad valorem taxes for educational purposes, approved May 13, 2025 (Ga. L. 2025, p. 3901), so as to remove the five year residency requirement for the homestead exemption for residents of such school district who are 75 years of age or older; to provide for definitions; to specify the terms and conditions of the exemption and the procedures relating thereto; to provide for applicability; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: H: House Date Signed by Governor

versions.name: Enrolled
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed between the introduced and enrolled versions. The only edits are header labels showing the bill passed the House and Senate. The bill's content is the same: it still removes the five-year residency requirement for the Walker County school tax homestead exemption, subject to a local vote.

bills.headline: Drops five-year residency rule for Walker County seniors' full school tax exemption.
bills.recap: This bill changes Walker County's senior homestead exemption from school taxes. It removes the five-year residency requirement for homeowners 75 and older, who can get a full exemption from school taxes on their homestead. Homeowners ages 70 to 74 keep a $50,000 exemption, and qualifying surviving spouses can continue to receive the benefit. Voters must approve it in November 2026, and it would take effect January 1, 2027, which could make Walker County more attractive to older buyers who are relocating there.

bills.title: Cartersville, City of; ad valorem tax for municipal purposes; provide homestead exemption
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to provide a homestead exemption from City of Cartersville ad valorem taxes for municipal purposes in the amount of $100,000.00 of the assessed value of the homestead for residents of that city; to provide for definitions; to specify the terms and conditions of the exemption and the procedures relating thereto; to provide for applicability; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: H: House Date Signed by Governor

versions.name: Enrolled
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed between the introduced and enrolled versions. The only edits are header labels showing the bill passed the House and Senate. The Cartersville homestead exemption from city property taxes reads the same, still applies to tax years starting January 1, 2027, and still requires a local election that the city pays for.

bills.headline: Creates a $100,000 Cartersville city homestead exemption, pending a November 2026 local vote.
bills.recap: This bill gives Cartersville homeowners a $100,000 exemption off the assessed value of their primary home for city property taxes. It only covers city taxes, not state, county, or school taxes, and it stacks on top of any other city homestead exemptions. Owners must apply once with the city, and the exemption then renews each year as long as they live in the home. City voters must approve it in November 2026, and if they do, it starts January 1, 2027, which could lower tax bills and be a selling point for buyers in Cartersville.

bills.title: Savannah, City of; ad valorem taxes for municipal purposes; homestead exemption; provisions
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend an Act providing for a homestead exemption from certain City of Savannah ad valorem taxes for municipal purposes in an amount equal to the amount by which the current year assessed value of a homestead exceeds the adjusted assessed value of such homestead for the taxable year immediately preceding the taxable year in which this exemption was first granted to the current owner of such homestead, approved April 13, 1999 (Ga. L. 1999, p. 4223), as amended, so as to prevent any increases in the adjusted base year assessed value of properties above the value set in tax year 2025; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Freezes Savannah homestead exemption base values at 2025 levels, if voters approve.
bills.recap: Savannah already offers a city homestead exemption that limits how fast a home's taxable value can grow, with the base value rising each year by inflation (CPI). This bill would stop that base value from rising above its 2025 level, so city taxable values for homesteads would effectively be frozen at 2025 amounts. It applies only to City of Savannah municipal property taxes and goes to city voters in November 2026, taking effect January 1, 2027 if approved. Realtors may care because it could lower long-term city tax bills for current owners and strengthen the incentive for owners to stay put, which may affect listing inventory.

bills.title: Hall County; ad valorem tax for educational purposes; homestead exemption; increase income cap
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend an Act providing for homestead exemptions from Hall County school district ad valorem taxes for educational purposes for certain residents of that school district who are senior citizens, approved April 6, 1998 (Ga. L. 1998, p. 4281), as amended, so as to increase the income cap on the homestead exemption provided to residents of the school district 62 years of age and older; to provide that any person 66 years of age or older shall receive a new exemption on the first $400,000.00 of the assessed value of the homestead; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: H: House Date Signed by Governor

versions.name: Enrolled
versions.changes: No meaningful changes were made between the introduced and enrolled versions of this bill. The only edits mark the bill as passed by the House and Senate and update the document code on each page. The Hall County school tax homestead exemption and its higher income cap stay the same as first introduced.

bills.headline: Expands Hall County senior school tax breaks on homes, pending a November 2026 vote.
bills.recap: This local law changes school property tax exemptions for older and disabled homeowners in the Hall County school district. It raises the income limit for the $30,000 exemption for residents 62 to 65 (and disabled residents) to $40,000. It adds a new exemption for homeowners 66 and older on the first $480,000 of assessed value (about $1.2 million in market value), and seniors don't have to reapply as they age into the next tier. Voters must approve it in November 2026, and it would take effect January 1, 2027, which could make Hall County more attractive to older buyers and help seniors stay in their homes.

bills.title: Hall County; ad valorem tax for county purposes; provide homestead exemption
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to provide a homestead exemption from Hall County ad valorem taxes for county purposes in the amount of $10,000.00 of the assessed value of the homestead for residents of that county; to provide for definitions; to specify the terms and conditions of the exemption and the procedures relating thereto; to provide for applicability; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: H: House Date Signed by Governor

versions.name: Enrolled
versions.changes: No meaningful changes were made between the introduced and enrolled versions. The only edits are labels showing the bill passed the House and Senate. The $10,000 Hall County homestead exemption from county property taxes and the rest of the bill's terms stay the same.

bills.headline: Gives Hall County homeowners a $10,000 homestead exemption from county property taxes.
bills.recap: This law creates a new $10,000 homestead exemption on the assessed value of a home for Hall County property taxes for county purposes, covering up to five contiguous acres. It does not apply to school, city, or state taxes, and it adds to any existing exemptions. Hall County voters must approve it in the November 2026 election, and if passed, it starts January 1, 2027. Homeowners who already have the statewide homestead exemption by December 31, 2026 get it automatically, which can lower carrying costs and is a good selling point for buyers in Hall County.

bills.title: Public Retirement Systems Investment Authority Law; provide certain retirement systems the option to invest in real estate
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Article 7 of Chapter 20 of Title 47 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, the "Public Retirement Systems Investment Authority Law," so as to provide certain retirement systems the option to invest in real estate; to provide for an increase in certain retirement systems allowable alternative investments; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Lets more large Georgia public pension funds invest up to 10% in real estate.
bills.recap: This bill lets large public retirement systems in Georgia invest up to 10 percent of their assets in real estate. The Employees' Retirement System and the Teachers Retirement System are left out of this change. If a fund's value drops, it can keep real estate it already owns. The bill also raises the general limit on alternative investments for eligible large retirement systems from 10 to 15 percent, which could bring more institutional money into Georgia property markets.

bills.title: Property; nonjudicial foreclosures on time-share estates; provisions
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Part 7 of Article 5 of Chapter 3 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to miscellaneous provisions relative to time-share projects and programs, so as to repeal provisions for nonjudicial foreclosures on time-share estates, subject to exceptions for time-share estates created during certain time periods; to provide for related matters; to provide for an effective date; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Limits special time-share foreclosure rules to time-shares created from mid-2023 to mid-2026.
bills.recap: This bill narrows Georgia's special nonjudicial foreclosure process for time-share estates. Those rules would only apply to time-shares created between July 1, 2023, and June 30, 2026. Owners' associations could still foreclose liens for unpaid assessments on time-shares created or amended on or after July 1, 2023, using the standard condo-style lien process, and mortgage lenders could foreclose using Georgia's regular power-of-sale foreclosure rules. Realtors who work with time-share buyers, sellers, or owners should know that the foreclosure process may differ depending on when the time-share was created.

bills.title: Fire protection and safety; improve government efficiency by updating provisions of office of the Safety Fire Commissioner
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Titles 8 and 25 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to buildings and housing and fire protection and safety, respectively, so as to improve government efficiency by updating provisions of the office of the Safety Fire Commissioner; to provide for procedures for rules promulgation, hearings, and appeals; to provide for the appointment of a deputy commissioner of safety fire; to provide for certain powers in suspected arson investigations; to provide for immediate reporting of fatalities caused by fire or smoke; to provide for suspension or revocation of a license; to provide for an increased reinspection fee; to provide for an effective date; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.lastAction: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute

timeline.text: H: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The committee version lowers the top fine for an occupant who fails to keep a smoke detector working from $250 to $100 per detector, up from $25 under current law, with a warning still required for a first offense. It lowers the manufactured home reinspection fee to $150 instead of $250, up from $15 today. It drops several original pieces: the Commissioner's new power to suspend or revoke manufactured home licenses, the shift of hearings and appeals to Insurance Department procedures and Fulton County Superior Court, the expanded subpoena power, and the rulemaking change. It adds a new law letting probate courts hear fire safety misdemeanors if the defendant gives up a jury trial in writing.

bills.headline: Updates fire marshal powers, adds building permit appeals board, and raises smoke detector fines.
bills.recap: This bill reorganizes the state Safety Fire office, adding a deputy commissioner and letting state officials order immediate evacuations of unsafe buildings, even ones without a certificate of occupancy. It creates an appeals board where builders and others can challenge local building permit rulings based on fire safety standards, including some stop-work orders. It raises the maximum fine for an occupant who fails to keep a working smoke detector from $25 to $100 per detector, with a warning first, and raises the manufactured home reinspection fee from $15 to $150. Realtors may care because it affects new construction timelines, occupied homes and rentals with faulty smoke detectors, and manufactured housing costs.

bills.title: Ad valorem tax; state-wide homestead exemption in an amount as determined from proceeds generated from collection of certain ad valorem property taxes on data centers
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Article 2 of Chapter 5 of Title 48 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to property tax exemptions and deferral, so as to provide for a state-wide homestead exemption from ad valorem taxes in an amount as determined from the proceeds generated from the collection of certain ad valorem property taxes on data centers; to provide for definitions; to specify the terms and conditions of the exemption and the procedures relating thereto; to provide for applicability; to provide for related matters; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, and automatic repeal; to provide for contingent repeal; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Creates a statewide homestead exemption funded by growth in data center property taxes.
bills.recap: This bill would create a new homestead exemption for Georgia homeowners, funded by property tax money from data centers. Each year, any increase in data center tax collections over a base year would be set aside and split equally among homesteads to lower their taxes the next year. If data center collections do not grow, the exemption is zero that year. Homeowners must apply, and the exemption renews automatically, stays with a surviving spouse, and does not transfer to a new owner. It starts in 2027 only if voters approve it in a statewide referendum in November 2026 and a related constitutional amendment also passes, so Realtors may get questions about future tax bills.

bills.title: Community Health, Department of; license supportive senior housing communities; provide
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Article 1 of Chapter 7 of Title 31 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to the regulation of hospitals and related institutions, so as to provide for the Department of Community Health to license supportive senior housing communities; to provide for COVID-19 requirements; to provide for employer based programs; to provide for influenza education information; to provide for residential care facilities for the elderly; to provide for hospice and palliative care; to provide background checks; to provide for the ombudsman program; to provide for remedies and protections of residents; to provide for the drug repository program; to provide for continuing care providers and facilities; to provide for related matters; to provide for an effective date; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Creates a new state license for Medicaid-focused supportive senior housing communities.
bills.recap: This bill lets the Department of Community Health license a new type of facility called a supportive senior housing community. These are 25-bed to 150-unit apartment buildings where each resident leases their own unit and more than half of residents are on Medicaid. The communities can offer help with daily living, medication help, limited nursing, housekeeping, and transportation, and they must meet staffing, training, and financial stability rules. The state must also build a payment rate that works for projects financed with low-income housing tax credits and seek a federal Medicaid waiver by June 30, 2026. That could encourage new affordable senior apartment development, which matters to agents working with seniors, families, developers, and investors.

bills.title: Petrea-Stephens-Franklin-Watson Tax Relief Act; enact
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to provide a homestead exemption from Bryan County school district ad valorem taxes for educational purposes in an amount equal to the amount by which the current year assessed value of a homestead exceeds the base year assessed value of such homestead; to provide for definitions; to specify the terms and conditions of the exemption and the procedures relating thereto; to provide for applicability; to provide a short title; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: H: House Date Signed by Governor

versions.name: Enrolled
versions.changes: Nothing of substance changed between the introduced and enrolled versions of HB 1440. The only edits are labels showing the bill passed the House and Senate (the "/AP" tag and "As Passed House and Senate"). The tax relief provisions, including the property tax exemption, read the same as when the bill was introduced.

bills.headline: Freezes Bryan County school taxes on homesteads at base-year value, pending November 2026 vote.
bills.recap: This local law creates a homestead exemption from Bryan County school district taxes that covers any rise in a home's assessed value above its base-year value, which works like a school tax value freeze. It covers up to five contiguous acres, but new improvements or added land are still taxed, and it does not touch state, county, or city taxes. Owners who already get the 2025 Bryan County school exemption or the statewide base-year exemption are enrolled automatically, with 2026 or their existing base year as the base. New owners must apply, and their base year resets to the year before they first get the exemption. Voters must approve it in November 2026, and it would start January 1, 2027. Realtors should know that a buyer's school taxes may differ from the seller's because the frozen value does not carry over to a new owner.

bills.title: Georgia Property Tax Fairness Fund; create
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapters 7 and 8 of Title 48 and Chapter 8 of Title 33 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to income taxes, sales and use taxes, and fees and taxes relative to insurance, respectively, so as to create the Georgia Property Tax Fairness Fund; to provide constitutional authorization; to provide for the calculation, application, and limitations on tax credits; to provide for rules and regulations; to provide for recoverability; to provide for the repeal of insurance premium tax credits and abatements; to provide for conforming changes; to provide for a contingent effective date and automatic repeal; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Creates a state fund giving tax credits to cost-burdened homeowners and renters.
bills.recap: This bill creates the Georgia Property Tax Fairness Fund, paid for by insurance premium taxes and sales taxes on data centers. It ends the sales tax break for new data centers and repeals several insurance premium tax credits. Lower- and middle-income homeowners whose property taxes plus homeowners insurance top 5% of income, and renters whose rent tops 33% of income, could get a refundable state income tax credit. Local sales tax collected from data centers would first go toward property tax bill credits of up to $2,500 on homesteads worth $500,000 or less in that area. It only takes effect if voters approve a constitutional amendment in November 2026.

bills.title: Bartow County; ad valorem tax for county purposes; increase homestead exemption
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend an Act to provide a homestead exemption from certain Bartow County ad valorem taxes for county purposes in the amount of $5,000.00 of the assessed value of the homestead for certain residents of that county, approved March 24, 1994 (Ga. L. 1994, p. 4058), as amended, particularly by an Act approved May 1, 2023 (Ga. L. 2023, p. 3891), so as to increase the exemption to $30,000.00; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: H: House Date Signed by Governor

versions.name: Enrolled
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed between the introduced and enrolled versions. The only edits are header labels showing the bill passed the House and Senate. The Bartow County homestead exemption increase reads the same as when it was introduced.

bills.headline: Raises Bartow County's homestead exemption for county taxes from $15,000 to $30,000, pending voter approval.
bills.recap: This local law doubles the Bartow County homestead exemption on county property taxes, from $15,000 to $30,000 of a home's assessed value. It applies to all Bartow County residents who claim a homestead. Voters must approve it on the November 2026 ballot, and if they do, it takes effect January 1, 2027. A bigger exemption means lower county tax bills for owner-occupants, which can help with affordability talks with buyers and sellers in Bartow.

bills.title: Hampton City of; ad valorem tax for municipal purposes; provide homestead exemption
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to provide a homestead exemption from City of Hampton ad valorem taxes for municipal purposes in the amount of the full assessed value of the homestead for residents of that city who have resided within the city for five years or more; to provide for definitions; to specify the terms and conditions of the exemption and the procedures relating thereto; to provide for applicability; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: H: House Date Signed by Governor

versions.name: Enrolled
versions.changes: Nothing of substance changed between the introduced and enrolled versions. The only edits are labels showing the bill passed the House and Senate. The homestead exemption from City of Hampton property taxes and the local voter referendum stay the same as first introduced.

bills.headline: Fully exempts long-time Hampton homeowners' homes from city property taxes, pending voter approval.
bills.recap: This bill gives City of Hampton homeowners who have lived in the city five years or more a full exemption from city property taxes on their homestead, covering up to five contiguous acres. It does not cut county, school, or state property taxes, and it replaces any other city homestead exemption rather than adding to it. Hampton voters must approve it in the November 2026 election, and it would start January 1, 2027. Homeowners who already have a city homestead exemption for five years get it automatically, and Realtors may see it as a selling point for long-term owners, though new buyers must wait five years to qualify.

bills.title: Senior Stabilization Act; enact
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 7 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to landlord and tenant, so as to provide for rent increase limits for certain senior citizens and senior housing; to provide for a short title; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Caps rent increases at 10 percent for certain senior tenants through 2028.
bills.recap: This bill limits rent increases for tenants age 62 or older whose main income is Social Security, if their lease was signed on or before June 30, 2026. From July 1, 2026, through December 31, 2028, landlords and developers building senior housing cannot renew or sign a new lease with these tenants that raises rent more than 10 percent above the rent in effect on June 30, 2026. Property managers and agents who handle rentals would need to check tenant age and income status before setting renewal rents. It would be a rare form of rent limit in Georgia, which could affect how investors value rental properties.

bills.title: Georgia Home Title Protection and Deed Fraud Prevention Act; enact
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Part 1 of Article 1 of Chapter 2 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to recording of deeds and other real property transactions, so as to provide for a statement form regarding the effect of quitclaim deeds; to provide for a short title; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Requires a bold warning on quitclaim deeds that the seller gives up ownership.
bills.recap: This bill would require any deed that transfers property without a title warranty, such as a quitclaim deed, to carry a bold, all-caps warning at the top of the first page. The warning says the person signing will no longer own the property once the deed is signed and recorded. The goal is to help prevent deed fraud and make sure owners understand what they are signing. Realtors may see this on family transfers, divorces, and other quitclaim deals, and it could help protect clients from being tricked out of their homes.

bills.title: Ad valorem tax; procedures for transmission of relevant information following a real estate closing to allow for the automatic granting of homestead exemptions; provide
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Code Section 48-5-45 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to application for homestead exemption and unlawful to solicit fee to file application for homestead for another, so as to provide procedures for the transmission of relevant information following a real estate closing to allow for the automatic granting of homestead exemptions; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Closing attorneys would send homestead exemption info to tax offices after home purchases.
bills.recap: This bill requires the attorney who closes a home purchase to send the local tax office all the information needed to grant the homestead exemption. The tax office would then grant the exemption without the buyer having to file a separate application. The tax office must notify the owner that the exemption was granted and which tax year it starts. Realtors may care because buyers would be less likely to miss out on tax savings, and closings would add a new step for attorneys.

bills.title: Covington, City of; ad valorem tax for municipal purposes; provide homestead exemption
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to provide a homestead exemption from City of Covington ad valorem taxes for municipal purposes for the total amount of the assessed value of the homestead for residents of that city; to provide for definitions; to specify the terms and conditions of the exemption and the procedures relating thereto; to provide for applicability; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: H: House Date Signed by Governor

versions.name: Enrolled
versions.changes: Nothing of substance changed between the introduced and enrolled versions. The only edits are labels showing the bill passed the House and Senate, plus updated document codes. The Covington city homestead exemption from municipal property taxes reads the same as when it was introduced.

bills.headline: Covington homeowners could pay zero city property tax on their homestead, pending voter approval.
bills.recap: This bill gives Covington residents a homestead exemption covering the full assessed value of their home, wiping out city property taxes for municipal purposes on it. It does not cover state, county, or school taxes, and it stacks on top of other city homestead exemptions. Homeowners must apply once, and the exemption renews automatically while they live in the home. City voters must approve it in November 2026, and if they do, it starts January 1, 2027. A Realtor might care because it could lower ownership costs and make Covington homes more attractive to buyers who plan to live in them.

bills.title: Local government; zoning procedures; operation of immigration detention centers; require special use permits
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 66 of Title 36 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to zoning procedures applicable to counties and municipal corporations, so as to require local governments that have adopted zoning ordinances to require special use permits for the operation of immigration detention centers; to provide for definitions; to provide for related matters; to provide for an effective date and applicability; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Requires special use permits for immigration detention centers in Georgia communities with zoning.
bills.recap: This bill says any Georgia city or county with a zoning ordinance must require a special use permit before an immigration detention center can be built or operated there. A permit would also be needed before land is transferred to the federal government to run such a center. This includes private facilities that hold detainees under federal contracts. Realtors may care because it affects how certain land can be used, sold, or developed, and gives local governments and neighbors more say over these sites. If passed, it takes effect July 1, 2026.

bills.title: Madison County; school district ad valorem tax; provide homestead exemption
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to provide a homestead exemption from Madison County school district ad valorem taxes for educational purposes in the amount of $75,000.00 of the assessed value of the homestead for residents of that school district who are 70 years of age or older; to provide for definitions; to specify the terms and conditions of the exemption and the procedures relating thereto; to provide for applicability; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, contingent effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: H: House Date Signed by Governor

versions.name: Enrolled
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed between the introduced and enrolled versions of this bill. The only edits are labels showing it passed the House and Senate. The Madison County school tax homestead exemption reads the same as when it was introduced.

bills.headline: Gives Madison County seniors 70 and older a $75,000 school tax homestead exemption.
bills.recap: This law creates a $75,000 homestead exemption from Madison County school district property taxes for homeowners age 70 or older. It does not apply to state, county, or city taxes, or to school bond debt payments, and it replaces any other school tax homestead exemption rather than adding to it. Seniors must apply once with the tax commissioner, and it then renews automatically while they live in the home. Voters must approve it in November 2026, and it will not take effect if a statewide amendment exempting homes from all school taxes passes that same election. If approved, it starts January 1, 2027, which could lower costs for older buyers and owners in the county.

bills.title: Revenue and taxation; sales to United States Department of Homeland Security or United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement; revise tax
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Article 1 of Chapter 6 of Title 48 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to real estate transfer tax, so as to revise the tax for sales to the United States Department of Homeland Security or United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement; to revise an exemption; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Imposes a 100% real estate transfer tax on property sales to DHS or ICE.
bills.recap: This bill changes Georgia's real estate transfer tax for one type of buyer. Any deed that transfers property to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security or Immigration and Customs Enforcement would be taxed at 100% of the sale price or property value. It also removes those two agencies from the current exemption that lets government buyers skip the transfer tax. The normal transfer tax rate for all other sales stays the same, so most Realtors would only see an effect on deals where DHS or ICE is the buyer.

bills.title: Rental Pricing Integrity Act; enact
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Part 2 of Article 15 of Chapter 1 of Title 10 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to the "Fair Business Practices Act of 1975," so as to prohibit certain practices by landlords and coordinators involving the use of nonpublic competitor data to influence rental price and occupancy decisions; to provide for annual certification and record retention; to provide for enforcement; to provide for a short title; to provide for legislative findings and intent; to provide for an effective date and applicability; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Bans rent-setting software that uses private competitor data from multiple landlords.
bills.recap: This bill makes it illegal for landlords, property managers, and software vendors to use rent-pricing tools that pull in private rental data from two or more competing landlords to set rents or occupancy. Any landlord or manager using a rent-setting tool must certify to the Attorney General each year that it follows this rule. They must also keep vendor contracts, data input records, pricing recommendations, and proof of independent pricing decisions for at least five years. Only the Attorney General can enforce it under the Fair Business Practices Act, so tenants cannot sue directly. Agents who manage rentals or advise investors should note the new paperwork and pricing limits.

bills.title: Gwinnett County; school district ad valorem tax; provide homestead exemption
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to provide a homestead exemption from Gwinnett County school district ad valorem taxes for educational purposes in the amount of 50 percent of the assessed value of the homestead for certain residents of that school district who are 65 years of age but less than 70 years of age and in the amount of the full assessed value of the homestead for certain residents of that school district who are 70 years of age or older; to provide for definitions; to specify the terms and conditions of the exemption and the procedures relating thereto; to provide for applicability; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Creates Gwinnett school tax homestead exemptions for seniors 65 to 69 and 70-plus.
bills.recap: This bill gives Gwinnett County homeowners aged 65 to 69 a 50 percent exemption from school district property taxes on their homestead. Homeowners 70 and older would pay no school district property taxes on their homestead. To qualify, seniors must have had a homestead exemption in the district for five of the last six years, and the exemption covers up to five acres. It needs voter approval in November 2026 and would start January 1, 2027. Realtors may see it shape older owners' choices to stay put or move, and newcomers would wait years to qualify.

bills.title: Franklin Springs, City of; ad valorem tax for municipal purposes; provide homestead exemption
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to provide a homestead exemption from City of Franklin Springs ad valorem taxes for municipal purposes for the full assessed value of the homestead for residents of that city who are 65 years of age or older; to provide for definitions; to specify the terms and conditions of the exemption and the procedures relating thereto; to provide for applicability; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

bills.headline: Franklin Springs seniors 65 and older could get full exemption from city property taxes.
bills.recap: This bill gives Franklin Springs homeowners age 65 or older a full exemption from city property taxes on their home. It does not cover state, county, or school taxes, and it replaces any other city homestead exemption. City voters must approve it in November 2026, and if they do, it starts January 1, 2027, with seniors needing to apply once. Realtors may find it useful when talking with older buyers and sellers in Franklin Springs about lower ongoing ownership costs.

bills.title: Bibb County; ad valorem tax for educational purposes; provide a homestead exemption
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to provide a homestead exemption from Bibb County school district ad valorem taxes for educational purposes in the amount of $17,000.00 of the assessed value of the homestead for residents of that school district who are between the ages of 65 and 74; to provide a homestead exemption from Bibb County school district ad valorem taxes for educational purposes in the amount of $32,000.00 of the assessed value of the homestead for residents of that school district who are between the ages of 75 and 84; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

bills.headline: Bibb County seniors could get bigger school tax breaks on their homes, if voters approve.
bills.recap: This bill creates age-based homestead exemptions from Bibb County school taxes. Homeowners aged 65 to 74 would get $17,000 off their home's assessed value, those 75 to 84 would get $32,000 off, and those 85 and older would pay no school tax on their homestead. Voters in the Bibb County school district must approve it in November 2026, and it would start January 1, 2027. Seniors apply once with the tax commissioner and it renews automatically. It replaces, not adds to, other school tax homestead exemptions and does not affect state, county, or city taxes. Realtors may find it useful when talking with older buyers and sellers about holding costs in Bibb County.
