bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to provide a homestead exemption from Macon-Bibb County ad valorem taxes for county purposes in the amount of $17,000.00 of the assessed value of the homestead for residents of that county who are between the ages of 65 and 74; to provide a homestead exemption from Macon-Bibb County ad valorem taxes for county purposes in the amount of $32,000.00 of the assessed value of the homestead for residents of that county who are between the ages of 75 and 84; to provide a homestead exemption from Macon-Bibb County ad valorem taxes for county purposes in the amount of the full assessed value of the homestead for residents of that county who are 85 years of age or older; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

Realtors may see more qualified first-time buyers who can cover upfront costs in pricier markets.

bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to provide a homestead exemption from Laurens County school district ad valorem taxes for educational purposes in the amount of the full assessed value of the homestead for residents of that school district who are 80 years of age or older; to provide for definitions; to specify the terms and conditions of the exemption and the procedures relating thereto; to provide for applicability; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

versions.name: Enrolled
versions.changes: Nothing of substance changed between the introduced and enrolled versions. The only edits are labels showing the bill passed the House and Senate. The Laurens County school tax homestead exemption and the local voter referendum stay exactly as first written.

bills.headline: Laurens County seniors 80 and older would pay no school property taxes on their homes.
bills.recap: This bill gives Laurens County homeowners age 80 or older a full exemption from school district property taxes on their homestead, covering the home and up to five connected acres. Owners must apply once with the county tax commissioner, and the exemption then renews each year while they live in the home. It does not affect state, county, city, or independent school district taxes, and it replaces, not adds to, other school tax homestead exemptions. Voters must approve it in November 2026; if they do, it starts January 1, 2027, which could help older owners afford to stay in their homes and may matter when advising senior clients on selling or staying.

bills.title: Gainesville, City of; ad valorem tax for municipal purposes; provide homestead exemption
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to provide a homestead exemption from City of Gainesville ad valorem taxes for municipal purposes in the amount of $10,000.00 of the assessed value of the homestead for residents of that city; to provide for definitions; to specify the terms and conditions of the exemption and the procedures relating thereto; to provide for applicability; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

versions.name: Enrolled
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed between the introduced and enrolled versions. The only edits are header labels showing the bill passed the House and Senate. The Gainesville city homestead exemption, its start date of tax years beginning January 1, 2027, and the local election requirement are the same as introduced.

bills.headline: Gives Gainesville homeowners a $10,000 homestead exemption on city property taxes, pending voter approval.
bills.recap: This law creates a $10,000 homestead exemption off the assessed value of a home for City of Gainesville property taxes. It only covers city taxes, not county, school, or state taxes, and it stacks on top of any other city homestead exemptions. Gainesville voters must approve it in the November 2026 election, and if they do, it starts January 1, 2027. Homeowners must apply once, and the exemption then renews automatically, so Realtors may want to remind Gainesville buyers to file after closing.

bills.title: Gainesville, City of; school district ad valorem tax; provide homestead exemption
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to provide a homestead exemption from City of Gainesville independent school district ad valorem taxes for educational purposes in the amount of $10,000.00 of the assessed value of the homestead for residents of that school district; to provide for definitions; to specify the terms and conditions of the exemption and the procedures relating thereto; to provide for applicability; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

versions.name: Enrolled
versions.changes: No meaningful changes were made between the introduced and enrolled versions. The only edits are header labels showing the bill passed the House and Senate. The homestead exemption for City of Gainesville school district taxes reads the same as when it was introduced.

bills.headline: Creates a $10,000 school tax homestead exemption for Gainesville city school district homeowners.
bills.recap: This law gives homeowners in the City of Gainesville school district a $10,000 exemption off the assessed value of their home for city school taxes. It only applies to those school taxes, not state, county, or city taxes, and it adds to any existing exemptions. Voters must approve it in the November 2026 election, and if they do, it starts January 1, 2027. Homeowners must apply once, and it renews each year. Realtors can remind buyers in the district to file for it after closing.

bills.title: Georgia First-Time Homebuyer's Savings Account Act; enact
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Title 7 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to banking and finance, so as to provide for the creation of first-time homebuyer savings accounts; to provide for contributions by account holders to accounts; to provide for transfer of beneficiaries; to provide for annual reporting; to provide for certain exemptions from certain requirements for financial institutions; to provide for tax deductions; to provide for tax deduction limits; to provide for unqualified withdrawal penalties and exceptions; to permit the Department of Revenue to impose penalties for fraudulent activity; to require the Department of Revenue to create certain forms; to provide for a short title; to provide for purpose; to provide for definitions; to provide for related matters; to provide for an effective date and applicability; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Creates tax-advantaged savings accounts to help Georgia first-time homebuyers save for a home.
bills.recap: This bill lets Georgians open a special savings account at a bank or credit union to save for a first home. Contributions can be deducted from state taxable income, up to $6,000 a year for single filers and $12,000 for joint filers, with lifetime caps of $60,000 and $120,000 per beneficiary. Interest and earnings are state tax-free when used for down payments, closing costs, inspections, appraisals, title insurance, and similar costs on a home of up to four units in Georgia. A first-time buyer is someone who has not owned a home in the past three years, and money used for other purposes faces added tax and a 10 percent penalty, with some exceptions; it would take effect January 1, 2027.

bills.title: House Study Committee on the Use of Local Fees to Support Affordable Housing; create
bills.description: A RESOLUTION creating the House Study Committee on the Use of Local Fees to Support Affordable Housing; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Creates a House study committee on using local fees to support affordable housing.
bills.recap: This resolution creates a five-member House study committee, appointed by the Speaker, to look at how local government fees could better support affordable housing. The committee may recommend changes to local fees or new laws, and it ends on December 1, 2025. It does not change any fees or rules by itself. Realtors may want to watch it, since future proposals could affect local fees tied to housing and development.

bills.title: Georgia Association of REALTORS®; REALTOR® Day at the Dome; February 18, 2025; recognize
bills.description: A RESOLUTION commending the Georgia Association of REALTORS® and recognizing February 18, 2025, as REALTOR® Day at the Dome; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: House honors Georgia REALTORS® and names February 18, 2025, REALTOR® Day at the Dome.
bills.recap: This ceremonial resolution commends the Georgia Association of REALTORS® and recognizes February 18, 2025, as REALTOR® Day at the Dome, when more than 1,000 Realtors visit the state capitol. It highlights the group's 105-year history, its more than 48,000 members, its continuing education scholarships, and over $600,000 in 2024 disaster relief grants. It does not change any laws, rules, or requirements. Realtors may care because it publicly recognizes their profession and their advocacy for private property rights.

bills.title: Local government; adopt an alternative method of appraisal and assessment of real property located within the county for taxation; provide - CA
bills.description: A RESOLUTION proposing an amendment to the Constitution so as to provide that the governing authority of any county or consolidated government shall be authorized to adopt an alternative method of appraisal and assessment of real property located within such county for taxation; to provide for conditions and limitations; to provide for legislative findings; to provide for related matters; to provide for the submission of this amendment for ratification or rejection; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Lets counties tax real property based on its most recent sale price.
bills.recap: This proposed constitutional amendment would let any county or consolidated government switch to a new way of valuing real property for property taxes. Values would be locked at the January 1 digest value after adoption, then change only when the property sells (to the new purchase price) or gets a substantial improvement worth more than $50,000. Counties could adopt it by a majority vote, with an optional local referendum, and could not revoke it for at least five years. For Realtors, this matters because buyers could inherit a fresh, often higher tax bill at closing, while long-time owners would see stable taxes, which could affect pricing, affordability and how often people move.

bills.title: Georgia Keys for Heroes Amendment; provide by law - CA
bills.description: A RESOLUTION proposing an amendment to the Constitution of the State of Georgia so as to authorize the General Assembly to provide by law for a homestead exemption for an additional 100 percent disabled veterans' homestead exemption for the full assessed value of a homestead in certain circumstances; to authorize municipalities to seek supplementary funding to offset lost revenue from the homestead exemption; to provide for a short title; to provide for submission of this amendment for ratification or rejection; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Proposed amendment would fully exempt eligible disabled veterans' homes from property taxes.
bills.recap: This proposed constitutional amendment would let lawmakers create an extra homestead exemption covering the full assessed value of a home for disabled veterans. It would apply when a disabled veteran finances new home construction, inherits a home, or buys an existing home to use as a primary residence. Cities could also seek extra funding to make up for lost tax revenue. Voters would have to approve it, and it could make buying a home more affordable for disabled veteran clients.

bills.title: Property; common interest ownership structure; provisions - CA
bills.description: A RESOLUTION proposing an amendment to the Constitution so as to provide that any property owner in a condominium, property owners' development, or similar common interest ownership structure shall have standing to bring an action to challenge the unauthorized possession of other property located within the same condominium, property owners' development, or other common ownership interest structure; to provide for related matters; to provide for the submission of this amendment for ratification or rejection; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Constitutional amendment lets condo and HOA owners sue over squatters on neighboring property.
bills.recap: This proposed change to the Georgia Constitution would let any owner in a condo, HOA community, or similar shared-ownership development go to court to stop someone from occupying another home there without permission. Today, usually only the owner of the affected property can bring that kind of case. If the legislature passes it, voters would decide on the statewide ballot. Realtors may care because it gives neighbors a new tool against squatters, which could help protect property values and the appeal of homes in these communities.

bills.title: State government; rate of ad valorem tax assessment of a single family residential property; provisions - CA
bills.description: A RESOLUTION proposing an amendment to the Constitution of the State of Georgia so as to set the rate of the ad valorem tax assessment of a single-family residential property to 100 percent of its fair market value when such property is owned by a business enterprise with an interest in at least 100 single-family residential properties within this state which are used primarily for the purpose of generating rental income; to provide for the subclassification of business enterprise property for ad valorem taxation purposes; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Proposes taxing large corporate single-family rental owners at 100% of market value.
bills.recap: This proposed constitutional amendment would create a separate property tax class for businesses that own at least 100 single-family rental homes in Georgia. Their property would be assessed at 100 percent of fair market value, instead of the usual 40 percent, which would sharply raise their tax bills. The Department of Revenue could appraise these properties, and lawmakers could set up a separate appeals process. Voters would have to approve it, and Realtors may care because it could change how large investors view buying and holding rental homes, which may affect competition for starter homes.

bills.title: State and local government; assist with reducing Wall Street landlord ownership of residential properties to help this state flourish
bills.description: A RESOLUTION encouraging state and local governments to assist with reducing Wall Street landlord ownership of residential properties to help this state flourish; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: House resolution urges state and local governments to reduce Wall Street landlord home ownership.
bills.recap: This resolution encourages Georgia's state and local governments to help reduce ownership of homes by large Wall Street landlords, such as Blackstone and Invitation Homes. It urges local governments to use their full home rule powers to make housing more affordable. It is a statement of support only and does not create new laws, rules, or penalties. Realtors may want to watch it as a sign of growing interest in limiting institutional investors, which could later affect investor buyers, sellers, and rental markets.

bills.title: Local government; sales and use tax for purpose of providing property tax relief; authorize - CA
bills.description: A RESOLUTION proposing an amendment to the Constitution so as to provide that the governing authority of any county or consolidated government shall be authorized to impose a sales and use tax in such county or consolidated government for the purpose of providing property tax relief in such county or consolidated government; to provide for conditions and limitations; to provide for legislative findings; to provide for related matters; to provide for the submission of this amendment for ratification or rejection; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Proposes letting counties add a 1% sales tax to cut property taxes.
bills.recap: This proposed constitutional amendment would let any county or consolidated government ask local voters to approve a 1 percent sales tax for up to five years. Every dollar raised must go toward a dollar-for-dollar cut in property taxes on real property in that county. The tax would not count toward the usual cap on local sales taxes, and it would apply to food and beverages too. Realtors may care because lower property tax bills can make homes cheaper to own and easier to sell, though statewide voters must first approve the amendment and then each county's voters must approve the tax.

bills.title: Homeowner's Incentive Adjustment clause; remove cap on benefits - CA
bills.description: A RESOLUTION proposing an amendment to the Constitution so as to remove the cap on benefits granted pursuant to the Homeowner's Incentive Adjustment clause; to provide for related matters; to provide for the submission of this amendment for ratification or rejection; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: H: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute
H: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The House Ways and Means Committee rewrote this proposed constitutional amendment. It still exempts all homestead properties from local and school property taxes by January 1, 2032, with optional local sales taxes to make up the lost revenue. The new version adds that homes may still be taxed to pay off existing local bond debt. If voters reject a required sales tax referendum after 2037, local governments could tax homesteads again. The new local finance assessments are no longer tied to each parcel of real property, and unpaid assessments would no longer become a lien on the property. Instead, the state could let local governments temporarily suspend the owner's homestead exemptions or use other ways to collect. Property tax rollbacks would only be required for assessments that pay for services, not for capital projects. Both the school and local government millage referendum rules would now apply to increases in property tax revenue, and the law would have to account for inflation and growth. The ballot question now promises "100 percent" instead of "complete" property tax relief.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The new substitute drops the plan to fully exempt all homesteads from local property taxes by 2032. Instead, it would lower the taxable value of homesteads from 40 percent of appraised value to 10 percent, cutting it by 3 percent each year starting in 2027, and local governments could speed this up. It also drops voter approval of millage increases and the new local finance assessments, and cuts the local homestead sales tax cap for cities and counties from 3 percent to 1 percent. If a later referendum on that sales tax fails, homesteads go back to 40 percent. New pieces include a full homestead exemption for 100 percent disabled veterans who build, buy, or inherit a home, and letting the state use dedicated money, such as sales tax from data centers, to fund homeowner tax relief grants.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The House Rules Committee replaced the Ways and Means version with its own. The new version adds a rule for local governments that don't assess homes at 40 percent of value: they must cut their assessment rate by a total of 75 percent over 10 years, in equal steps starting in 2027. It also lets the state give grants to local governments and school systems to replace money lost from lower home assessments. The local homestead sales tax is now tied directly to making up that lost revenue, with the 1 percent local government share split based on each government's loss. The ballot question now mentions the 10-year phase-in and the goal of offsetting lost property tax revenue.

bills.headline: Constitutional amendment would cut homestead taxable value from 40% to 10% over ten years.
bills.recap: This proposed constitutional amendment would lower the taxable value of homestead properties from 40% to 10% of appraised value, dropping 3 points a year starting in 2027. Local governments could speed up the cut. To make up lost revenue, counties, cities and school systems could add a new local homestead option sales tax, up to 2% for schools and 1% for local governments. It also removes the $18,000 cap on the Homeowner's Incentive Adjustment and adds a full homestead exemption for 100% disabled veterans who buy, build or inherit a primary home. It also caps school sales taxes at a combined 2%. For Realtors, this could greatly lower property tax bills for owner-occupants and change the cost of owning a home, but voters must approve it first.

bills.title: General Assembly; provide by general law for local grant and adjustment programs; authorize
bills.description: A RESOLUTION proposing an amendment to the Constitution so as to remove the cap on benefits granted pursuant to the Homeowner's Incentive Adjustment clause; to authorize the General Assembly to provide by general law for local grant and adjustment programs; to provide for related matters; to provide for the submission of this amendment for ratification or rejection; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Proposed constitutional amendment lifts cap on homeowner tax relief and allows local relief programs.
bills.recap: This resolution asks voters to change Georgia's Constitution on the Homeowner's Incentive Adjustment, a property tax break for people who claim the statewide homestead exemption. It would remove the current cap, which limits the benefit to the value of an $18,000 homestead exemption or the homeowner's tax bill, whichever is lower. It would also let lawmakers allow cities, counties, and school systems to set up their own grant programs and use local tax money for added homeowner tax relief. Realtors may care because bigger tax breaks could lower ownership costs for buyers and current homeowners, but details would depend on later laws and voter approval.

bills.title: Ad valorem tax; business enterprises; rate of assessment of 1,000 or more single family residential properties used for rental income; provisions - CA
bills.description: A RESOLUTION proposing an amendment to the Constitution of the State of Georgia so as to provide that any business enterprise, including, but not limited to, private equity, having an interest in 1,000 or more single-family residential properties within this state used primarily for purposes of generating rental income shall be subject to an ad valorem tax assessment of 100 percent; to provide for related matters; to provide for submission of this amendment for ratification or rejection; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Proposes taxing big single-family rental owners at full value to cut homestead taxes.
bills.recap: This proposed constitutional amendment would let lawmakers create a separate property tax class for companies, including private equity, that own 1,000 or more single-family rental homes in Georgia. Those properties would be taxed on 100 percent of fair market value instead of the usual 40 percent. The extra tax money would first go toward lowering property tax bills on homesteads in the same area. Realtors may care because it could change the math for large investors buying homes and lower taxes for owner-occupants; voters would have to approve it on the ballot.

bills.title: Ad valorem tax; qualified low-income building projects may be classified as a separate class of property; provide - CA
bills.description: A RESOLUTION proposing an amendment to the Constitution so as to provide that qualified low-income building projects may be classified as a separate class of property for ad valorem property tax purposes, and different rates, methods, and assessment dates may be provided for such building projects; to provide for the submission of this amendment for ratification or rejection; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Proposes letting Georgia tax qualified low-income housing projects as a separate property class.
bills.recap: This proposed constitutional amendment would let lawmakers treat qualified low-income housing projects as their own class of property for property tax purposes. These are projects that meet the federal Low-Income Housing Tax Credit definition. If approved, the state could set different tax rates, valuation methods, and assessment dates for them, under rules set later by law. Voters would have to approve it on a statewide ballot. Realtors working with affordable housing developers, investors, or landlords may want to watch it, since it could change how these properties are valued and taxed.

bills.title: State-wide sales and use tax; property tax relief in counties or consolidated governments; provide - CA
bills.description: A RESOLUTION proposing an amendment to the Constitution so as to impose a 1 percent, state-wide sales and use tax for which the proceeds shall be distributed to the governing authorities of the counties and consolidated governments of this state on a population basis for the purpose of providing property tax relief in such counties or consolidated governments; to provide for conditions and limitations; to provide for legislative findings, determinations, and declarations; to provide for related matters; to provide for the submission of this amendment for ratification or rejection; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Proposes a 1% statewide sales tax to cut property taxes, homesteads first.
bills.recap: This proposed constitutional amendment would add a 1 percent statewide sales and use tax, including on food and beverages. The money would go to counties and consolidated governments based on population and must be used for a dollar-for-dollar cut in property taxes on real property. Homestead property taxes get reduced first, then all other real property, and any money left over can be used for other county purposes. Voters would have to approve it on the ballot. Realtors may care because lower property tax bills could make owning a home more affordable, though shoppers would pay more sales tax.

bills.title: General Assembly; assessment and taxation of affordable housing use property; provide - CA
bills.description: A RESOLUTION proposing an amendment to the Constitution so as to provide for assessment and taxation of affordable housing use property; to provide for definitions, methods of assessment and taxation, and conditions; to provide for related matters; to provide for the submission of this amendment for ratification or rejection; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Proposes constitutional amendment allowing special property tax treatment for affordable single-family homes.
bills.recap: This proposed change to the Georgia Constitution would let the General Assembly set up special property tax assessment for 'affordable home use property.' It covers single-family homes on up to five acres meant to be sold to a single low-income family. To get the tax break, the owner must sign a covenant that limits the home's purchase price so it stays affordable to lower-income households. If the covenant is broken within ten years, the tax savings would be taken back and other penalties could apply. Voters would have to approve it on a statewide ballot, and Realtors may see resale price limits on these homes.

bills.title: General Assembly; expend or authorize expenditure of public funds for Georgia Property Tax Fairness Fund; provide by law - CA
bills.description: A RESOLUTION proposing an amendment to the Constitution of the State of Georgia so as to provide that the General Assembly shall be authorized to provide by law to expend or authorize the expenditure of public funds for the Georgia Property Tax Fairness Fund without the need for benefit in return; to increase the cap on benefits granted pursuant to the Homeowner's Incentive Adjustment clause; to authorize the General Assembly to provide by general law for local grant and adjustment programs; to provide for related matters; to provide for submission of this amendment for ratification or rejection; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Proposed constitutional amendment creates a property tax relief fund and raises homeowner tax relief cap.
bills.recap: This proposed change to Georgia's Constitution would create a Georgia Property Tax Fairness Fund, paid for with tax collections from high-tech data centers and the insurance premium tax. The money would give refundable income tax credits to people living in "qualifying homes," which lawmakers would define later. It would also raise the cap on the Homeowner's Incentive Adjustment from the equivalent of an $18,000 homestead exemption to $150,000, and let local governments and school systems fund their own homeowner relief. Voters would have to approve it on a statewide ballot, and it could lower the yearly cost of owning a home for many Georgia homeowners.

bills.title: Condominium associations, property owners' associations, and any other corporations or voluntary entities; provide transparency to members; urge
bills.description: A RESOLUTION urging condominium associations, property owners' associations, and any other corporations or voluntary entities formed for the purpose of exercising the powers of a homeowners' or property owners' association governing a common interest community to provide transparency to members of such associations; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: House resolution urges HOAs and condo associations to share clear assessment and fee information.
bills.recap: This resolution asks condo associations, HOAs, and similar groups to be more open with their members about fees. It urges them to post contact info for account statement requests where it is easy to find, such as on a public website. It also urges them to quickly provide detailed statements listing assessments, due dates, amounts owed, and upcoming fees. It is non-binding and creates no new legal duties, but Realtors may care because buyers often don't know about fees or unpaid dues on a property, and better information can help avoid closing surprises and members losing homes over unpaid dues.

bills.title: Property Insurance Policies; notice required to be given a policyholder before the nonrenewal of his or her homeowners' insurance policy; increase the number of days
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Code Section 33-24-46 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to cancellation or nonrenewal of certain property insurance policies, so as to increase the number of days of notice required to be given a policyholder before the nonrenewal of his or her homeowners' insurance policy; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: S: Senate Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute
S: Senate Date Signed by Governor

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The Senate Insurance and Labor Committee replaced the original bill with a substitute. The core idea stays the same: insurers must give homeowners more days' notice before they choose not to renew a homeowners' insurance policy. The new version adds a start date of January 1, 2026. The longer notice rule would apply only to policies issued, delivered, or renewed in Georgia on or after that date.

versions.name: Engrossed
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed in this version. The only edits are formatting. The header now lists the sponsoring senators and marks the bill as passed by the Senate, and page labels were added. The rules on how much notice an insurer must give before not renewing a homeowners' policy are the same as in the committee version.

versions.name: Enrolled
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed between the Engrossed and Enrolled versions of SB 35. The only edits are document labels, such as the header code and the status line changing from "As Passed Senate" to "As Passed." The bill's rules on how much notice insurers must give before not renewing a homeowners' policy are the same as in the earlier version.

bills.headline: Insurers must give homeowners 60 days' notice, up from 30, before nonrenewing policies.
bills.recap: This law doubles the notice an insurer must give before refusing to renew a homeowners' insurance policy, from 30 days to 60 days. The notice must be mailed or delivered to the insured and to the lienholder, where applicable, and must state the reasons for nonrenewal. It takes effect January 1, 2026, for policies issued or renewed on or after that date. Realtors may care because more lead time helps homeowners and sellers find new coverage and avoid insurance gaps that could delay a sale or put a mortgage at risk.

bills.title: City of Cartersville; independent school district ad valorem taxes for educational purposes; provide a homestead exemption
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to provide a homestead exemption from City of Cartersville independent school district ad valorem taxes for educational purposes in an amount equal to the amount by which the current year assessed value of a homestead exceeds the adjusted base year assessed value of such homestead; to provide for definitions; to specify the terms and conditions of the exemption and the procedures relating thereto; to provide for applicability; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The Senate committee version makes one real change. For homeowners who first get this Cartersville school tax homestead exemption in 2026, the starting (base year) value is now their home's 2024 assessed value instead of the 2025 value. Using the earlier year could lock in a lower starting value for those owners. Everything else is formatting and header updates.

versions.name: Engrossed
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed between the committee substitute and the version that passed the Senate. The edits only update headers and labels: the bill now lists its sponsors (Senators Hufstetler and Setzler), is marked "As Passed Senate," and adds page labels. The homestead exemption for City of Cartersville school district taxes, its January 1, 2026 start date, and the local vote requirement are unchanged.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The House committee version adds a five-year sunset to the Cartersville school tax homestead exemption. The exemption would now apply only to tax years 2026 through 2030, ending December 31, 2030, instead of continuing with no end date. The ballot question for the November 2025 vote was also updated to tell voters about the five-year sunset. The rest of the bill, including how the exemption caps yearly increases in taxable home value, is unchanged.

versions.name: Enrolled
versions.changes: The final version moves the job of running this Cartersville school tax homestead exemption from the Bartow County tax commissioner to the City of Cartersville. The city now takes applications, sets the yearly inflation rate, picks the better exemption if a homeowner qualifies for more than one, and must be told if a homeowner is no longer eligible. The November 2025 vote is now run and paid for by the city and limited to voters in the Cartersville school district, and the ballot now names that district instead of the Bartow County school district. The exemption itself is unchanged: it still limits taxable value growth for 2026 through 2030 and still applies automatically to homeowners who had a homestead exemption in 2025.

bills.headline: Caps yearly school tax value increases on Cartersville homesteads at inflation, pending voter approval.
bills.recap: This bill creates a homestead exemption from Cartersville city school district taxes, so a home's taxable value for school taxes can only rise each year by the rate of inflation, plus the value of any major improvements. For homesteads first getting the break in 2026, the starting value is the 2024 assessed value, and current homestead holders get it automatically without a new application. The break needed approval from city school district voters in November 2025, and it would run from 2026 through 2030. It does not move to a new owner, so buyers start with a fresh base value, which matters when you explain tax bills to clients.

bills.title: Bartow County; school district ad valorem taxes for educational purposes; provide a homestead exemption
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to provide a homestead exemption from Bartow County school district ad valorem taxes for educational purposes in an amount equal to the amount by which the current year assessed value of a homestead exceeds the adjusted base year assessed value of such homestead; to provide for definitions; to specify the terms and conditions of the exemption and the procedures relating thereto; to provide for applicability; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

versions.name: Engrossed
versions.changes: The only change is a new label marking the bill "As Passed Senate." The Senate approved SB 83 with no changes to its wording. The bill still proposes a homestead exemption from Bartow County school district property taxes for educational purposes.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The House local legislation committee's substitute adds a sunset to the Bartow County school tax homestead exemption. The exemption would now apply only to tax years 2026 through 2030 instead of having no end date. The ballot question was also updated to tell voters the exemption has a five-year sunset. Everything else, including the referendum and the January 1, 2026 start date, stays the same.

versions.name: Enrolled
versions.changes: Nothing of substance changed between the committee substitute and the enrolled version. The only edits are labels: the header now reads "Senate Bill 83, As Passed" with the sponsors' names (Senators Hufstetler and Setzler), and the page footers drop "(SUB)." The Bartow County school tax homestead exemption reads the same as in the committee version.

bills.headline: Caps yearly school tax value increases on Bartow County homesteads to inflation, pending voter approval.
bills.recap: This bill creates a homestead exemption from Bartow County school district taxes that limits how much a home's taxable value can rise each year to the rate of inflation, plus any value from major improvements. It applies to tax years 2026 through 2030 and only takes effect if Bartow County school district voters approve it in a November 2025 referendum. Homeowners who already had a homestead exemption in 2025 get it automatically, while new owners must apply, and the benefit does not transfer to a buyer. Realtors should know that buyers will start with a new base value, so their school taxes may be higher than the seller's.

bills.title: Landlord and Tenant; Code Section 44-7-19; repeal
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Article 1 of Chapter 7 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to landlord and tenant in general, so as to repeal Code Section 44-7-19, relating to restrictions on rent regulation by local governments; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Repeals Georgia's state ban on local rent control rules.
bills.recap: This bill would repeal Code Section 44-7-19, the Georgia law that stops cities and counties from regulating rents. The bill itself does not create rent control. It would remove the state ban and leave the door open for local governments to pass their own rent rules. That could affect landlords, investors, renters, and the value of rental properties in areas that choose to act, so agents who work with investment property should watch it.

bills.title: Specialized Land Transactions; protections of homeowners in community associations; provide
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 3 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to regulation of specialized land transactions, so as to provide for protections of homeowners in community associations; to provide for the monitoring of elections for boards of directors for community associations; to provide for annual registration of community associations and related fees; to provide for applicability; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: S: Senate Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The Senate committee version changes the HOA and condo foreclosure rules. The original bill barred association foreclosure on liens under $2,000; the new version instead bars foreclosure when the lien is less than the total assessments charged on the unit in the past 12 months. Foreclosure on fines alone is still barred. The new version also bars the association, its related companies, and any current or former board member from buying the unit at the foreclosure sale, and it gives owners 180 days instead of 120 to buy back (redeem) the home after the sale. Because associations can no longer buy at these sales, the separate payoff rules for association-purchased units were removed, leaving one set of redemption costs that applies to every buyer. The rest of the bill is unchanged, including the hardship assessment waivers, the new Community Association Ombudsman, and the $25-per-unit annual registration fee.

bills.headline: Limits HOA and condo foreclosures and creates a state ombudsman for community associations.
bills.recap: This bill limits when HOAs and condo associations can foreclose on a home over unpaid dues. They could not foreclose over fines alone, or for less than $2,000 or less than a year of assessments, and the association and its board members could not buy the home at the sale. Owners would get 180 days after a foreclosure sale to buy the home back, and newer associations would have to waive dues for at least 12 months for owners who become disabled with financial hardship or who die with an insolvent estate. It also creates a state Community Association Ombudsman to handle complaints and monitor board elections, paid for by an annual $25-per-unit registration fee on associations. Realtors should note the added protections for owners in HOA and condo communities, possible fee pass-throughs to owners, and the 180-day buyback period on HOA foreclosure sales.

bills.title: Manufactured or Mobile Homes; limited exceptions to circumstances under which a manufactured home shall become real property; provide
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Subpart 1 of Part 4 of Article 2 of Chapter 2 of Title 8 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to general provisions for manufactured or mobile homes, so as to provide for limited exceptions to circumstances under which a manufactured home shall become real property; to provide for preservation of rights and remedies of prior holders of a lien or security interest in certain manufactured homes; to provide for notice and application requirements; to provide for related matters; to provide for an effective date and applicability; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: S: Senate Date Signed by Governor

versions.name: Engrossed
versions.changes: The only change is a label noting that the bill passed the Senate. The wording of the bill itself did not change. The rules on when a manufactured or mobile home becomes real property, and the limited exceptions, are the same as in the introduced version.

versions.name: Enrolled
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed between these two versions. The only edit is in the header, where "AS PASSED SENATE" became "AS PASSED." That shows the bill passed both chambers in final form. The rules on when a manufactured or mobile home becomes real property stay the same.

bills.headline: Changes how manufactured homes become real property and protects existing lenders' rights.
bills.recap: Under this law, only the homeowner, not every lienholder, must sign and file the Certificate of Permanent Location that turns a manufactured home into real property. A lender who held a lien on the home before the conversion keeps its personal property rights and priority until the loan is paid off. That lender can repossess and remove the home without the landowner's or mortgage holder's consent, and it or a buyer from it can get a new title. Realtors listing or selling land with a converted manufactured home should check for unpaid prior liens on the home itself, since they can survive the conversion; the law applies to contracts made on or after July 1, 2025.

bills.title: "Georgia Supporting those Who Sacrificed for Service Act"; enact
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Part 1 of Article 2 of Chapter 5 of Title 48 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to property tax exemptions, so as to increase the amount of a state-wide homestead exemption for certain totally disabled veterans; to create new state-wide homestead exemptions for certain partially disabled veterans and partially or totally disabled first responders; to provide for definitions; to provide for related matters; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a short title; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, and automatic repeal; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: S: Senate Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The Senate Finance Committee changed who counts as a disabled first responder for the new homestead tax exemptions. Before, police officers, firefighters, and public EMTs qualified if they got line-of-duty disability payments under a state law (Code Section 45-9-85). Now they qualify if they received workers' compensation benefits in Georgia for a partial or total permanent disability suffered in the line of duty. To apply, they now file written proof from the State Board of Workers' Compensation instead of a letter from the Department of Administrative Services. The exemption amounts, the veterans' provisions, and the November 2026 statewide vote are unchanged.

versions.name: Engrossed
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed in this version. The Engrossed copy only adds formatting, such as the sponsor names, an "As Passed Senate" label, and page headers. The property tax exemption rules and other content are the same as in the committee substitute.

bills.headline: Expands property tax homestead exemptions for disabled veterans and disabled first responders.
bills.recap: This bill would make totally disabled veterans fully exempt from property taxes on their home, up from the current fixed-dollar exemption, and would extend this to their unremarried surviving spouses or minor children. It creates a new exemption for partially disabled veterans equal to their VA disability percentage times the home's assessed value. It also creates new exemptions for police, firefighters, and public EMTs disabled in the line of duty: 100% for total disability and 50% for partial disability. Voters must approve it statewide in November 2026, with an effective date of January 1, 2027, so Realtors working with these buyers should note the possible large tax savings that could affect affordability.

bills.title: Gordon County; school district ad valorem taxes for educational purposes; provide homestead exemption
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to provide a homestead exemption from Gordon County school district ad valorem taxes for educational purposes in an amount equal to the amount by which the current year assessed value of a homestead exceeds the adjusted base year assessed value of such homestead; to provide for definitions; to specify the terms and conditions of the exemption and the procedures relating thereto; to provide for applicability; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

versions.name: Engrossed
versions.changes: The only change is a new label showing the bill passed the Senate. The wording of the Gordon County school tax homestead exemption is the same as when it was introduced. For agents, nothing about the exemption itself is different. The bill has simply moved forward in the process.

bills.headline: Caps yearly school tax value increases on Gordon County homesteads at inflation, pending voter approval.
bills.recap: This bill creates a homestead exemption from Gordon County school district taxes that limits how much a home's taxable value can rise each year to the rate of inflation. Increases from improvements or additions still count, and the cap does not apply to school bond debt taxes or to county, city, or state taxes. For homeowners claiming it for 2026, the starting value is the 2024 assessed value, and the exemption does not transfer to a new owner. Gordon County voters must approve it in November 2025. For Realtors, it means long-time owners may see steadier tax bills, while buyers should expect taxes to reset to current value after a sale.

bills.title: Consumer Transactions; increased consumer protection for homeowners entering into contracts with contractors following natural disasters; provide
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Code Section 10-1-393 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to unfair or deceptive practices in consumer transactions unlawful and examples, so as to provide increased consumer protection for homeowners entering into contracts with contractors following natural disasters; to provide for certain contractual requirements; to provide for notice language; to amend Code Section 33-6-5 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to unfair methods of competition and unfair or deceptive acts or practices, so as to prohibit the assignment of benefits in certain circumstances; to provide for definitions; to provide for related matters; to provide for legislative findings; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: S: Senate Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute
H: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute
S: Senate Agreed House Amend or Sub
S: Senate Date Signed by Governor

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The Senate Insurance and Labor Committee made two small changes to the bill. First, it removed the phrase "according to a reasonable-person standard" from the list of unfair contractor practices after a natural disaster. That means those listed actions, such as not starting work within one year, would count as violations without that extra test. Second, a contractor whose contract is canceled can now collect only a "reasonable" amount for emergency services, not just any amount due. The rest of the changes are formatting only.

versions.name: Engrossed
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed between the committee version and the version passed by the Senate. The only edits are formatting: new header labels, the sponsor names, an "As Passed Senate" note, and page markers. The rules for contractors working on homes after natural disasters and for insurers stay the same.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The House Agriculture and Consumer Affairs Committee's version adds a new unfair practice for contractors after a natural disaster: doing work that does not meet state minimum building codes or accredited industry standards. It also defines 'natural disaster' directly in the insurance section that bars policies allowing homeowners to assign insurance proceeds to a contractor within one year of a disaster. The new version sets start dates. The insurance rule takes effect January 1, 2026, for policies issued or renewed on or after that date, and the rest of the bill takes effect July 1, 2025.

versions.name: Enrolled
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed between the House committee substitute and the final enrolled version of SB 201. The only edits are labels: the header now lists the Senate sponsors and says "As Passed," and the page footers drop the "(SUB)" tag. The bill's protections for homeowners hiring contractors after natural disasters stay exactly as they were in the committee version.

bills.headline: Adds protections for homeowners hiring contractors to repair natural disaster damage.
bills.recap: For one year after a natural disaster, contractors repairing disaster damage to a home commit an unfair practice if they fail to substantially start work within a year, do substandard work, ignore state building codes, or take an assignment of the homeowner's insurance money. Homeowners can cancel the contract until midnight on the fifth business day after their insurer says all or part of the claim is not covered, and contractors must give a boldface cancellation notice and form. Contractors can still collect a reasonable amount for emergency work the homeowner approved in writing. Starting January 1, 2026, insurers cannot sell homeowner's policies that allow assigning proceeds to a contractor within a year of a disaster; Realtors may see this affect how storm-damaged homes get repaired before a sale.

bills.title: Condominiums; maximum amount of insurance deductibles payable by unit owners; remove the limitation
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Article 3 of Chapter 3 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to condominiums, so as to remove the limitation on the maximum amount of insurance deductibles payable by unit owners; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.lastAction: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute

timeline.text: S: Senate Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute
S: Senate Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute
H: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The committee version no longer removes the cap on how much of the association's insurance deductible can be charged to a single condo owner. Instead, it raises the cap from $5,000 to $25,000 per covered loss. It also adds a new rule: associations must promptly notify all unit owners in writing of any major change to the master policy deductible. The notice goes by first-class mail, or in person, by email, or by fax if the owner agrees in writing.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The only change is the document tracking code in the header, updated from a 2025 draft number (25 LC 46 1174S) to a 2026 draft number (26 LC 46 1447S). The wording of the bill itself did not change. Rules on condo insurance deductibles paid by unit owners, and on owner votes not to restore a damaged unit, stay the same as in the earlier version.

versions.name: Engrossed
versions.changes: No meaningful changes were made to the bill's content between the committee version and the version that passed the Senate. The updates only add the sponsors' names (Senators Still, Anavitarte, Harbin, Harbison, and Walker III), mark the bill as passed by the Senate, and add page labels. The rules on condo insurance deductibles paid by unit owners are the same as in the committee version.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The House Insurance Committee turned this condo bill into a broader package called the "Real Estate Security and Title Act." The condo change stays the same: the most an association can charge one unit owner toward the master policy deductible rises from $5,000 to $25,000 per loss, and owners must get written notice of big deductible changes. New parts let the lender or holder of the loan being foreclosed make a credit bid at a foreclosure sale instead of paying cash or certified funds. Other new parts make government offices hide home addresses, parcel numbers, and personal phone numbers of judges and their spouses, with an exception for title insurers and their attorneys, and set new experience and residency rules for special masters in quiet title cases.

bills.headline: Raises condo owner deductible cap to $25,000 and updates foreclosure, title, and judge privacy rules.
bills.recap: This bill, called the Real Estate Security and Title Act, raises the most a condo association can charge one unit owner toward the master policy insurance deductible from $5,000 to $25,000 per loss. Associations must also notify owners in writing of any big change in the master policy deductible. The bill lets the lender foreclosing on a property make a credit bid at a judicial sale instead of paying cash, and it sets stricter experience rules for special masters in some quiet title cases. It also expands privacy protections that hide judges' and their spouses' home addresses and parcel numbers in public records, while still letting title insurers and their attorneys get full copies for title work, so Realtors may want to remind condo buyers and owners to check their HO-6 coverage.

bills.title: City of Dalton; independent school district ad valorem taxes for educational purposes; provide a homestead exemption
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to provide a homestead exemption from City of Dalton independent school district ad valorem taxes for educational purposes in an amount equal to the amount by which the current year assessed value of a homestead exceeds the adjusted base year assessed value of such homestead; to provide for definitions; to specify the terms and conditions of the exemption and the procedures relating thereto; to provide for applicability; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed between these two versions. The only edit is a header label, which went from "AS PASSED SENATE" to "AS PASSED" to show the bill cleared both chambers. The Dalton school tax homestead exemption itself reads the same as before.

bills.headline: Caps yearly taxable value growth on Dalton homes for city school taxes, pending voter approval.
bills.recap: This bill creates a homestead exemption from City of Dalton school district taxes that limits how much a home's taxable value can rise each year to the rate of inflation. The base year is 2024 for owners first getting it in 2026, and owners with a 2025 homestead exemption get it automatically. Improvements like additions still raise the value, and the benefit does not transfer to a new owner, so buyers start with a fresh base year. It only takes effect if Dalton school district voters approve it in November 2025, and it would start January 1, 2026.

bills.title: Whitfield County; school district ad valorem taxes for educational purposes; provide a homestead exemption
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to provide a homestead exemption from Whitfield County school district ad valorem taxes for educational purposes in an amount equal to the amount by which the current year assessed value of a homestead exceeds the adjusted base year assessed value of such homestead; to provide for definitions; to specify the terms and conditions of the exemption and the procedures relating thereto; to provide for applicability; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: S: Senate Date Signed by Governor

versions.name: Engrossed
versions.changes: The only change is a label noting the bill passed the Senate. The wording of the Whitfield County school tax homestead exemption is the same as when it was introduced. Nothing in the bill's substance changed.

versions.name: Enrolled
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed between these two versions. The only edit is a header label, from "As Passed Senate" to "As Passed," which shows the bill cleared both chambers. The Whitfield County school tax homestead exemption reads the same in both versions.

bills.headline: Caps yearly taxable value increases on Whitfield County homes for school taxes, if voters approve.
bills.recap: This bill creates a homestead exemption from Whitfield County school district taxes that limits how much a home's taxable value can rise each year, tied to inflation. The base year is 2024 value for owners who get the exemption in 2026, and owners who already had a homestead exemption in 2025 get it automatically. It covers up to five acres, adds value for major improvements, and does not transfer to a new buyer, so a buyer's taxes may reset to current value. It needed approval by Whitfield County voters in November 2025 and would start January 1, 2026.

bills.title: "Quality Basic Education Act,"; certain students whose parents or guardians are on active duty are eligible for enrollment in the public school of the attendance zone in which they intend to reside; provide
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Code Section 20-2-150 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to eligibility for enrollment under the "Quality Basic Education Act," so as to provide that certain students whose parents or guardians are on active duty in the United States armed forces are eligible for enrollment in the public school of the attendance zone in which they intend to reside regardless of whether they have entered into a lease, purchased a house, or otherwise secured housing within such attendance zone; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: S: Senate Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute
H: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The committee version keeps the main idea: children of active-duty military families can enroll in the school for the attendance zone where they plan to live, using their military orders, before they have a lease or home there. The change is about what happens if the family ends up living somewhere else. The family must move the student to the school where they actually live and show proof of that address by the end of the current school year. High school juniors and seniors may stay at their current school until they graduate, even if the family's address changes.

versions.name: Engrossed
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed between these two versions. The engrossed version only updates header labels, adds the sponsor names, and marks the bill as passed by the Senate. The rule letting children of active-duty military parents enroll in their future attendance-zone school before moving in stays the same.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The House Education Committee's version makes early school enrollment for military children provisional. Families still may enroll a child in the school zone where they plan to live, before they have a lease or home, by showing military orders. Now they must give the principal written proof within 90 days that they have set up residency, or made enough good-faith efforts to do so, in that zone. If they don't, the child must move to the school where the family actually lives at the end of the 90-day period, instead of at the end of the school year as in the Senate version.

bills.headline: Lets military kids enroll in a school zone before their family secures housing there.
bills.recap: This bill lets children of active-duty military parents with orders to move into or within Georgia enroll in the school for the zone where they plan to live, even before signing a lease or buying a home. Enrollment is provisional, and parents must show within 90 days that they have moved in or made good faith efforts to do so. If they end up living elsewhere, the child must switch to the school where they actually live, though high school juniors and seniors may stay put until graduation. Realtors working with relocating military families may find this gives buyers and renters more time to find the right home in their preferred school zone.

bills.title: "Fair Business Practices Act of 1975,"; rent pricing for residential properties; encourage transparency and fairness
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Part 2 of Article 15 of Chapter 1 of Title 10 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to the "Fair Business Practices Act of 1975," so as to encourage transparency and fairness with respect to rent pricing for residential properties; to prohibit landlords from failing to disclose the total rental price of any residential property and charging deceptive fees for any residential property; to provide for definitions; to provide for statutory construction; to provide for related matters; to provide for an effective date and applicability; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Requires landlords to show total rent upfront and bans deceptive rental fees.
bills.recap: This bill makes it an unfair business practice for landlords to advertise or quote rent without clearly showing the total price, including all mandatory and government fees. Landlords must disclose that total before signing a lease or taking payment, and the total must be shown more prominently than other pricing. It bans 'deceptive fees,' such as fees above actual cost, fees for unused services, fees for things landlords must already provide, fees for not using a preferred vendor, or fees not written in the lease. It covers long-term rentals plus hotels and short-term or vacation rentals, so Realtors who list or manage rentals would need to update ads and fee practices.

bills.title: Department of Human Services; adopt and implement affordable family housing assistance programs; authorize local governments
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapters 2 and 3 of Title 49 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to Department of Human Services and county and district departments, boards, and directors of family and children services, respectively, so as to authorize local governments to adopt and implement affordable family housing assistance programs; to provide for reporting requirements; to provide for the determination of median annual gross household incomes; to authorize the promulgation of rules and regulations; to provide definitions; to provide for related matters; to provide for an effective date; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Lets Georgia cities and counties create state-approved affordable family housing assistance programs.
bills.recap: Starting January 1, 2026, cities and counties could choose to set up affordable family housing programs, funded through a separate local trust fund and approved by the state Division of Family and Children Services. Programs could give loans, grants, or guarantees to builders who create or fix up affordable homes or apartments. Builders getting help would have to reserve at least 40% of units for rent to low-income families and 20% for very low-income families, and programs could also help these families pay security deposits and first and last month's rent. Realtors may see more affordable rental supply and more qualified renters in areas that adopt these programs.

bills.title: Landlord and Tenant; requiring tenants to provide income information; prohibit
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Article 1 of Chapter 7 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to general provisions regarding landlord and tenant, so as to prohibit landlords from requiring tenants to provide income information; to authorize tenants to withhold rent payments under certain conditions; to provide for liability of landlords; to prohibit certain late fees; to provide for habitability; to prohibit retaliation; to provide for fair housing; to provide for definitions; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Adds tenant repair rights, rent withholding, voucher protections, and source-of-income fair housing rules.
bills.recap: SB 272 defines a home 'fit for human habitation' as one with working electrical, plumbing, hot and cold water, safe appliances, working detectors, no mold, and no pests. It also adds cooling to the utilities a landlord must provide. If a landlord ignores two repair notices for a serious problem, tenants could withhold rent, make the repair and deduct the cost, or end the lease. Ten days is presumed to be a reasonable time to fix the problem, and landlords could not retaliate against tenants who use these rights. Landlords also could not require voucher holders to earn three times the rent, and the bill adds 'source of income' as a protected class in sales, rentals, ads, and MLS access, which affects agents and property managers directly.

bills.title: Peach County; ad valorem taxes for county purposes; provide a homestead exemption
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to provide a homestead exemption from Peach County ad valorem taxes for county purposes in the amount of 10 percent of the assessed value of the homestead for residents of that county; to provide for definitions; to specify the terms and conditions of the exemption and the procedures relating thereto; to provide for applicability; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: S: Senate Date Signed by Governor

versions.name: Engrossed
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed between the introduced and engrossed versions. The only difference is a new label noting the bill passed the Senate. The Peach County homestead exemption itself is the same as when it was introduced.

versions.name: Enrolled
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed between these two versions. The only edit is the header label, which went from "As Passed Senate" to "As Passed" to show the bill cleared both chambers. The Peach County homestead exemption itself is the same.

bills.headline: Creates a 10 percent homestead exemption from Peach County taxes, if voters approve.
bills.recap: This law gives Peach County homeowners a property tax break equal to 10 percent of their home's assessed value on county taxes. It does not cover school, state, city, or county bond debt taxes, and it stacks on top of other homestead exemptions. Owners must apply once with the tax commissioner, and it renews each year while they live in the home. It only takes effect if Peach County voters approve it in November 2025, starting with the 2026 tax year, so Realtors may want to tell buyers to file for their homestead exemption.

bills.title: Enforcement Methods; investigations or inspections of certain residential rental property when there is a reasonable suspicion of a code violation; provide
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Code Section 36-74-30 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to other enforcement methods and probable cause for investigation required, so as to provide for investigations or inspections of certain residential rental property when there is a reasonable suspicion of a code violation; to provide for the registration of certain residential rental property; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Lets local governments inspect larger rentals on reasonable suspicion and register big landlords' properties.
bills.recap: Right now, Georgia local governments can only inspect rental property when there is probable cause of a code violation, and they cannot require rental registration at all. This bill would let them inspect rental properties with four or more units, with adequate notice to the owner, when there is a 'reasonable suspicion' of a code violation, which is a lower bar. It would also let local governments require registration of rental property owned directly or indirectly by anyone who owns at least 20 rental properties in Georgia. Realtors who work with investors, multifamily owners, or property managers should note the possible new inspections and registration steps.

bills.title: Contracts; certain agreements involving parallel pricing coordination as unenforceable contracts in general restraint of trade with respect to residential rental properties; prohibit
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 8 of Title 13 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to illegal and void contracts generally, so as to prohibit certain agreements involving parallel pricing coordination as unenforceable contracts in general restraint of trade with respect to residential rental properties; to provide for a civil penalty; to provide for educational materials informing residents in this state of the provisions of this Act; to provide for statutory construction; to provide for an effective date and applicability; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Bans landlords from using shared rent-pricing software or agreements to coordinate rents.
bills.recap: This bill makes it illegal for two or more landlords to agree to raise, lower, or hold rents, including through software or AI tools that collect rent and vacancy data from several landlords and recommend prices. Any such agreement would be void, and anyone who takes part, including property managers and software providers, could face a $1,000 civil penalty per violation, enforced by the Attorney General or district attorneys. The Department of Community Affairs would publish materials explaining the law to residents, and actions under affordable or low-income housing programs are exempt. Realtors who manage rentals or advise landlord clients should review any pricing tools they use, since 'landlord' includes agents and property managers.

bills.title: "Georgia Civil Rights Act of 2025"; enact
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Titles 8, 10, 34, 35, 45, and 50 of the O.C.G.A., relating to buildings and housing, commerce and trade, labor and industrial relations, law enforcement officers and agencies, public officers and employees, and state government, respectively, so as to provide comprehensive state civil rights laws protecting individuals from discrimination in housing, public accommodations, and employment on the basis of race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, age, disability, familial status, or national origin; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Adds sexual orientation, gender identity, and age to Georgia's fair housing protections.
bills.recap: This bill creates a broad state civil rights law covering housing, public places, and jobs. In housing, it adds sexual orientation, gender identity, and age to the groups protected under Georgia's Fair Housing Act. That covers selling, renting, lending, appraisals, advertising, and access to MLS and Realtor organizations. Realtors, brokers, landlords, and lenders would need to update their practices and ads to avoid treating anyone differently on these grounds. If passed, it would take effect January 1, 2026.

versions.changes: The committee version changes one key point: the new Atlanta school tax homestead exemption would now be added on top of any other homestead exemption the owner already gets on Atlanta school district taxes, instead of replacing them. This makes the exemption more valuable for eligible homeowners, since they would not have to give up an existing exemption to get this one. The sponsor list also changed, with Senator Orrock added and Senator Halpern no longer listed. The rest of the bill, including the January 1, 2026 start date and the local voter approval requirement, is unchanged.

The updates are formatting only: the header now says "As Passed Senate," page labels were added, and the sponsor list changed slightly (Senator Halpern was added and Senator Orrock is no longer listed). The homestead exemption, the January 1, 2026 start date, and the local election requirement all stay the same.

bills.headline: Creates a $50,000 Atlanta school tax homestead exemption for homeowners 65 and older.
bills.recap: This bill gives Atlanta homeowners age 65 or older a $50,000 exemption on the assessed value of their home for Atlanta Public Schools property taxes. Total exemptions are capped at about $487.8 million a year, and if claims go over that, each senior's break is reduced proportionately. Seniors must apply once, and it renews each year as long as they live in the home. The exemption needed voter approval in a November 2025 referendum and, if approved, starts January 1, 2026. It does not cover state, county, or city taxes, and Realtors working with older Atlanta buyers and sellers may want to mention it.

bills.headline: Freezes Chickamauga school tax assessments on homesteads at base-year value, pending voter approval.
bills.recap: This bill creates a homestead exemption from City of Chickamauga school district taxes that covers any rise in a home's assessed value above its base year value. In effect, it freezes the school-tax value of a homestead (up to five acres) while the owner lives there, though new improvements or added land are still taxed. Owners must apply once, and the exemption renews automatically, but a new owner gets a new base year. Voters must approve it in November 2025, and it would start January 1, 2026. Realtors may want to note that buyers will reset the base year, so their school taxes may be higher than the seller's.

bills.recap: This bill creates a homestead exemption from City of Trion independent school district taxes that covers any rise in a home's assessed value above its base-year value.
