Owners must apply once with the City of Trion, and the exemption renews automatically while they live in the home. Voters in the school district must approve it in November 2025 for it to start January 1, 2026. bills.headline: Freezes Chattooga County school tax assessments on homesteads at base-year value, pending voter approval.
bills.recap: This bill creates a new homestead exemption from Chattooga County school district taxes that blocks increases in a home's assessed value above its base year value. The base year is the year before the current owner first gets the exemption, so the freeze resets when a home sells. New improvements and added land are still taxed, the exemption covers up to five acres, and surviving spouses keep it. Voters must approve it in November 2025, and it would start January 1, 2026. Realtors should note that buyers would start a new base year, so a seller's tax bill may not match what a buyer will pay.

bills.headline: Freezes Dade County school taxes on homesteads at base-year assessed value, if voters approve.
bills.recap: This bill creates a homestead exemption from Dade County school district taxes that covers any rise in a home's assessed value above its base-year value. In practice, it freezes the school tax value of a homestead, except for new improvements or added land, on up to five contiguous acres. Owners must apply once with the Dade County tax commissioner, and the exemption renews automatically and continues for a surviving spouse who stays in the home. It needed voter approval in a November 2025 referendum and, if approved, applies starting January 1, 2026. Realtors should note that the base year resets for each new owner, so buyers may face higher school taxes than sellers paid.

bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to provide a homestead exemption from Jasper County school district ad valorem taxes for educational purposes in the amount of $40,000.00 of the assessed value of the homestead for residents of that school district who are 65 years of age or older; to provide for definitions; to specify the terms and conditions of the exemption and the procedures relating thereto; to provide for applicability; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

bills.headline: Creates a $40,000 school tax homestead exemption for Jasper County seniors 65 and older.
bills.recap: This bill gives Jasper County homeowners age 65 or older a $40,000 exemption off the assessed value of their home for school district property taxes. The home can include up to five acres, and owners must apply once with the county tax commissioner, after which it renews automatically. It replaces, rather than adds to, any other school tax homestead exemption, and it does not affect state, county, or city taxes. Voters must approve it in November 2025, and it would start January 1, 2026, which could lower costs for older owners and matter to agents working with senior buyers and sellers there.

bills.title: Paulding County; school district ad valorem taxes for educational purposes; provide a homestead exemption
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to provide a homestead exemption from Paulding County school district ad valorem taxes for educational purposes in an amount equal to the amount by which the current year assessed value of a homestead exceeds the adjusted base year assessed value of such homestead; to provide for definitions; to specify the terms and conditions of the exemption and the procedures relating thereto; to provide for applicability; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

bills.headline: Caps yearly school tax value increases on Paulding County homesteads at inflation, if voters approve.
bills.recap: This bill creates a homestead exemption from Paulding County school district taxes. Each year, a home's taxable value for school taxes can rise only by the inflation rate, plus the value of improvements like additions. For homeowners who first get it in 2027, the starting value is the home's 2024 assessed value. Homeowners who already have a homestead exemption for 2026 get it automatically. The break does not transfer to a new buyer, who starts over at the current value. A surviving spouse who has not remarried keeps it. Voters must approve it at the 2026 primary, and it would start January 1, 2027. Realtors should note that buyers may face higher school tax bills than the sellers paid.

bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to provide a homestead exemption from Polk County school district ad valorem taxes for educational purposes in the amount of the greater of 50 percent or $60,000.00 of the assessed value of the homestead for residents of that school district who are 65 years of age or older, in the amount of the greater of 75 percent or $80,000.00 of the assessed value of the homestead for residents of that school district who are 70 years of age or older, and in the amount of the full assessed value of the homestead for residents of that school district who are 77 years of age or older, all with a temporary cap on the annual aggregate exemption amount; to provide for definitions; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

versions.name: Engrossed
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed in the bill's content between the Introduced and Engrossed versions. The only difference is a new label showing the bill passed the Senate. The Polk County school tax homestead exemption reads the same as before.

bills.headline: Creates senior school tax homestead exemptions in Polk County, pending a local vote.
bills.recap: This bill cuts Polk County school property taxes for seniors on their homes, if local voters approve it in November 2025. Owners 65 to 69 get the greater of 50 percent or $60,000 of assessed value exempt. Owners 70 to 76 get the greater of 75 percent or $80,000 exempt, and owners 77 and older pay no school tax on homes worth up to $500,000. Total exemptions are capped at $150 million in 2026, with cuts shared if claims go over, and Realtors working with older buyers or sellers in Polk County may find these savings a selling point.

bills.title: Property Owners' Associations; authorization of liens and use of assessments; provide
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Article 6 of Chapter 3 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to property owners' associations, so as to provide for authorization of liens and use of assessments; to provide for registration of property owners' associations; to provide for rules and regulations regarding administrative hearings and escrow of funds; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Limits HOA lien foreclosures, requires HOA registration, and creates a state dispute hearing process.
bills.recap: This bill makes it harder for property owners' associations (HOAs) to foreclose on a lot for unpaid dues. The association would need written approval from the Secretary of State first, and the unpaid amount would have to be at least $4,000 instead of $2,000. HOAs also could not use assessment money to pay foreclosure costs. HOAs would have to register with the Secretary of State and update that registration every year. The Secretary of State would set up hearings for owner-HOA disputes, with the filing fee paid back to the winner. The Department of Banking and Finance would set rules for how HOAs hold funds in escrow. Realtors may care because this affects HOA-governed communities, owner protections, and what buyers can learn about an association.

bills.title: Ad Valorem Taxation; make the state-wide base year homestead exemption mandatory for all political subdivisions

timeline.text: S: Senate Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute
H: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute
H: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The Senate Finance Committee's version keeps the original changes: it makes the statewide base year homestead exemption mandatory and removes the homestead exemption condition for calling a special district sales tax (FLOST) vote. It adds a new section on how that sales tax money lowers property taxes. Each year, the local roll-back rate must be cut by the millage equal to the net sales tax money received in the prior tax year or through June 30 of the current year. Tax bills must still show how much property tax was reduced, and the state commissioner cannot certify a local tax digest if the money is not used only for tax relief.

versions.name: Engrossed
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed between the committee version and the version that passed the Senate. The only edits are labels: the bill now lists its sponsors, Senator Hufstetler and others, is marked "As Passed Senate," and has updated page headers. The rules on the statewide base year homestead exemption are the same as in the committee version.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The House Ways & Means substitute turns a short Senate bill into a broad property tax overhaul called the "Homeownership Opportunity and Market Equalization Act of 2026." It still makes the statewide base-year homestead exemption mandatory, but it no longer applies where a local base-year or adjusted base-year homestead exemption is already in effect. Starting January 1, 2028, the LOST, HOST, EHOST, and RHOST sales taxes convert into a new 1% Local Homestead Option Sales Tax (LHOST) for homestead property tax relief, FLOST can be adopted by resolution instead of a referendum, and the local sales tax cap becomes 5%. Starting 2028, local governments and school boards that raise property tax revenue by more than 3% or inflation (not counting growth) need voter approval or a local Act of the General Assembly, and votes on revenue increases are limited to certain election dates. For homeowners, the bill sets a 50% penalty for failing to report losing homestead eligibility, bars back-billing for homestead mistakes that were not the owner's fault, adds a statewide homestead database, and ends the estimated roll-back rate shown on assessment notices.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The new House committee version drops the plan to convert local sales taxes (LOST, HOST, EHOST, RHOST) into a new Local Homestead Option Sales Tax. It also drops the higher school reserve cap, the limits on special election dates, the homestead penalty and statewide database rules, and the ban on billing owners for back taxes when a homestead exemption was applied by mistake. Instead, the statewide homestead exemption changes from a base-year (value freeze) exemption to a flat cut in the home's taxable value. That cut is 10% in 2027 and rises 10 points a year to 50% in 2031. The exemption no longer applies to school taxes and becomes mandatory, though the bill still contains opt-out wording from current law. Other changes: the 5% local sales tax cap and the 3% revenue limits on local budgets now start in 2027 instead of 2028, and FLOST money can cover losses from the homestead exemption. Sales tax returns must also show where the tax was collected. The bill adds a nonbinding November 2026 statewide ballot question on full property tax relief for homeowners and states an intent to use certain data center equipment sales tax, starting in 2029, for homestead tax relief grants.

bills.headline: Replaces Georgia's base-year homestead exemption with a mandatory exemption phasing up to 50%.
bills.recap: This House substitute changes the statewide homestead exemption from a cap on assessment increases to a flat cut in taxable home value. The cut starts at 10% in 2027 and rises to 50% by 2031. It applies to all counties and cities with no opt-out, but no longer applies to school taxes. It also lets local sales taxes total up to 5% to replace lost revenue, with FLOST adoptable by resolution instead of a vote. Local budgets that raise property tax revenue by more than 3% or inflation, whichever is greater, would need voter approval or a local act of the General Assembly. The exemption does not transfer to a new owner, and the bill adds a November 2026 advisory vote on fully eliminating homeowner property taxes. Realtors should note the big cut in owner-occupied tax bills and the higher sales taxes that may come with it.

bills.title: "HOA Accountability and Training Act"; enact
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Article 6 of Chapter 3 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, the "Georgia Property Owners' Association Act," so as to prohibit a property owners' association from exercising enforcement authority over traffic laws, ordinances, or regulations; to authorize requests to law enforcement agencies to enforce traffic laws, ordinances, or regulations within a privately owned residential area; to provide for training; to provide for rules and regulations; to provide for a short title; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Bars HOAs from enforcing traffic laws and requires training for HOA board members.
bills.recap: This bill says property owners' associations (HOAs) cannot enforce state or local traffic laws, including parking violations. An HOA may instead ask local police to enforce those laws in its private neighborhood. It also requires the Secretary of State to set up a training program of at least four hours by January 1, 2028. New HOA board members would have to finish it within 90 days of joining the board, covering topics like money management, record keeping, conflicts of interest, and following HOA rules. Realtors may care because it changes how HOA communities handle parking and traffic, and it aims to make HOA boards better run.

bills.title: "Georgia Property Owners' Bill of Rights Act"; enact
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Title 43 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to professions and businesses, so as to require the registration of property owners' associations; to provide for renewals and amendments; to provide for appeals; to provide for a State Board for Review of Complaints Regarding Property Owners' Associations; to provide for review of complaints; to amend Code Section 44-3-232 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to assessments against lot owners as constituting lien in favor of association, additional charges against lot owners, procedure for foreclosing lien, and obligation to provide statement of amounts due, so as to provide for authorization of liens and use of assessments; to provide for a short title; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: S: Senate Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute
H: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute
S: Senate Agreed House Amend or Sub
S: Senate Date Signed by Governor

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The committee version lets an HOA choose not to register with the Secretary of State, but an unregistered HOA could not collect fines or fees. Registered HOAs would only need to register before collecting fines or fees, filing liens, or foreclosing, not before collecting dues. The complaint board gets more power: it can hold hearings, impose civil fines, issue cease-and-desist orders, and hear owner complaints filed within 180 days, with appeals to superior court. The new version also makes HOAs apply owner payments to dues first, then fees, then fines. It drops the earlier ban on the HOA and its insiders bidding at foreclosure sales. It sets the foreclosure minimum at the lesser of $4,000 or 12 months of past-due dues, not counting collection fees or fines, and extends the lien life from four to six years. The owner rights list no longer includes one vote per lot or the rights to display flags, political signs, and religious or holiday signs.

versions.name: Engrossed
versions.changes: The Senate passed this version with two real changes; the rest is formatting and line numbering. First, members of the new state complaint board for property owners' associations cannot work for, or have major business ties with, a law firm that represents association boards or a property management firm that serves associations. Second, the foreclosure threshold is clarified: an association can foreclose on a lot owner's lien only if the amount owed is the lesser of $4,000 or 12 months of past-due dues, and that amount must also be at least $2,000, not counting collection fees or fines.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The House Judiciary Committee version drops the proposed five-member state complaint review board. Instead, homeowners file complaints with the Secretary of State, who appoints a hearing officer. Appeals go to magistrate court for smaller amounts or superior court for larger ones, and the losing side pays a $100 fee. It also covers common interest communities, requires associations to file their governing documents when they register, defines regular, special, and specific assessments, and bans accelerated assessments and refusing partial payments. Payments must now go first to regular dues, then special assessments, then specific assessments, then fees and fines, unless an association's declaration recorded by June 30, 2026 says otherwise. For foreclosure, notice time grows from 30 to 90 days, and paying within 90 days stops the foreclosure. Owners can get a one-time stay of up to 90 days while an appeal is pending, and the association can bid only up to the lien amount. Before an association can collect attorney's fees, it must send a certified notice, give the owner 30 days to pay, and provide an itemized fee list, and a judge must find the fees reasonable. Most of the bill takes effect January 1, 2027, and the attorney's fee rules take effect July 1, 2026. The satellite dish right was removed.

versions.name: Introduced
versions.changes: This newer version (a Rules Committee substitute) keeps the core HOA plan: associations must register with the Secretary of State, owners can file complaints and get hearings, owners get a set of listed rights, and payments must go to regular dues first. Filing a complaint now automatically pauses collection of the disputed fines or fees until the hearing officer rules, and owners can also see the HOA's bank statements. The foreclosure notice period rises from 30 to 60 days instead of the 90 days in the prior version, and the one-time pause of foreclosure during an appeal is dropped. New sections let existing HOAs opt into the Georgia Property Owners' Association Act with an 80 percent vote, add an emergency exception to the attorney's fee notice rules, remove protection for older declarations on payment order, and let courts seal certain eviction records when the tenant wins, pays in full, or after seven years.

versions.name: Enrolled
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed between the introduced version and the enrolled version. The differences are only formatting: an updated document code, a new header listing the sponsors and marking the bill "As Passed," and page labels. The substance of the bill, including the HOA registration rules, owner rights, lien limits, and eviction record changes, stays the same.

bills.headline: Requires HOAs to register with the state and adds new homeowner protections.
bills.recap: Starting January 1, 2027, homeowner and condo associations must register each year with the Secretary of State ($100 fee) before they can collect fines or fees, file liens, or foreclose. Associations that opt out cannot charge fines, fees, or accelerated assessments. Owners gain a list of rights, including access to three years of financial records, a state complaint process that pauses collection of disputed fines, and a rule that payments go to regular dues first, then special assessments, then fines. HOA lien foreclosures now require 60 days' notice and a higher minimum debt that excludes fines, and starting July 1, 2026, associations must give written notice and 30 days to pay before collecting attorney's fees; judges can also seal certain eviction records, which matters for buyers, sellers, and renters in HOA communities.

bills.title: "Insurers' Use of Aerial or Satellite Images Act"; enact
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 9 of Title 33 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to regulation of rates, underwriting rules, and related organizations, so as to provide for homeowner protections with regard to insurance companies' use of aerial or satellite images; to provide for definitions; to provide for certain procedures; to require that homeowners be allowed 60 days to correct; to provide for regulations; to provide for related matters; to provide for a short title; to provide for an effective date and applicability; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: S: Senate Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The Senate Insurance and Labor Committee made one real change to the bill. Before, any aerial or satellite photos a homeowner sent to dispute an insurer's denial, cancellation, or nonrenewal had to match the quality of the insurer's own images. Now the homeowner's photos can be of equal or better resolution and quality. The other edits are only formatting and spacing fixes.

versions.name: Engrossed
versions.changes: Nothing in the bill's actual rules changed between the committee version and the version that passed the Senate. The only edits are formatting: the header now lists the sponsors (Senators Walker III, Harbin, Robertson, Kirkpatrick, Harbison and others), marks the bill as passed by the Senate, and adds page labels. The rules on how insurers may use aerial or satellite images for home insurance stay the same.

bills.headline: Gives homeowners rights when insurers use drone or satellite photos to drop or raise coverage.
bills.recap: When a home insurer uses drone, aircraft, or satellite images to cancel, not renew, cut coverage, or raise premiums on a primary residence, it must send dated photos (taken within nine months) showing the problem and explain how to fix it. Insurers must give homeowners at least 60 days to make repairs, set up a contact person and an appeal process, and offer renewal or reverse the decision once the fix is proven. The rules also apply to Georgia's FAIR Plan and would cover policies issued or renewed on or after October 1, 2026. Realtors may care because these protections can help clients keep insurance in place during a sale and avoid surprise coverage problems at closing.

bills.title: Landlord and Tenant; residential rental or lease agreement terminations if a tenant or a legal occupant of a residence experienced residential firearm violence; provide
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Article 1 of Chapter 7 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to general provisions regarding landlord and tenant, so as to provide for residential rental or lease agreement terminations if a tenant or a legal occupant of a residence experienced residential firearm violence or reasonably fears such tenant or a legal occupant would experience such violence at such residence; to provide for definitions; to provide for written notice; to provide for procedures; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Lets renters end leases early after gun violence at or near their home.
bills.recap: This bill expands Georgia's existing early lease termination law, which now covers family violence and stalking orders, to include tenants or legal occupants who were victims of firearm violence at or near their rental home. The tenant gives the landlord written notice, and the lease ends 30 days later. The notice must include proof, such as a police record, medical record, a letter from a victim services provider, or a sworn statement from a qualified person like a counselor or clergy member. The tenant still owes prorated rent and any past-due amounts, but no early termination fees or damages, and the lease cannot waive these rights, so landlords and property managers should update their forms and practices.

bills.title: "Fair Business Practices Act of 1975"; transparency and fairness with respect to rent pricing for residential properties; encourage
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Part 2 of Article 15 of Chapter 1 of Title 10 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to the "Fair Business Practices Act of 1975," so as to encourage transparency and fairness with respect to rent pricing for residential properties; to prohibit landlords from failing to disclose the total rental price of any residential property and charging hidden fees for any residential property; to provide for definitions; to provide for statutory construction; to provide for related matters; to provide for an effective date and applicability; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Requires landlords to disclose total rent upfront and bans hidden rental fees.
bills.recap: This bill would make it an unfair business practice for a landlord to sign a lease or take payment before clearly showing the total rental price, including all required fees and taxes. It also bans hidden fees, such as fees that cost more than the actual service, fees for services not provided, fees for things the landlord must already provide, fees tied to required vendors, or fees not written in the lease. It covers long-term rentals as well as hotels, vacation rentals, and short-term rentals, and applies to new leases, renewals, and changes signed after it takes effect. Realtors who handle leasing or property management would need to review fee structures and advertising so the total price is shown most prominently.

bills.title: "Housing for Heroes Act"; enact
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Article 1 of Chapter 7 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to landlord and tenant in general, so as to limit the monthly income requirement for disabled veterans to qualify as tenants; to provide for definitions; to provide for related matters; to provide for a short title; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Caps landlord income requirements for disabled veterans at twice the monthly rent.
bills.recap: This bill, called the Housing for Heroes Act, bars landlords from requiring a disabled veteran to earn more than two times the monthly rent to qualify as a tenant. Many landlords now ask for three times the rent, so this would lower the bar for qualifying veterans. It covers veterans with certain severe or 100 percent service-related disabilities, as defined in the bill, and measures income using federal adjusted gross income. Agents who handle leasing or property management would need to adjust screening rules for these applicants.

bills.title: Specialized Land Transactions; business enterprises or business enterprises controlled by natural born persons from owning an interest in more than 500 single-family residential properties; prohibit
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 3 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to regulation of specialized land transactions, so as to prohibit business enterprises or business enterprises controlled by natural born persons from owning an interest in more than 500 single-family residential properties; to prohibit foreign investment vehicles from owning any interest in a single-family residential property to be used as rental property; to provide a private cause of action against a business enterprise that owns an interest in more than 500 single-family residential properties and foreign investment vehicles; to provide for the disclosure of information by brokers; to provide an effective date and applicability; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.lastAction: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute

timeline.text: S: Senate Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute
H: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The committee version keeps the original limits: starting January 1, 2027, a business that does not build its own homes cannot own interests in more than 500 single-family homes, foreign investment vehicles cannot own single-family rentals, and people harmed can sue for $100,000 per violation. It adds new tax penalties. Businesses over the 500-home limit, not counting homes they built, would lose certain Georgia tax credits, including the housing tax credit. They would also lose some depreciation deductions (Section 179) and some investment expense deductions on those homes. Brokers working with business clients who are buying or leasing homes must also tell those clients in a timely way that they may lose these tax credits.

versions.name: Engrossed
versions.changes: Nothing in the bill's actual rules changed between the committee version and the version that passed the Senate. The only edits are labels: the header now lists the sponsors and says "As Passed Senate," and each page is marked "S. B. 463." The limits on business enterprises owning interests in more than 500 single-family rental homes, and the related tax provisions, read the same as before.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The House Judiciary Committee replaced the entire bill. All of the Senate-passed version is gone: the 500-home limit on companies, the ban on foreign investment vehicles owning rental homes, the related tax credit and depreciation limits, and the broker disclosure duty. The new bill is the "Georgia Anti-Squatting Act of 2026." It lets owners or their agents file a sworn complaint so law enforcement can quickly remove squatters, and it makes showing a fake lease or deed to stay on a property a felony with at least one year in prison. It also lets magistrate courts hear squatting cases anywhere in the county and gives hotels a faster way to remove guests whose stay has ended. It shortens the wait from 14 to 7 days before a landlord can hire off-duty officers to carry out an eviction, and it takes effect when signed.

bills.headline: Creates a fast sheriff process for owners to remove squatters and tightens squatting penalties.
bills.recap: This House substitute, called the Georgia Anti-Squatting Act of 2026, replaces the original bill's limits on large corporate home ownership. It lets a property owner or their authorized agent file a sworn complaint with the sheriff or another certified officer to have squatters removed quickly, without a full eviction case, if conditions are met: no lease, no family tie, and no pending lawsuit. Showing a fake lease or deed to stay in a property becomes a felony with at least one year in prison, and convicted squatters must pay the owner back based on fair market rent. The bill also gives innkeepers faster removal of guests whose stays have ended and lets landlords use off-duty officers if a writ of possession is not carried out within 7 days instead of 14. Owners who wrongly use the process can owe damages and attorney's fees. Realtors handling vacant listings or investor properties should know this new tool exists.

bills.title: Office of the Safety Fire Commissioner; update provisions
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Titles 8 and 25 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to buildings and housing and fire protection and safety, respectively, so as to improve government efficiency by updating provisions of the office of the Safety Fire Commissioner; to provide for an effective date; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.lastAction: Senate Agreed House Amend or Sub As Amended

timeline.text: S: Senate Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute
H: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute
S: Senate Agreed House Amend or Sub As Amended

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The Senate Public Safety Committee's version makes two real changes; the rest is formatting. First, the fire safety appeals board grows from four to six members appointed by the Commissioner, adding two seats the Commissioner chooses, alongside the state fire marshal as chair. Second, the rule on fire deaths is rewritten: the county coroner or medical examiner must report fire or smoke deaths to the Safety Fire Division, and only coroners or medical examiners (no longer firefighters or police) are barred from moving the body until state fire officials allow it. The earlier text requiring a state investigation before the body is moved, and letting officials decline to investigate, is removed.

versions.name: Engrossed
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed between the committee version and the version that passed the Senate. The only edits are formatting: the bill now lists its sponsors (Senator Robertson and others), is labeled "As Passed Senate," and has updated page headers. The rules on fire safety and building inspections are the same as in the committee version.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The House committee version cuts the smoke detector fine for occupants who don't keep detectors working from $250 to $100 per detector (it is $25 today; a first offense still gets a warning). It also lowers the new reinspection fee for manufactured homes from $250 to $150, and drops the Senate's power to suspend or revoke manufactured home licenses. Appeals of fire marshal decisions would go to the local superior court instead of only Fulton County, and the Senate's changes to hearing procedures and to the arson subpoena power were removed. The House version also adds new fireworks rules: permanent and temporary sales facilities, up to three tents for qualifying distributors, a $500 local license fee, fines of up to $5,000 for selling from an unapproved tent, and probate court power to hear fire-law misdemeanors.

bills.headline: Reorganizes the state fire office, adds building permit appeals, and raises smoke detector fines.
bills.recap: This bill restructures the Safety Fire Commissioner's office, adds a deputy commissioner, and creates a new appeals board for local building permit rulings tied to fire safety standards. The board includes the state fire marshal, local officials, and licensed residential and commercial contractors, and it can overturn local stop-work orders that do not pose an imminent danger. It also lets the Commissioner order immediate evacuations of unsafe buildings, raises the fine for occupants who fail to maintain a working smoke detector from $25 to $100 per detector after a warning, and raises the manufactured home reinspection fee from $15 to $150. Realtors may care because builders gain a faster path to challenge permit holds, while homeowners, renters, and manufactured home makers face higher fees and fines. Much of the rest of the bill covers fireworks sales rules.

bills.title: "Community Housing Options Increase Efficiency (CHOICE) Act"; enact
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Titles 12, 32, and 50 of the O.C.G.A., relating to conservation and natural resources, highways, bridges, and ferries, and state government, respectively, so as to provide for a system whereby certain local governments may seek certifications from the Department of Community Affairs upon the enactment of certain policies that can be used to receive priority in grant and loan applications submitted to state agencies; to provide for related matters; to provide a short title; to provide legislative findings; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Rewards local governments that ease zoning and building rules with priority for state grants.
bills.recap: This bill sets up a voluntary program where larger or higher-income cities and counties can earn state certification for adopting pro-housing policies. Examples include allowing duplexes and ADUs where single-family homes are allowed, smaller minimum lot and home sizes, fewer parking rules, faster permits, and not requiring HOAs in new developments. Certified places, at three levels starting with 10 policies, get priority for grants and loans from DCA, GEFA, and the state recreational trails program. The top tier also skips local matching funds for certain road grants. Realtors may see more housing types, more supply, and changing zoning rules in communities that take part, starting July 1, 2027.

bills.title: Specialized Land Transactions; a residency requirement for board members and officers of condominium associations and property owners' associations; establish
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 3 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to regulation of specialized land transactions, so as to establish a residency requirement for board members and officers of condominium associations and property owners' associations; to require the instruments and bylaws of each condominium association and property owners' association to provide for such residency requirement; to provide for construction; to provide for definitions; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Requires condo and HOA board members and officers to live in the community.
bills.recap: Starting January 1, 2027, board members and officers of Georgia condo associations and property owners' associations must be owners who have lived in their unit or lot as their main home for at least six months of the prior year. Active-duty military owners who can't live there because of orders, deployment, or training still qualify. Current board members can finish their terms, and associations must update their governing documents and bylaws to include the rule. Realtors may care because owners who rent out their property, investors, and second-home buyers would no longer be able to serve on these boards, though their voting and property rights stay the same.

bills.title: Georgia Property Tax Fairness Fund; create
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapters 7 and 8 of Title 48 and Chapter 8 of Title 33 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to income taxes, sales and use taxes, and fees and taxes relative to insurance, respectively, so as to create the Georgia Property Tax Fairness Fund; to require that high-technology data center and insurance premium tax collections be deposited into such fund; to provide for rules and regulations; to provide for recoverability; to provide for the repeal of insurance premium tax credits and abatements; to provide for conforming changes; to provide for a contingent effective date and automatic repeal; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Creates a state fund giving tax credits to cost-burdened homeowners and renters.
bills.recap: This bill creates the Georgia Property Tax Fairness Fund, paid for with insurance premium taxes and sales taxes from data centers. It ends new sales tax breaks for data centers and repeals some insurance company tax credits. Lower- and middle-income homeowners whose property taxes plus homeowners insurance top 5% of income, and renters whose rent tops 33% of income, could get refundable state income tax credits. Homes worth up to $500,000 near data centers could also get up to $2,500 off their property tax bill. It only takes effect if voters approve a constitutional amendment in November 2026.

bills.title: Butts County; a homestead exemption from Butts County ad valorem taxes for county purposes; provide
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to provide a homestead exemption from Butts County ad valorem taxes for county purposes in the amount of $70,000.00 of the assessed value of the homestead for residents of that county who are 62 years of age or older; to provide for definitions; to specify the terms and conditions of the exemption and the procedures relating thereto; to provide for applicability; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: S: Senate Date Signed by Governor

versions.name: Engrossed
versions.changes: The only change is a label noting the bill passed the Senate. The wording of the Butts County homestead exemption from county property taxes did not change. For agents and buyers, the proposal is the same as when it was introduced.

versions.name: Enrolled
versions.changes: The only change is a label at the top of the bill, from "As Passed Senate" to "As Passed." This shows the bill has passed both chambers and is in its final form. The Butts County homestead exemption itself was not changed.

bills.headline: Creates a $70,000 county property tax homestead exemption for Butts County seniors 62 and older.
bills.recap: This bill gives Butts County homeowners age 62 or older a $70,000 exemption off the assessed value of their home for county property taxes. It does not apply to school, state, or city taxes, and it stacks on top of other homestead exemptions. Seniors must apply once with the county tax commissioner, and it renews automatically while they live in the home. Voters must approve it in November 2026, and it would start January 1, 2027, which could lower carrying costs for older buyers and owners in Butts County.

bills.title: Butts County; a homestead exemption from Butts County ad valorem taxes for county purposes; provide
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to provide a homestead exemption from Butts County ad valorem taxes for county purposes in the amount of $50,000.00 of the assessed value of the homestead for residents of that county; to provide for definitions; to specify the terms and conditions of the exemption and the procedures relating thereto; to provide for applicability; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: S: Senate Date Signed by Governor

versions.name: Engrossed
versions.changes: No meaningful change. The only difference is a new label showing the bill passed the Senate. The Butts County homestead exemption itself was not changed.

versions.name: Enrolled
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed between these two versions. The only edit is the header label, which changed from "As Passed Senate" to "As Passed" to show the bill cleared both chambers. The Butts County homestead exemption itself is the same.

bills.headline: Offers Butts County homeowners a $50,000 homestead exemption from county property taxes, pending voter approval.
bills.recap: This law creates a $50,000 homestead exemption on the assessed value of a primary home in Butts County, applied to county property taxes. It does not cut school, state, or city taxes, and it adds to any other existing exemptions. Voters must approve it in the November 2026 election, and it would take effect for tax years starting January 1, 2027. Homeowners must apply once with the county tax commissioner, so Realtors can remind buyers to file and point out the lower county tax bill when talking about costs.

bills.title: "Fair Business Practices Act of 1975"; any person from facilitating noncompete agreements between residential rental property owners or managers, including by use of algorithmic coordinating functions; prohibit
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Part 2 of Article 15 of Chapter 1 of Title 10 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to the "Fair Business Practices Act of 1975," so as to prohibit any person from facilitating noncompete agreements between residential rental property owners or managers, including by use of algorithmic coordinating functions; to prohibit rental property owners or managers from setting or adjusting rental prices, lease renewal terms, occupancy levels, or other lease terms and conditions based on recommendations from software, data analytics service, or algorithmic devices; to provide for definitions; to provide for related matters; to provide an effective date and for applicability; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Bans landlords from using shared-data algorithm software to set rents and lease terms.
bills.recap: This bill makes it an unfair and deceptive trade practice under Georgia's Fair Business Practices Act to help rental owners or managers agree not to compete, including by running or licensing software that pools data from multiple landlords and recommends rents or lease terms. It also makes it unlawful for landlords and property managers to set or adjust rents, renewal terms, occupancy levels, or other lease terms based on such software's recommendations. Tools used to set rent or income limits for government affordable housing programs are exempt. Brokers who manage rentals or advise investors should review their pricing tools, since the rules would apply to contracts entered into on or after July 1, 2026.

bills.title: "Georgia Human Trafficking Prevention Training Act"; enact
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Article 1 of Chapter 21 of Title 43 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to rights, duties, and liabilities of innkeepers, so as to provide for a required human trafficking training program for inns and short-term rental properties; to provide for definitions; to provide for training policies and procedures; to provide for the retention of certain records; to provide for limitations; to provide for penalties; to provide an effective date; to provide a short title; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: S: Senate Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute
H: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute
S: Senate Agreed House Amend or Sub
S: Senate Date Signed by Governor

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The Senate Public Safety Committee version makes one real change: short-term rental hosting platforms now help create the required human trafficking awareness training. Before, only the Criminal Justice Coordinating Council and the Georgia Hotel and Lodging Association were named. Everything else stays the same, including the training, reporting policy, posting and record-keeping duties for inns and short-term rentals, the fines of $500, $1,000, and $2,000, and the July 1, 2026 start date.

versions.name: Engrossed
versions.changes: Nothing of substance changed between the committee version and the version that passed the Senate. The only edits are formatting: a new header listing the sponsoring senators, an "As Passed Senate" label, and page markers. The training rules and penalties read the same as before.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The House Judiciary Committee version narrows the short-term rental rules. Training now applies only to rentals run by a paid third-party property manager. Rentals managed directly by the owner are exempt, even if they use Airbnb-type platforms, and so are rentals offered fewer than 15 days a year. The Attorney General's office, not the Criminal Justice Coordinating Council, now develops the training, collects records, and imposes and keeps the fines ($500, $1,000, then $2,000 for willful violations). Training records must be kept one year after employment ends instead of three, and the Georgia trafficking hotline was dropped from required contacts. Local sheriffs or police must help enforce the posting rules.

versions.name: Enrolled
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed between the House committee substitute and the enrolled version. The only edits are on the cover page and page footers, which now list the Senate sponsors and mark the bill "As Passed." The rules for human trafficking awareness training at inns and short-term rental properties stay the same as in the committee version.

bills.headline: Requires human trafficking training for hotel staff and third-party short-term rental managers.
bills.recap: Starting July 1, 2026, on-site hotel employees and paid third-party managers of short-term rentals must take yearly human trafficking awareness training approved by the Attorney General's office. Owners, operators, or managers must adopt reporting policies, post required trafficking notices, and keep training records for the length of employment plus one year. Willful violations can bring fines of $500, $1,000, and then $2,000 for repeat offenses. Owners who manage their own rentals, and rentals offered fewer than 15 days a year, are exempt, so Realtors and brokers who manage short-term rentals for clients should take note.

bills.title: City of Metter; ad valorem taxes for municipal purposes; provide a homestead exemption
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to provide a homestead exemption from City of Metter ad valorem taxes for municipal purposes in the amount of $2,000.00 of the assessed value of the homestead for residents of that city; to provide for definitions; to specify the terms and conditions of the exemption and the procedures relating thereto; to provide for applicability; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: S: Senate Date Signed by Governor

versions.name: Engrossed
versions.changes: The only change is a label noting the bill passed the Senate. The content of the bill is the same as when it was introduced. It still proposes a homestead exemption from City of Metter property taxes for city purposes.

versions.name: Enrolled
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed between these two versions. The only edit is the header label, which went from "As Passed Senate" to "As Passed" to show the bill cleared both chambers. The homestead exemption for City of Metter property taxes reads the same as before.

bills.headline: Creates a $2,000 city homestead exemption for Metter homeowners, if voters approve.
bills.recap: This law gives homeowners living in the City of Metter a $2,000 exemption off the assessed value of their home for city property taxes. It does not lower state, county, or school taxes, and it stacks on top of any other city homestead exemptions. Homeowners must apply once with the city, and the exemption renews each year as long as they live there. It only takes effect if city voters approve it in November 2026, starting with the 2027 tax year, which gives Realtors a small selling point for buyers in Metter.

bills.title: City of Metter; ad valorem taxes for municipal purposes; provide a homestead exemption
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to provide a homestead exemption from City of Metter ad valorem taxes for municipal purposes in the amount of $4,000.00 of the assessed value of the homestead for residents of that city who are 65 years of age or older and whose income does not exceed $10,000.00; to provide for definitions; to specify the terms and conditions of the exemption and the procedures relating thereto; to provide for applicability; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: S: Senate Date Signed by Governor

versions.name: Engrossed
versions.changes: The only change is a label noting the bill passed the Senate. The wording of the bill itself did not change. It still deals with a homestead tax break on city property taxes in the City of Metter.

versions.name: Enrolled
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed between these two versions. The only edit is the header label, which now reads "As Passed" instead of "As Passed Senate," showing the bill cleared both chambers. The homestead exemption from City of Metter property taxes is the same in both versions.

bills.headline: Creates a $4,000 Metter city tax homestead exemption for low-income seniors 65 and older.
bills.recap: This law gives Metter homeowners age 65 or older a $4,000 cut in the assessed value of their home for city property taxes, if household income is $10,000 or less. It covers city taxes only, not county, school, or state taxes, and it adds to any other exemptions. Seniors must apply once with the city, and it renews each year while they live in the home. City voters must approve it in a November 2027 referendum before it takes effect, and the bill sets it to apply to tax years starting January 1, 2027.

bills.title: Ad Valorem Taxation; assessment of tangible real property used for community housing provider properties; provide
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Article 1 of Chapter 5 of Title 48 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to general provisions relative to ad valorem taxation of property, so as to provide for assessment of tangible real property used for community housing provider properties; to provide for supporting affidavits; to provide for definitions; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

timeline.text: S: Senate Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The Senate Finance Committee's version tightens who can qualify as a community housing provider. An S corporation, LLC, or partnership now qualifies only if it owns no more than 500 properties in Georgia, directly or through shared ownership. The original bill allowed up to 2,000. The rest of the changes are formatting and document numbering, so the special property tax assessment rules for these providers stay the same.

bills.headline: Lets counties tax large single-family rental owners' homes at full value, not 40 percent.
bills.recap: Georgia normally taxes property at 40 percent of its fair market value. This bill says single-family rental homes owned by larger investors may be taxed at 100 percent of value. Homes owned by "community housing providers" stay at the normal 40 percent rate. That group covers individuals, nonprofits, charities, and S corporations, LLCs, or partnerships owning 500 or fewer properties in Georgia. Larger rental owners would have to give tax assessors income data on request. Assessors could also ask smaller owners for a sworn affidavit by April 1. Realtors working with institutional investors or rental buyers should watch how this could change holding costs and investor demand.

bills.title: Property; the minimum amount required for a foreclosure on a lien on a property under the "Georgia Condominium Act" and the "Georgia Property Owners' Association Act"; increase
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to property, so as to increase the minimum amount required for a foreclosure on a lien on a property under the "Georgia Condominium Act" and the "Georgia Property Owners' Association Act"; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Raises the minimum unpaid HOA or condo dues before foreclosure from $2,000 to $20,000.
bills.recap: This bill raises the minimum lien amount a condo association or property owners' association must reach before it can foreclose on a home for unpaid assessments. The threshold jumps from $2,000 to $20,000 under both the Georgia Condominium Act and the Georgia Property Owners' Association Act. Other rules stay the same, including the 30-day notice requirement and the four-year expiration of assessment liens. Realtors may care because it protects owners behind on dues from losing their homes over small debts, but associations may have less leverage to collect, and unpaid liens could still show up at closing.

bills.title: "Georgia Landowners Protection Act"; enact
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 66 of Title 36 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to zoning procedures, so as to provide for the maximum period of time a local government may enforce certain moratoria; to prohibit reimposition of certain moratoria within a certain period of time; to waive sovereign immunity on claims related to damages arising from moratoria exceeding such limitations; to provide for recoverable damages and attorney's fees; to provide for legislative findings; to provide a short title; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Limits local zoning and permit moratoria to 90 days and lets landowners sue.
bills.recap: This bill caps local government moratoria on zoning decisions and on permits for residential or commercial property at 90 days. A zoning moratorium of the same type cannot be reimposed within 365 days, and any moratorium needs 45 days of public notice with data-backed reasons. Owners whose property loses value from a moratorium lasting past 90 days could sue the local government for lost development value, carrying costs, higher property taxes, and possibly attorney's fees. Emergencies, natural disasters, and imminent public health or safety threats are exempt, and Realtors working with builders, developers, and land sellers may see fewer long approval delays.

bills.title: City of Hampton; homestead exemption; ad valorem taxes for municipal purposes; provide
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to provide a homestead exemption from City of Hampton ad valorem taxes for municipal purposes for the total amount of the assessed value of the homestead for residents of that city who have resided at such homestead for at least five years; to provide for definitions; to specify the terms and conditions of the exemption and the procedures relating thereto; to provide for applicability; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

versions.name: Engrossed
versions.changes: The only change is a new label marking the bill "As Passed Senate." This shows SB614 cleared the Senate. The bill's content did not change, including the City of Hampton homestead exemption from city property taxes.

bills.headline: Fully exempts long-time Hampton homeowners' homes from city property taxes, if voters approve.
bills.recap: This bill would exempt the full assessed value of a home from City of Hampton property taxes for owners who have lived there as their main home for at least five years. It covers city taxes only. County, school, and state property taxes still apply. Owners must apply once with the city, and the exemption renews each year while they live there. Hampton voters must approve it in a November 2027 election. If they do, it applies to tax years starting January 1, 2027. Realtors should note that long-time owners may be slower to sell, and buyers will not get the break until they have lived in the home for five years.

bills.headline: Creates a $50,000 city homestead exemption for City of Dallas homeowners, pending voter approval.
bills.recap: This bill gives City of Dallas residents a $50,000 exemption on the assessed value of their homestead for city property taxes. It does not cut state, county, or school taxes, and it stacks on top of any other city homestead exemptions. Owners must apply once with the city, and the exemption then renews each year while they live in the home. Dallas voters must approve it in November 2026 for it to start January 1, 2027. A lower city tax bill could make homes in Dallas a bit more affordable to own, which is a useful point for buyers and sellers.

bills.description: A RESOLUTION encouraging the Department of Community Affairs to investigate the abusive practices of homeowners' associations, particularly their impact on the elderly and other vulnerable residents in a community; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Senate resolution urges state agency to investigate abusive homeowners' association practices.
bills.recap: This resolution asks the Georgia Department of Community Affairs to look into abusive practices by homeowners' associations (HOAs), with a focus on elderly and other vulnerable residents. It cites concerns about retaliation, financial exploitation, unlicensed property management, and the spread of short-term rentals in neighborhoods. It is only a request and does not create new laws, rules, or penalties. Realtors may care because it signals growing interest in HOA oversight, which could lead to future rules affecting HOA communities and buyers' decisions.

bills.description: A RESOLUTION proposing an amendment to the Constitution so as to authorize the General Assembly to provide by general law for the assessment of property taxes on property used primarily for the manufacturing, assembly, processing, or storage of products or the housing of electronic equipment primarily used to process, store, or transmit digital information and data; to provide for related matters; to provide for the submission of this amendment for ratification or rejection; and for other purposes.

Local governments and school systems could still tax data center property at different rates or values to ease the tax burden on other property, if lawmakers and voters approve. bills.headline: Proposes constitutional amendment letting local governments tax data centers differently to ease other property taxes.
bills.recap: This resolution asks voters to amend the Georgia Constitution so lawmakers can treat data center property as its own tax class. Counties, cities, and school systems could then tax data centers at different rates or values. The stated goal is to reduce the property tax burden on other property, which could include homes. Realtors may care because it could affect local property tax bills and the cost of owning a home in areas with data centers.

bills.description: A RESOLUTION proposing an amendment to the Constitution of the State of Georgia so as to provide that the General Assembly shall be authorized to provide by law to expend or authorize the expenditure of public funds for the Georgia Property Tax Fairness Fund without the need for benefit in return; to provide for related matters; to provide for submission of this amendment for ratification or rejection; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Proposed constitutional amendment creates a property tax relief fund and raises homeowner tax relief cap.
bills.recap: This resolution would ask Georgia voters to amend the state constitution to create a Georgia Property Tax Fairness Fund. Money collected from high-tech data centers and the insurance premium tax could fund refundable state income tax credits for people living in 'qualifying homes,' which lawmakers would define later. It also raises the cap on the Homeowner's Incentive Adjustment from the equivalent of an $18,000 homestead exemption to $150,000, and lets local governments and school systems fund their own adjustments. For Realtors, this could mean lower yearly costs for homeowners with a homestead exemption, which may help affordability and owner appeal.

bills.recap: This resolution asks the Department of Community Affairs not to adopt the 2024 International Energy Conservation Code for home construction. It urges the state to keep using the 2015 code with Georgia amendments. The resolution cites cost modeling showing the newer code would add thousands of dollars per home, and says each $1,000 price increase prices out more than 5,000 Georgians. Eligible stores include grocery stores, corner stores, convenience stores, farmers' markets, and small food retailers. The credit starts with tax years beginning January 1, 2026, can only be claimed in the year the store opens, and unused amounts can carry forward five years. Realtors who work in commercial leasing or sales may see more demand for retail space in these areas, since the credit can lower the cost of buying or leasing property there.

bills.recap: This law updates many parts of Georgia's banking code. For mortgage companies, it sets minimum net worth and cash requirements: $50,000 for brokers, and $100,000 plus $1 million in liquidity for most lenders. Lenders must get a yearly outside audit, and both lenders and brokers must have a board of directors, a risk management program, and internal audits. bills.headline: Lets surviving spouses and minor children of disabled veterans keep their tax exemption after moving.
bills.recap: Today, the unremarried surviving spouse or minor children of a qualified disabled veteran can keep the veteran's homestead tax exemption only on the home they already live in. This bill lets them carry the exemption to any future homestead they own and live in, as long as they file once in the new county. A child's exemption ends at the end of the tax year they turn 18, and tax assessors can ask for proof of eligibility no more than once every three years. It needs a two-thirds vote in both chambers and statewide voter approval in November 2026, taking effect January 1, 2027. For Realtors, it means these surviving families can sell and buy a new home without losing a major property tax break.

It lets Georgia counties ask voters to approve a new 1% local sales tax, paired with a local act creating an extra homestead exemption that could cover up to 100% of a home's assessed value for county taxes. Up to 25% of the money can go to road projects and city capital projects. The rest must lower county taxes on primary homes, with any leftover used to roll back the county tax rate. Both the tax and the exemption must pass in the same vote, and they end after 10 years unless voters renew them. bills.headline: Tweaks Georgia's homestead tax freeze, opt-out rules, tax bills, and assessment notices.
bills.recap: This new law updates the statewide base-year homestead exemption from HB 581 (2024), which limits how fast a home's taxable value can rise. Local governments that opted out must repeat public hearings and refile by March 1, 2027 to stay opted out, can reverse their opt-out through 2029, and must print a bold notice on homeowners' tax bills saying they opted out. Surviving spouses do not need to reapply. Assessment notices must now use a statewide form and show each local government's estimated roll-back rate, and tax bills must flag when the adopted rate is higher. Realtors can use this to explain property tax relief, and future tax bills, to buyers and sellers in different counties.

bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Code Section 48-5-7.4 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to preferential assessment for bona fide conservation use property and bona fide residential transitional property, so as to remove a limitation on leased property as to certain entities; to provide for related matters; to provide for an effective date and applicability; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Lets more farm businesses lease conservation use land without losing the tax break.
bills.recap: Georgia's conservation use program lowers property taxes on farm and timber land. Before, the land lost that break if it was leased to someone who could not qualify for it. This law lets owners lease to certain registered farm businesses and keep the break. The business must be owned only by U.S. citizens, focus on farming or timber, and earn at least 80% of its income from those uses in Georgia, or have a member who owns at least 25% of the leased land and qualifies. The bill also renews a film postproduction tax credit through 2030 and applies starting in tax year 2026. Agents who sell or list farm and timber land may want to know about the new leasing option.

bills.recap: This law raises the limit on bonds and notes the Georgia Housing and Finance Authority (GHFA) can have outstanding for its single-family housing program, from $3 billion to $6 billion. These bonds help fund the state's home loan programs, such as Georgia Dream. A higher cap gives the state room to finance more mortgages for eligible buyers. Realtors working with first-time or moderate-income buyers may see these programs stay available longer. The law took effect when the Governor signed it.

bills.headline: Cuts state sales tax on manufactured homes converted to real property by half.
bills.recap: Starting July 1, 2026, this law exempts 50% of the sales price of a manufactured home from Georgia state sales tax. To qualify, the home must be properly installed and converted to real property within 30 days of the sale. It must also be a dwelling of at least 650 square feet with an angled roof. The seller must file a Certificate of Permanent Location with the clerk of superior court within 30 days, or pay 1.5 times the tax that was exempted. The home cannot later be turned back into personal property unless the exempted tax is repaid. Local sales taxes still apply. Realtors working with manufactured homes on land may see lower purchase costs for buyers.

bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 3 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to regulation of specialized land transactions, so as to prohibit condominium associations and property owners' associations from retaliating against property owners for taking certain actions; to provide for circumstances that are not considered retaliation; to provide definitions; to provide for remedies; to provide for a defense; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Bars condo and HOA boards from retaliating against owners who complain or assert rights.
bills.recap: This bill stops condo associations and property owners' associations from punishing owners who file complaints, give feedback, use their legal rights, or organize other owners. Banned retaliation includes raising an owner's fees, cutting services, blocking use of their home or common areas, or suddenly suing or filing to foreclose on a lien. If an owner raised a life, health, safety, or habitability concern and the association acted against them within three months, that counts as early proof of retaliation. Owners could use retaliation as a defense to a lien foreclosure and recover one month's fees plus $500, court costs, and attorney's fees, which matters for Realtors working with buyers and sellers in HOA and condo communities.

bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Title 17, Title 19, and Title 44 of the O.C.G.A., relating to criminal procedure, domestic relations, and property, respectively, so as to extend certain protections for victims of family violence and stalking with respect to residential leases; to provide for an effective date and applicability; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Expands lease protections for family violence and stalking victims, including removing abusers from shared rentals.
bills.recap: This bill lets a tenant protected by a family violence or stalking order end their own lease on a shared rental with 30 days' written notice, without ending the lease for other tenants. It also lets the victim ask the landlord to end only the abuser's lease, with at least 72 hours' posted notice to the abuser. Landlords cannot raise rent, add deposits, or charge early termination fees to remaining tenants. Landlords also cannot refuse to rent to, refuse to renew, or evict someone for being a victim, or face a lawsuit. Property managers and leasing agents should know these rules apply to leases signed or renewed after the law takes effect and cannot be waived in the lease.

bills.headline: Freezes Newnan city property tax assessments on homesteads at base-year value, pending voter approval.
bills.recap: This bill creates a City of Newnan homestead exemption that blocks city taxes on any rise in a home's assessed value above its base-year value. It covers up to five contiguous acres. New improvements or added land are still taxed, and city taxes for bond debt, county, school, and state taxes are not affected. Homeowners must apply once, and the exemption renews each year while they live there. The base year resets when a home sells, so buyers start fresh at the new value. The exemption needed approval from Newnan voters in November 2025 and would start January 1, 2026.

Before, only a sheriff, deputy, or county constable could serve the summons and affidavit. Now an approved process server can do it too, using the same rules for hand delivery, leaving papers with an adult at the home, or posting and mailing them. Landlords and property managers may see faster service and fewer delays in eviction cases.

bills.headline: Cracks down on deceptive mortgage solicitations using credit-check 'trigger leads' sold to other lenders.
bills.recap: When a buyer applies for a mortgage, the credit check can be sold as a 'trigger lead' to other lenders, who then call or mail the buyer with competing offers. This law makes it an unfair or deceptive practice for those lenders and brokers to hide that they are not tied to the buyer's original lender, skip making a firm offer of credit, contact people on the do-not-call list or who opted out of prescreened offers, or advertise rates and terms they know will change for the worse. Violations can be punished under Georgia's Fair Business Practices Act and are also grounds for action against a mortgage license. Realtors may care because it helps protect buyer clients from confusing or bait-and-switch calls during the loan process, which can reduce surprises before closing.

bills.recap: This bill would raise the basic statewide homestead exemption from $2,000 to $5,000 of a home's value for owner-occupied primary residences. It applies to state, county, and school property taxes, but not to city taxes, city school taxes, or taxes used to pay off bonds. It needs a two-thirds vote in both chambers and approval by statewide voters by November 2026; if approved, it takes effect January 1, 2027. Realtors may care because it would modestly lower yearly property tax bills for homeowners, which can help with owning costs.

bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Article 2 of Chapter 6 of Title 15 and Article 1 of Chapter 17 of Title 45 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to clerks of superior courts and general provisions regarding notaries public, respectively, so as to provide for remote online notaries public and remote online notarizations; to provide requirements for electronic journaling; to amend Part 2 of Article 15 of Chapter 1 of Title 10, Part 1 of Article 1 of Chapter 2 of Title 44 and Article 4 of Chapter 18 of Title 50 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to the "Fair Business Practices Act of 1975," recording of deeds and other real property transactions and inspection of public records, respectively, so as to provide for an unfair or deceptive practice in consumer transactions in the recording of certain residential real estate documents; to provide for related matters; to provide an effective date; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Allows remote online notarization and electronic witnessing for Georgia real estate documents.
bills.lastAction: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute
bills.recap: This bill creates a new class of remote online notaries who can notarize documents by live video, including deeds and other real estate documents, starting with state standards due by January 1, 2027. Notaries must take a course, pass an exam, carry a $2,000 bond, verify signer ID through set checks, keep a 10-year electronic journal and video recording, and may charge up to $25 per notarization. It also lets unofficial witnesses sign real estate documents electronically or by video, and tells clerks to record documents that show both witness signatures without digging further. The bill keeps the rule that a Georgia attorney must supervise closings and makes it an unfair business practice to knowingly record a 1-4 family home document that came from the unauthorized practice of law, which matters to agents working with remote or out-of-state buyers and sellers.

bills.recap: This bill repeals Code Section 44-7-19, the state law that restricts cities and counties from regulating rent. The bill itself does not create rent control. It removes the state-level barrier, which could let local governments adopt their own rent rules. Realtors who work with landlords, investors, or rental properties may want to watch this closely, since local rent rules could affect rental income and property values.

bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 60 of Title 36 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to general provisions applicable to counties and municipal corporations, so as to provide procedures for real property owners to make claims for compensation from local governments for loss of property value or expenses incurred due to the local government's failure to comply with or nonenforcement of certain laws, ordinances, and resolutions or due to the local government maintaining a public nuisance; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Lets property owners seek payment from local governments that ignore certain laws or nuisances.
bills.recap: This new law lets property owners and leaseholders file a written claim against their city or county if it has a policy or pattern of not enforcing laws on things like illegal camping, loitering, panhandling, public drug use, or shoplifting, of not following state immigration rules, or of maintaining a public nuisance. Owners can ask for either documented costs to deal with the problem or the drop in their property's fair market value, but payment is capped at the local property taxes paid on that parcel the prior year. If the local government rejects the claim or does not act within 30 days, the owner can sue, the government must prove its case, and a winning owner gets attorney fees. Realtors may see clients ask about this option when nearby conditions hurt home values, and claims are limited to once per tax year per parcel.
