bills.title: Local government; procedures for real property owners to make claims for compensation for loss of property value or expenses incurred; provisions

versions.changes: The committee version narrows when property owners can claim money from a city or county for lost property value or costs caused by non-enforcement of laws (like illegal camping or panhandling) or a public nuisance. It defines "policy, pattern, or practice" as a widespread, organized practice, so one-off or isolated failures do not count. It caps payments at the property taxes that local government collected over the prior two years, leaving out school taxes, and lets the government defend itself by showing it took reasonable steps to address the nuisance. It also makes an owner pay the government's legal fees if they keep filing after two unsuccessful claims on the same property, and it says claims are handled under an existing tax refund process (Code Section 48-5-380).
versions.name: Comm Sub

versions.changes: The new substitute changes the claim deadline. Owners now must file within the same tax year the events happened, instead of within 24 months. It also changes the payment cap: compensation can't exceed the local property taxes paid on the parcel in the prior tax year, instead of the old cap tied to taxes from the two years before the claim. Owners whose claims are denied as incomplete may now revise and resubmit them. The penalty for repeat claims is tougher: after just one unsuccessful claim on a parcel (down from two), the local government recovers its legal fees and costs on any later failed claim. Repeat claims in later years now require ongoing money damages rather than just 'injury,' and the rest of the changes are wording cleanups and a new Code section number.

The rules on how property owners can claim compensation for lost property value or expenses were not changed.

versions.changes: The final version keeps the core plan: property owners can ask their city or county to pay them back for cleanup costs or lost property value caused by things like ignored illegal camping, panhandling, or immigration sanctuary policies, capped at the prior year's local property taxes. New sections let anyone harmed by a local sanctuary policy, or by a jail that ignores a federal immigration detainer, ask a superior court to order compliance, and those cases get priority. The rule making repeat losing claimants pay the local government's legal fees now applies only to claims that were complete when filed, so incomplete paperwork won't count against an owner. The bill title also mentions public disclosure of certain state documents, but no section in this version actually does that.

bills.headline: Revises Georgia zoning procedures and lets superior court zoning rulings be appealed directly.
bills.recap: This bill lets final superior court rulings on local zoning decisions be appealed directly to Georgia's higher courts. It also changes zoning rules for cities and counties: it removes the power of staff officers to make quasi-judicial zoning calls, shortens hearing notice for boards like zoning appeals boards from 30 to 15 days, and requires those boards to adopt written decision standards. It treats special use permits as zoning decisions handled by elected officials and shortens the gap between the two votes needed to allow multifamily uses in single-family zones from 21 to 15 days. bills.recap: This bill creates a homestead exemption from Bryan County school district taxes that limits how much a home's taxable value can rise each year to the rate of inflation, plus any value from improvements. It covers up to five contiguous acres and starts January 1, 2026, if Bryan County school district voters approve it in a November 2025 referendum. Homeowners who already have a 2025 homestead exemption get it automatically, but the benefit does not transfer to a new owner. Credits run from 2026 through 2030 and are capped at $10 million a year statewide, with each organization limited to $2 million a year. Individuals can claim up to $5,000, couples up to $10,000, and corporations up to 30% of their tax bill. The bill does not say how the money must be used, but it could mean more funding for exempt lenders that help buyers get mortgages.

bills.recap: This bill lets Georgia cities and counties create a free registry of residential rental property, but only for owners who own or control at least 10 contiguous units in that area. Properties with more than 20 units, certain state-licensed homes, and short-term rentals under 30 days are excluded. Owners or property managers would list contact details, the property address and parcel number, and deed information, update it within 30 days of changes, and disclose any foreign adversary ownership. Fines can run from $500 to $1,000 per violation, with exemptions for deployed military, serious illness, heirs, and disaster hardship. Notices of code violations could also go to the property manager, which matters for licensees who manage rentals.

It also leaves out homes licensed by the Department of Community Health, multifamily properties with more than 20 units, and short-term rentals. Owners can list either their own or their property manager's contact information. Property managers may also handle updates and the foreign ownership disclosure, and the list of foreign adversaries now follows the U.S. Commerce Department's list instead of naming specific countries.

bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to property, so as to prohibit condominium associations, property owners' associations, and homeowners' associations from preventing property owners from installing solar energy devices on common roofs or roof structures; to provide for the burden of costs for removal and reinstallation of solar energy devices; to allow for repair of common roofs or roof structures; to provide for definitions; to provide for applicability; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Bars HOAs and condo associations from blocking owners' rooftop solar installations.
bills.recap: This bill stops condo associations, property owners' associations, and HOAs from banning or restricting solar energy devices on an owner's roof, even when the roof is a common area the association maintains. Associations could not require a permit or charge a fee for installing or using solar, and any rule or covenant that conflicts would be void. If the roof needs maintenance later, the owner who installed the solar must pay to remove and reinstall it. The rules would apply to covenants, documents, and association rules made, renewed, or changed on or after January 1, 2026, which matters for agents advising buyers and sellers in HOA and condo communities.
bills.title: Property; prohibit homeowners' associations from preventing property owners from installing solar energy devices; provisions

bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to property, so as to enhance protections for homeowners and tenants by revising or repealing certain provisions inhibiting housing stability; to provide for definitions; to provide for related matters; to provide for an effective date and applicability; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Limits HOA liens, bans big REIT home buys, allows local rent control, curbs foreclosures.
bills.recap: This bill removes the automatic lien that condo and property owners' associations get for unpaid fees, which also removes their power to foreclose over those debts, though owners would still owe the money. It voids any sale of a single-family home or townhome to a real estate investment trust that already owns at least $30 million or 12,000 units of rental homes in Georgia. It repeals the state ban on local rent control and blocks non-court (power of sale) foreclosures against borrowers who are 65 or older or under guardianship, for loans made or changed after the law takes effect. Realtors should watch this closely: it could change HOA payoff letters at closing, cut off a major group of buyers, and change how foreclosures and rental markets work.
bills.title: Property; enhance protections for homeowners and tenants by revising or repealing certain provisions inhibiting housing stability

bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Titles 12, 32, and 50 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to conservation and natural resources, highways, bridges, and ferries, and state government, respectively, so as to provide for a system whereby certain local governments may seek certifications from the Department of Community Affairs upon the enactment of certain policies that can be used to receive priority in grant and loan applications submitted to state agencies; to provide for statutory construction; to provide that the Georgia Environmental Finance Authority give priority to certified local governments when awarding grants and loans; to provide definitions; to provide exceptions; to provide for related matters; to provide a short title; to provide legislative findings; to provide an effective date; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Rewards local governments with grant priority for adopting zoning reforms that boost housing supply.
bills.lastAction: House Committee Favorably Reported By Substitute
bills.recap: The CHOICE Act lets larger or higher-income Georgia cities and counties earn a state certification starting July 1, 2027, by adopting a set number of pro-housing policies. Examples include allowing duplexes, ADUs, townhomes, and cottage courtyards in single-family zones, smaller minimum home sizes and lot sizes, reduced parking and setbacks, faster permits, and not requiring HOAs for new developments. Certified communities would get priority for certain state grants and loans from DCA, GEFA, and the recreational trails program, and top-tier ones would not need matching funds for some road grants. Participation is voluntary, but Realtors could see more housing types, more building, and new development options in communities that sign on.

bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Article 1 of Chapter 7 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to landlords and tenants in general, so as to require certain residential landlords to have in-state staff to manage tenant communications related to such properties; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Out-of-state landlords of single-family homes and duplexes must hire a Georgia-licensed broker.
bills.recap: Landlords who live outside Georgia and own or operate single-family or duplex rentals here must hire a broker licensed in Georgia. If that broker lives out of state, the broker must have at least one person in Georgia to handle tenant calls about repairs and other issues. These landlords can no longer use the owner and full-time employee exemptions to skip licensing. The bill also lets code enforcement officers, when they have probable cause of a violation, ask tenants for the property manager's name, license number, and contact info. For Realtors, this could create new property management business and adds accountability for licensed managers.

bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to property, so as to enact the "Homeowners Protection Act"; to provide for a rental intention affidavit regarding dispossessory proceedings; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Lets owners file an affidavit to speed removal of squatters from their property.
bills.recap: This bill creates the "Homeowners Protection Act." It lets a property owner file a sworn statement with the county superior court clerk saying the property is not rented and asking that any unlawful occupant be removed within one calendar day once the statement is confirmed. That statement can then be used as the basis to demand possession in an eviction (dispossessory) case. Realtors may care because it gives owners of vacant homes, listings, and investment properties a faster tool against squatters.
bills.title: Homeowners Protection Act; enact

bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 5 of Title 48 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to ad valorem taxation of property, so as to provide for an additional period to appeal certain property assessments; to require the annual notice of assessment for property taxes to include an estimate of the current year's taxes and a statement regarding such estimate; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Gives property owners a second chance to appeal assessments after receiving their tax bill.
bills.recap: This bill lets property owners appeal their assessed value within 45 days of the assessment notice or within 30 days of getting their actual tax bill. It also requires the yearly assessment notice to include an estimate of the current year's taxes, based on the prior or most applicable millage rate, along with a bold statement that the real bill may differ and may not include all exemptions. Forest land conservation use applications would follow the same appeal deadlines. Realtors may care because owners and recent buyers get more time to challenge high valuations and clearer early estimates of their tax costs.
bills.title: Ad valorem tax; additional period to appeal certain property assessments; provide

bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to provide a homestead exemption from Bryan County school district ad valorem taxes for educational purposes in an amount equal to the amount by which the current year assessed value of a homestead exceeds the adjusted base year assessed value of such homestead; to provide for definitions; to specify the terms and conditions of the exemption and the procedures relating thereto; to provide for applicability; to provide for a short title; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Caps Bryan County school tax increases on homesteads to inflation, if voters approve.
bills.recap: This local bill creates a homestead exemption from Bryan County school district taxes. It limits yearly increases in a home's taxable value to the rate of inflation, plus the value of major improvements. It covers up to five acres and starts January 1, 2026, but only if Bryan County school district voters approve it in a November 2025 referendum. Current homestead owners get it automatically, but it does not carry over to a new owner, so buyers should expect the school tax bill to reset after a sale.

bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 3 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to regulation of specialized land transactions, so as to prohibit business enterprises from owning an interest in more than 2,000 single-family residential properties or ten multifamily residential properties; to provide for the forfeiture of rental payments paid in connection with an unlawful lease of residential property; to provide a private cause of action for the return of rental payments paid in connection with an unlawful lease of residential property; to provide for the disclosure of information by brokers; to provide an effective date; to provide a short title; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Caps business ownership at 2,000 single-family homes or ten multifamily properties in Georgia.
bills.recap: Starting January 1, 2026, this bill would make it illegal for a business, counting its affiliates, to own more than 2,000 single-family homes (including townhouses and condos) or more than ten apartment properties with four or more units in Georgia. Anyone harmed could sue for actual damages or $15,000 per property, plus attorney's fees. The Attorney General or a district attorney could force a public sale of homes held over the limit, and businesses over the cap could not lease those homes; tenants could sue to get their rent back but keep their leases. Brokers working with business clients buying or leasing out homes must tell them about these limits, so it adds a new disclosure duty for agents and could shift investor demand in many markets.

Condos now count as single-family residences, so they fall under the 2,000-home cap on business ownership. The meaning of 'business enterprise' now names 'issuers' as covered, and only an 'aggrieved' person can sue. The bill now says each home held over the limit by a business or one of its shareholders counts as a separate violation. The $15,000-per-violation damages, forced public sale, lease limits, and the rule that brokers must tell business clients about these limits all stay the same.

bills.headline: Ends Georgia's Section 179 tax deduction for single-family rental property starting in 2026.
bills.recap: Starting with tax years beginning January 1, 2026, this bill stops letting owners use the Section 179 expensing deduction on their Georgia taxes for single-family rental homes. Any Section 179 amount already taken on single-family rentals would have to be added back to Georgia taxable income. The change applies to corporations, and the bill text also changes the rules for individual taxpayers. Realtors who work with investors buying single-family rentals may see clients face higher state tax bills, which could affect how attractive these purchases look.

bills.headline: Requires home sellers to disclose flood damage, claims, and repairs; fines frivolous mechanic liens.
bills.recap: Starting January 1, 2027, sellers of one-to-four family homes in Georgia must give buyers a written statement confirming or denying any flood damage, flood insurance claims, flood repairs, repetitive loss notices, or federal flood insurance requirements during their ownership, including approximate flood dates and the type of repairs. A willful failure to disclose counts as a violation of the Fair Business Practices Act. Sellers and their agents do not have to investigate beyond what the seller already knows. The bill also sets a $1,500 fine per lien, plus attorney's fees or court costs, for mechanic liens filed without good faith or with malice.

bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 8 of Title 13 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to illegal and void contracts generally, so as to prohibit certain agreements involving rental price-fixing as unenforceable contracts in general restraint of trade with respect to residential rental properties; to provide for a criminal penalty; to provide for statutory construction; to provide for a short title; to provide for an effective date and applicability; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Bans landlords from using shared data or software to coordinate rental prices.
bills.recap: This bill makes it illegal for competing landlords to agree to set rents using shared rental data run through pricing software, including AI tools. Such agreements would be void, and anyone who enters into one could face a felony with 1 to 5 years in prison, fines of $1,000 to $5,000, or both. Landlords also could not set rents based on that kind of pooled-data pricing. The rules cover owners and their agents, including property managers. Work done under affordable or low-income housing programs is exempt. Realtors who manage rentals or advise investors should watch how this could change the pricing tools they use.

bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Titles 8, 10, 34, 35, 45, and 50 of the O.C.G.A., relating to buildings and housing, commerce and trade, labor and industrial relations, law enforcement officers and agencies, public officers and employees, and state government, respectively, so as to provide comprehensive state civil rights laws protecting individuals from discrimination in housing, public accommodations, and employment on the basis of race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, age, disability, familial status, or national origin; to provide for related matters; to provide for a short title; to provide for an effective date; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Creates a Georgia civil rights law and adds sexual orientation and age to fair housing protections.
bills.recap: HB670 would create the Georgia Civil Rights Act of 2025, banning discrimination in housing, public places, and jobs based on race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, age, disability, familial status, or national origin. For real estate, it adds sexual orientation and age to the Georgia Fair Housing Act. That covers sales, rentals, lending, advertising, appraisals, and access to MLS and Realtor organizations. Agents, brokers, landlords, lenders, and appraisers would need to update their practices and ads to follow the wider rules, which would take effect January 1, 2026.

bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Article 5 of Chapter 3 of Title 8 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to housing trust fund for the homeless, so as to establish a homelessness prevention program; to provide for an application process and minimum standards; to provide for the use of certain funds; to provide for disbursements; to require contracts and assurances; to provide for definitions; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Lets Georgia's homeless housing trust fund pay for eviction and homelessness prevention programs.
bills.recap: This bill adds homelessness prevention programs to what the state housing trust fund for the homeless can pay for. Approved groups could get money for short-term rent and utility help, free legal help for low-income tenants facing eviction, landlord-tenant mediation, and a single portal for emergency rent aid applications. Eligible groups include nonprofits, legal aid offices, mediation providers, and local housing authorities, and they must sign a contract and show financial assurance before getting funds. Realtors and landlord clients may care because more rent aid and mediation could mean fewer evictions and more rent paid on time.

bills.headline: Requires landlords to give tenants an itemized list of all lease fees before deposits.
bills.recap: Before a tenant pays a security deposit, landlords already must give them a list of existing damage to the rental. This bill adds that the list must also itemize all fees tied to the tenant's lease, and the tenant keeps a copy. Tenants can still inspect the unit, sign the list, or write down what they disagree with. Agents and property managers handling leases would need to update move-in paperwork to show every fee up front.

bills.headline: Bans fire sprinkler mandates in one- and two-family homes, including by local governments.
bills.recap: Current Georgia law keeps the state building code from requiring fire sprinklers in homes with one or two units, but lets cities and counties adopt their own sprinkler rules. This bill removes that local option. It says neither the state code nor any local code adopted after May 24, 2010 may require sprinklers in single-family homes or duplexes. Realtors may care because sprinkler mandates can raise the cost of building new homes, so this could help keep new construction prices down.

bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Titles 10 and 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to commerce and trade and property, respectively, so as to provide certain limits on increases in rental amounts charged for residential properties; to prohibit landlords from charging rental amounts in excess of such limits as an unlawful, unfair, and deceptive trade practice; to provide for definitions; to provide for statutory construction; to provide for an affirmative defense; to provide for an effective date and applicability; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Caps residential rent increases at 3 percent yearly and requires 120 days' notice.
bills.recap: This bill would limit rent increases on most Georgia homes and apartments to 3 percent over the lowest rent charged in the prior 12 months, with 120 days' notice required, and no increases mid-lease unless the lease allows it. Rent hikes for qualifying students and seniors would be capped at 2 percent, and some low-income seniors renting the same place over five years could freeze their rent for up to five years. Buildings built after 2024 are exempt for 15 years, as are government-subsidized and state college housing. Violations would count as unfair trade practices, and tenants could use overcharges as a defense in evictions, so landlords, property managers, and investor clients would face new limits.

bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 7 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to landlord and tenant, so as to provide for limitations on rent increases for seniors and veterans; to provide for definitions; to provide for defense in dispossessory actions; to provide for an automatic repeal; to provide for applicability; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Caps yearly rent increases for seniors and veterans living mainly on federal benefits.
bills.recap: This bill limits how much a landlord can raise rent in a 12-month period when renewing or re-signing a lease with an existing tenant who is 62 or older, or a veteran, and whose main income is Social Security or veterans' benefits. The cap is the lower of 5% plus the yearly change in the Consumer Price Index, or 10%, measured against the lowest rent charged in the past 12 months. Rent includes most fees, but not security deposits. If a landlord charges more than allowed, the tenant can use that as a defense and counterclaim in an eviction case. The rule would apply to leases signed or renewed on or after July 1, 2025, and would end on January 1, 2035. Property managers and leasing agents would need to track tenant eligibility and limit renewal increases.

L. 2005, p. 3719), so as to increase the income cap related to qualifying for such exemption to $60,000.00; to increase the value of the exemption to $30,000.00 of the assessed value; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, and automatic repeal; to provide for mandatory execution of election and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

It applies to homeowners age 65 or older whose household income (with a spouse living there) is $60,000 or less for the prior year, up from the old $30,000 limit. City voters had to approve it in November 2025, and if passed, it takes effect January 1, 2026. Realtors may want to mention this lower city tax bill when working with older buyers and sellers in Peachtree City.

bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Article 4 of Chapter 3 of Title 8 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to fair housing, so as to provide for artificial intelligence or automated decision tools in actions for discriminatory housing practices; to prohibit the use of certain defenses in actions for discriminatory housing practices; to prohibit the use of artificial intelligence or automated decision tools without human oversight in making certain housing determinations; to prohibit making certain housing determinations using artificial intelligence or automated decision tools without certain disclosures; to provide for enforcement by Attorney General; to provide for fines; to provide for a short title; to provide for definitions; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Bans housing decisions made by AI tools without human review and disclosure.
bills.recap: This bill adds AI and automated decision tools to Georgia's fair housing law, so discrimination caused by these tools counts as illegal discrimination. Relying on AI is not a defense against a discrimination claim. Anyone using AI for decisions about selling, renting, financing, or brokerage services for homes must have a person review those decisions and must tell affected people that AI was used. The Attorney General could fine violators up to $10,000, so agents, brokers, landlords, and lenders using AI screening or pricing tools should take note.

bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Article 1 of Chapter 5 of Title 48 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to general provisions regarding ad valorem taxation of property, so as to prohibit ad valorem property tax bills from including any nontax related fees or assessments; to provide for applicability; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Bans non-tax fees like stormwater and trash charges from property tax bills.
bills.recap: This bill says property tax bills on real estate can only include the property tax itself. Fees like stormwater, trash, water and sewer charges, plus late fees or interest on those items, must be billed separately. Costs tied to collecting late property taxes can still appear on the tax bill. It would apply to bills issued on or after January 1, 2026, and could change how agents explain annual tax costs, escrow amounts, and closing prorations to clients.

bills.headline: Lets renters repair-and-deduct and doubles key eviction deadlines from 7 to 14 days.
bills.recap: If a landlord does not respond to a needed repair within five days, the tenant could hire a licensed professional and take the cost out of rent, capped at 50 percent of any one payment and backed by receipts. The bill also gives tenants 14 days instead of 7 to answer an eviction notice or pay back rent to stop the case. It also delays writs of possession to 14 days after judgment instead of 7. It would apply to residential leases signed or renewed on or after July 1, 2025, so agents who manage property or represent investors should watch it closely.
bills.title: Renters' Bill of Rights Act; enact

bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Code Section 44-7-13 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to landlord's duties as to repairs and improvements, so as to provide for landlord duties regarding certain rental agreements; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Sets specific minimum habitability standards Georgia landlords must meet for rental housing.
bills.recap: This bill expands Georgia's basic landlord repair duty into a detailed list of minimum living standards. Rentals would need to be structurally sound, with safe water, working heat and cooling, ventilation, lighting, safe electrical service, sanitary bathrooms and kitchens, and a second way out in case of fire. Each occupied level would need a working smoke detector, with special alarms for hearing-impaired tenants, and common areas like laundry rooms and hallways would also need detectors. Realtors who work with investors, property managers, or renters should know these standards could raise compliance costs for landlords and give tenants clearer grounds to demand repairs.

bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Article 2A of Chapter 8 of Title 48 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to homestead option sales and use tax, so as to provide for an alternative homestead option sales tax; to provide for a distribution of the proceeds from the levy of an alternative homestead option sales and use tax; to provide for the levy of a special purpose local option sales and use tax in certain counties; to provide for a referendum; to provide for procedures, conditions, and limitations; to provide for a short title; to provide for definitions; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Lets counties adopt a 1% sales tax to fund bigger homestead property tax exemptions.
bills.recap: This bill lets Georgia counties ask voters to approve a new 1 percent local sales tax, with the money used to cut county property taxes on primary homes through an added homestead exemption of up to 100 percent of assessed value. Up to 25 percent of the money can go to capital projects (county share limited to roads), and any leftover funds would roll back the county tax rate. Voters must approve both the sales tax and a matching local homestead exemption, and the deal ends after 10 years unless renewed. Counties already levying a similar existing local sales tax cannot use it, and only the home plus up to five surrounding acres qualifies. For Realtors, it could noticeably lower property tax bills for owner-occupants, which may affect affordability and how homes are marketed.

bills.headline: Freezes Bryan County school taxes on homesteads at base-year assessed value, if voters approve.
bills.recap: This local bill creates a new homestead exemption from Bryan County school district taxes. It covers any rise in a home's assessed value above its base-year value, so school taxes are based on a frozen value. The base year is the year before the current owner first gets the exemption, and it covers up to five acres. New improvements and added land are still taxed, and owners must apply once with the tax commissioner. Voters had to approve it in November 2025, and it would apply starting January 1, 2026. For Realtors, it matters because a buyer's base value resets at purchase, so a seller's low school tax bill may not carry over to the new owner.

bills.headline: Raises Norcross city homestead exemptions to $45,000, or $90,000 for seniors 65+.
bills.recap: This bill raises the City of Norcross homestead exemption on city property taxes from $9,000 to $45,000 for residents who own and live in their homes. It only takes effect if Norcross voters approve it in the November 2025 election, and would then apply starting with the 2026 tax year. Realtors may care because lower city tax bills can make owning a home in Norcross more affordable and appealing to buyers and current owners.

bills.headline: Caps yearly taxable value increases on Greensboro homesteads for city taxes, if voters approve.
bills.recap: This bill creates a homestead exemption from City of Greensboro property taxes that limits how much a home's taxable value can rise each year, generally to inflation plus 0.25 percent. For people first getting it in 2026, the base value is the home's 2024 assessed value, with adjustments for additions or improvements. It covers up to one acre and does not apply to state, county, or school taxes or to taxes for paying off bonds. The exemption does not transfer to a new buyer, who starts with a new base value. A surviving spouse who stays in the home keeps it, and current homestead holders get it automatically. It takes effect January 1, 2026, only if city voters approve it in the November 2025 election. Realtors should know that long-time owners may pay lower city taxes than a buyer will after a sale.

bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Article 1 of Chapter 7 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to landlord and tenant in general, so as to require landlords and managers of apartment buildings or complexes to provide local police and fire departments certain information; to provide for a penalty; to provide for an effective date and applicability; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.
bills.headline: Requires apartment landlords to give police and fire after-hours contacts, with steep fines.
bills.recap: This bill requires landlords or managers of apartment buildings and complexes to give local police and fire departments current after-hours maintenance and management phone numbers. Failing to do so brings a $2,000 fine per violation, and the fine repeats every five days the problem continues. Landlords or managers must also answer any police or fire department contact within one hour or face a $5,000 fine, with all fines going to Clayton County Public Schools' homeless education department. Agents who manage or sell apartment properties should note these new duties and penalties, which would start July 1, 2025 if passed.
